I'm not really a Dragon Ball Z fan. As a child, I was never into the whole "screaming 'till my hair grows 'n glows" shtick, and all of my friends would talk about the Kame-hame-whoosits at the lunch table with me staring into the infinite.
Knowing this, why did I ever buy this game?
Really, all it took for me was the concept of character customization.
I don't know anything about the Dragon Ball Z universe, but judging by how long the show has been going on, the amount of movies it has produced, the enormous fanbase the series has garnered, and the number of games it has created, just the thought of a dirty peasant like myself making a character that bounces around and inserts himself into this grand menagerie of bulging biceps and pulsating pecs fills in some sort of... primal need that I never filled in as a child. Making me feel involved in important parts of such a long-lived series is the sort of Skyrim type immersion I really enjoy in a game.
The character customization was pretty standard in terms of depth, with plenty of different facial features and color options to choose from. My only minor gripe is that I can't make my Earthling character smile, he's just stuck in a permanent scowl, like somebody just ate the last donut. Like I said though, this is only a minor gripe, and I'm sure there are different options for the other races.
In terms of gameplay, I'm a complete novice when it comes to the Dragon Ball Z themed fighting games, due to the aformentioned lack of interest as a child. It was impressive on how easily I was able to get into the mechanics of the game, even with the extremely frenetic pace of the combat. Punches roll out extremely fast, I zip around everywhere in the blink of an eye, and HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥I JUST SHOT A MAGIC MISSILE OUT OF MY HAND. Due to the cathartic nature of this type of combat, however, I more often than not forget about blocking or evading my enemies attacks, and just throw myself into the enemy with reckless abandon - but I'm sure that's something I'll eventually learn as I progress through the game.
One really annoying feature, however is the dowsing ability gained when your character gets a scouter headset thingy. I understand the part about using the scouter to see enemy players' power levels, but using the scouter to locate and pick up hidden items in each area is just plain tedious. Scanning around in first player mode to locate hidden nodes and then slowly hovering to that location (as far as I know, you can't fly fast in scouter FPS mode) completely breaks the flow of effortlessly zipping around like a jet plane and beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of other people. I just hope that all the items that are found this way are merely consumables and I can just bypass looking for them altogether.
The way the game ties the fighting and the customization and stat-building together is through a central hub. Here your character can buy new outfits, accessories, skills, consumables, and other stuff I didn't bother looking into yet. I'm not a huge fan of having outfits that provide stat boosts in a fighting game like this, since it limits my choice of customization. I would've much preferred some sort of non-aesthetic equippable that provided the same stat boosts instead to allow me to wear the clothes I wanted without worrying about optimizing my character for a specific fighting style.
I can't really comment on the multiplayer aspect of the game, since I didn't try it out yet, but if I'm correct, I can join up with up to 2 of my friends online to tackle more difficult missions and punch some bodybuilders together. It's an beat-em-up style multiplayer experience I can get around. Also, if me and my friends get bored being carebears, we can just try to beat each other up with our self-inserts, or using other prominent characters in the series, like the other Dragon Ball Z games. Neat.
As a person who doesn't really understand the Dragon Ball Z universe, do I recommend this game to friends? That depends. If I know that my friends are Dragon Ball Z fans? Sure, I recommend it if they aren't going to break the bank with the 40$ current price tag. For the 10 people out there that don't know anything about Dragon Ball Z? I have to make sure they like screaming, punching, and long trips to the barber.

The one hit kills and one hit deaths make the game extremely tense at almost every battle, coming at it over and over, figuring out a way to win, it's an interesting learning curve but it can be intensely frustrating, especially towards the end. But that frustration is worth it in the end for that sheer sense of accomplishment.
The environment design is excellent, it might be a bit big and walking back to bosses can get a bit frustrating, but the way it's set out, some neat background details that help tell parts of the story, it genuinely feels like you're walking around a long forgotten world. The tidbits of story you pick up, especially when replaying after unlocking a certain mode, create an interesting "Fill in the gaps" kind of deal that, as I mentioned, reminds me of Dark souls.
Soundtrack is also excellent. I especially like how the boss music can start at two different places so it doesn't get too stale for the short time you get to enjoy it.
Overall, it's an atmospheric experience of a game that, if you like boss battles, is a must have.

Ah, would it be lovely to move your whole house when it gets too hot in summer, to just pick it up, literally and just move to a cooler climate. Just needs someone to invent a Trans-Warp Locator. Or when the neighbourhood gets real bad, just point your TWL, poof and there you have it, your house is no-where near Justin Bieber.
Ok, in the mean time, while we wait for science to catch up with our reality, Mind Crew have taken upon themselves to find a way to move the whole Earth, just in case Mr Bieber decides to step out for a moment and if by coincidence, the Sun happens to go full Nova on us, at the same time.
Space Warp is a maze runner game with a twist. The Sun is super heating the solar system and you need to move Earth out of danger, by warping space near our little blue marble, to manoeuvre it to a new system. Screw up and earth becomes a steaming hot Quarter Pounder (Would you like fries with that).
The more you warp space in a certain direction, the faster Earth will move in that direction, need to slow down, simply warp space on the opposite side of the Earth. It’s that easy…. NOT!  Remember, you are moving around 5.972 × 10^21 tons of dirt with 7 Billon back seat drivers screaming at you to hit the brakes (all this going around and around, just gets so…..yesterday!!), so your not going to be stopping on a dime.
Instead you are going to be drifting the world around corners and through some pretty tight areas, the Swedish rally way, that even Per-Gunnar Andersson will give you a nod. And you need to do it in the fastest time possible.
Slow and steady or like a banshee on steroids it’s up to you how fast you go, but your time is your make or break, especially seeing your time is on an updated leader board. Yep your get to see who you need to beat, like the real world rally, just, with the real world as your car.
Also to help or hinder you along are solar winds which can blow you into walls, backwards or even speed you up. There are yellow areas which will slow or bog you down, so they are the sandpits of the cosmos. Walls that move or can even crush the world (bringing true the Flat Earth Society).
Another great feature of this game is the ghost car….. I mean ghost earth. You can see how well you do against yourself or any of the other players by having a ghost to compare/compete with. You have a whole 60 levels spread across 8 zones to try or fry Earth to your hearts content.
The graphics are good and clean, they get the job done. Options are also good and clean with the standard sound & music on/off, windowed or full screen but no other graphic options. Music is not too overbearing and suits the game. But like most Inde games, lacks variety so I recommend cranking up some Mega Death in the back ground.  The game play is good fun and Space Warp will be a great time waster, while you have a break from the nine to five grind. But beyond wanting to beat everyone’s time, there is not a lot of replay value.
So until a TWL gets invented, I need to finish strapping some jet packs onto my house and get ready to fly south for the summer. Hmmm, South pole look good at this time of the year.

I don't review many games, but I felt this one was warranted. Rimworld feels more stable and 'finished' in this alpha state, then some of the triple A games to have come out lately. When you combine that with the fact that it has a very solid modding community, and a very active developer, you can make a safe bet this game will shine on full release.
Rimworld has become the game that I wanted Clockwork Empires to be. It has been enjoyable enough that I have sunk over 65 hours into playing an early access game. Obviously everything isn't perfect, and bad luck will sometimes give you a mighty slap right across your face. I found myself getting attached to certain colonists, much like I did in the Xcom games, and went to great lengths to keep them safe. For me, that is one of the marks of a good game.
As the game progresses I'd love to see even more variety in craftable objects and tiles. I also hope the devleopers take note of some the most popular mods, and include some of the ideas in the base game, such as more visible tile textures for gravel and better hospitality for visitors. None of the current issues are game breaking, which should be obvious by the overwhelmingly positive reviews.
If you are like I was, and on the fence about spending your money on yet another Steam early access game, take note. This one won't let you down. I'm looking forward to full release and seeing what else they decide to add to this already time and soul devouring game.

Don't get me wrong the game is good and playing on expert should be frustratingly hard... but there is a broken progression system here in the campaign and it isnt a curve, it's a cliff edge.
I can do hard strategy, but this is not right, at all.
Take imminent crisis for example, first 3 planets are no brainer without any difficulty selection.
Deneb on expert is workable, spam as many units as possible and send them north, there is enough time to do what you like.
Yorkshire on expert is workable, play it like a classic macro RTS and rush the points before your enemies can tech up. Treat this one like a skirmish, not a campaign.
So far, there is clear logic required to win.
Then we get to Calethaon and the imbalance for expert shows.
Method 1: BALANCED
a: send a couple of units to cap top middle to aim for critical mass, send the remaining starter units to the lower capture point.
b: make factories and medium level factories for balanced army.
RESULT: enemy rush obliterates balanced set-up time required.
Method 2: TURTLE
a: a: send a couple of units to cap top middle to aim for critical mass, send the remaining starter units to the lower capture point.
b: build anti air turrets north, build sentinels lower main base mixed with a few smarties
c: build brutes to defend turrets
RESULT: attrition kills at red bar before critical mass.
Method 3: SUPER CHEESE TURTLE STYLE
a: Spam smarty systems
RESULT: Seems just as effective if not sligtly better as the other turtling method and loses at same point, probably too effective considering how absolutely cheesy it is, all the other methods simply don't compare to this.
Method 4: PUSH OUT AND HOLD
a: do the basic setup tropes, 2-3 fatories, armory
b: scatter various air defences at back
c: rush forward and hold forward defence point, place extractors down around it

Overall a solid entry in a the Total Annihilation sub genre of Real Time Strategy games.  Graphically the game can be a little cluttered but that is largely down to the epic scale that is core to the game play and is something that is handled well by the abstraction of the GUI that occurs when zoomed out far enough.  The design choices are not brave, largely refining existing game play from titles like Supreme Commander but what it does it does very well.  Like other titles in this sub genre the single player is very satisfying marrying the concepts of real time strategy with large scale strategy, however multiplayer is dulled greatly by the unlikeliness of comebacks and a very large gap between both identifying when you have won or lost and the actual conclusion of the game.  I feel like the game would have been better with fewer global abilities and tying global abilities into the same resource pool as upgrades was a poor decision that does not work in multiplayer with too many branching decision points and a serious resource inflation problem.
The game is designed to be played at a much slower pace than other RTS's with very low movement speeds barring air units.  Your chances of success is dependent on advanced scouting, securing resources and setting up reinforcement lines.  There is little room for micro management outside of the first ten minutes of a game as you are incentivized to group your units into armies that bind your units into a formation.  While the very early stages of the game might play like Supreme Commander the late game is reduced to the strategic depth of a total war game with resource management and buildings.  Additionally the granularity of unit choices feels off, each building will have 3-15 unit choices each, with your economy only being able to support 3-4 buildings generating units at a time and a very long reinforcement pipeline.  It makes it very difficult to anticipate what you will need and core support units only being produced once every few minutes.  This results in situations where you have the wrong unit composition and can discover this fact several minutes before you will suffer the consequences of it with no way to address it,
I highly recommend the game as a single player experience but I personally will not be investing a lot of time into the multiplayer.

I've really enjoyed my time playing UnEpic, and at this point, I haven't even finished the actual game yet. It has a decent level of feeling both grindy and not grindy at times; I had trouble approaching some of the mobs in the game when they were just large groups (especially when they learned how to use ladders), but I felt that the bosses were fair. Bosses in the game were not necessarily long affairs, but slipping up during one of them could prove very punishing. If they were long (>5 minutes), it would be tedious, but I like the balance achieved.
There are a few flaws (in my opinion) in this game that I don't think will get 'fixed' for the final product, and in a sense, game balance is one of them. There isn't quite as much freedom as I'd want out of a game like this; the character page looks as if you can follow archetypes such as a mage, but it really won't work for the game as a whole. My character used a balance of range, melee, and magic, and I don't know how I'd fare if I didn't use all three of those. Fortunately, you have enough skill points to have strengths in all those areas. It just means that you, as a player, are quite capable of making a character that might just not be able to stand up to specific challenges.
Multiplayer seems like a great idea, and I think the tools used in it show a lot of potential. Better yet, it appears as though the multiplayer is getting the bulk of the attention. Unfortunately, only a really small crowd plays multiplayer; try and get a couple friends to play with you if possible, and it would definitely enhance, if not create, the experience. As of writing this, I haven't quite done that yet. That being said, when I have played with others through finding/making games, I have found the other people to be easy to work with. That might not be the experience across the board, but I imagine that a game like this has less trolls on the multiplayer compared to more popular titles.
As for the early access part...I wouldn't have noticed that it was in this stage if it wasn't plastered over the steam page. The single player has always been completely done, and the multiplayer, again, only suffers from lack of players. I could see fear in playing a game nowhere near completion, but the early access was a solid product.
All in all, I've played this game for a good amount of time for its price, and I think it makes to be a fun game. It's unforgiving at times, but when it really matters, you can know that you were accountable for messing up most of the time. This game deserves to have a larger crowd, because it's pretty solid; even in its early access. There is a lot of fun to be had.

Animated wallpapers are always something I thought would be a neat idea - and this program actually makes that thought a reality (and doubles it). Sure, there's probably a way to do this without paying for this program, but even if I could get that set up, the amount of workshop content is enough of a plus to warrant the purchase of this instead.
Speaking of the workshop content, there's a lot of it. A lot. It's really not hard to find the wallpaper of your dreams, and if you can't, you can make your own pretty easily. Everything is available here, and it's not even just animated wallpapers (like videos), there's even interactive wallpapers. Categories can be filtered in the search, and there's plenty of content for anyone to enjoy - don't listen to the reviews that say it only has anime.
There's just no end to the awe of seeing a wallpaper that actually moves. In fact, it's actually quite hard to go back when I'm on a computer that doesn't have the engine installed. There's plenty of power-saving options available, and the wallpaper will turn off when a full-screen game opens to free the RAM. Crashes can be common after some updates, but this is early access, and for what you get, it's well worth it.
All in all, this is an amazing piece of software at a very affordable price. Whether you want to see particles fly around the screen as you move your mouse, or have Hatsune Miku dance around your app icons, you will be right at home.

I have to say that I really enjoy the premise behind this game, but it feels mechanically unpolished. A few examples of things that took me out of it:
-A group called me and offered payment for certain services. They never paid me, and my character never brought this up in conversation when they asked for more services.
-Achievements pop up for certain character deaths when the criteria for their death is met, but this can be well before they officially revealed to have died.
-I paid for intelligence to help me out in a quest, but I was unable to find where it put this intelligence and had to look it up online.
-Tenants don't notice you blatantly running out of their rooms as they approach.
-The voice-over for the slide-show cutscenes does not match up with dialogue, and even includes some mistakes (like when describing how the country sent its "able-boiled youth" off to war)
-Based on certain decisions, a character can show up to kill you. Should you ignore them however, they will simply stand in the same spot for the rest of the game with a dialogue notification over their head.
This game clearly draws inspiration from games like "Papers Please" and "This War of Mine" what with the setting, the tough choices, and the eventually overwhelming amount of laws to keep track of and punishment for failing from "Papers Please", and the permadeath and resource management of "This War of Mine". The choices are almost impossible to evaluate, making them dice rolls, and based on my experience, tend to be overall generally negative.
The game held numerous financial goals over my head that I was clearly meant to meet a minimal number of, resulting in some interesting decision making. I met none of them. Undoubtedly I could have done better, but this was all while keeping on top of the game's mechanics and doing my due diligence to earn. Then it charged me for not meeting them, rubbing salt in the wound and offsetting the sacrifices I made to try and earn my keep.
This game is brutal. And I can dig that, there's nothing wrong with having a narrative that's dark or mechanics that are demanding and require mastery. But the game frequently frames these consequences as being your own failings while setting you up to fail. Games can be art, but this feels like a clear cut case of art compromising the game aspect. I dig what they're going for, there's a lot of potential depth to the game, lots of moving pieces, and lots of charm. It's easy to find stuff to be impressed with here. But the end result, for all its potential, falls flat due to the fact that it just isn't that fun to play.

A few key things can make an action game really enjoyable for me. Those include: fast and fun gameplay, a plot that gives you a reason to embark on the various missions that you go on, and a varied mission structure that surprises you and puts you in unique situations throughout the game. Wolfenstein: The New Order does all of these things, and does them so well that it easily ranks right up there with DOOM (2016) as one of the best first person shooters that I have ever played.
Wolfenstein's premise of an alternate history where the Nazis took over the world is one that is very interesting and fun. This game does not make any attempt to go for depth in its story; it simply gives you a reason to want to go kick some♥♥♥♥♥ and it does that at the highest level. This game makes the Nazis that you fight so incredibly hatable that I actually found pleasure in killing every single one of them, even the simple grunts that you encounter in most fights. There was never a moment of sorrow or grief over slaughtering thousands of Nazi soldiers, and for a game like this, that is just fine.
Killing those enemies is very fun, too. Fighting is fast, and you are given a wide variety of options for approaching a fight. Basic stealth exists, as you are capable of sneaking around areas to silently take down enemies, which is often a useful approach. Most fighting areas are open, and give you opportunities to use multiple obvious and hidden routes to traverse a battlefield. Your arsenal is quite wide, and most weapons can be duel wielded, providing you with multiple fun ways to go in guns blazing.
The story in the game doesn't do anything ground breaking, but it serves its purpose well. As I mentioned, your enemy is very hatable. Thankfully, allies are quite likeable. You will be part of a small resistance, and each of your missions are meant to weaken Nazi forces, but more importantly to strengthen your own. Some of my objectives in these missions were so ridiculous that they could only put a smile on my face. This game is the perfect mixture of grounded and over-the-top.
The thing that really made this game a joy from start to finish was the wide variety of missions. After a weak opening level, pretty much every embarkment after that was unique and interesting in some way. I never felt as if things were becoming to repetitive, and I think that the game ended right where it should have, without overstaying its welcome.
If you enjoy a good single player FPS, you should absolutely play Wolfenstein: The New Order. I would struggle to recommend anything more than this game.

Beautiful, challenging, and mysterious.
Take a deep breath, fire your singular arrow, and awake the slumbering beast.
Titan Souls has no intention of grasping your sweaty palm.
Observation is key to discovering the weaknesses of the imaginative and vastly varied Titans. Avoid their attacks and your opportunity will reveal itself, though how and when to exploit it often remains unclear. Fortunately, you have infinite lives to try different tactics, because you will quickly burn through many of them. As unforgiving as this process is, I've rarely felt truly frustrated - I've simply not understood what needed to be done, or failed to execute it within the narrow window. You face a short walk back to the battle arena after defeat. I used this time to reflect on why I'd failed and how I could change my approach to succeed. Still, over time these treks become marathons, and an option to cut straight to the action would have avoided this. Controls are tight and responsive, provided you heed the strong recommendation of a game pad. Seriously, keyboard controls are futile here.
The world is pretty and detailed, yet feels slightly hollow - its a lonely journey. This was most likely to convey the isolation of your vulnerable protagonist, and this works, but some rewarding exploration would have created a more vibrant world, rather than just a hub leading to battles.
The score is glorious. Wistful, ethereal music accompanies the main world, ominously fading to silence once you enter a dungeon, replaced with pounding tribal beats and darting strings once battle initiates.

When that perfectly aimed arrow connects and the giant is slain, it is satisfaction and disbelief combined. Only one task remains - retrieve your lone weapon.
An immensely rewarding game, it deserves to be valued on its own merit, not stand in the "Shadow" of any other.

Space Warp is one of those games you play to fill time, usually while you are waiting for a bus, or already on a bus... let's just call it a "bus game".
The premise is that the Earth has once again entered one of it's natural states in games, being in big trouble. Not an entirely new or original situation to be fair, but not one commonly done with this genre.
Anyways, the Earth is in danger of being microwaved by space radiation and it is up to you to steer the Earth to safety by bending space and time in a 2D environment stricken with a kind of gellatinous radioactive jelly often found in the back of student dorm refridgerators, which kindly creates neat little passageways for your suddenly mobile Earth to steer through, in 2D, to the safe zone of each level... in 2D.
If I seem hung up on the 2D aspect of this, it is for a good reason. Space is very infrequently represented well in 2D. Much in the same way I do not like 2D mining games, 2D space games need to have a LOT of fantastic gameplay to compensate for cutting out an entire dimension before I can begin to feel like I haven't been ripped off.
Space Warp does not have fantastic gameplay. It is what you would expect from the marble-maze genre (yes I made that up). It does it's job but the theme chosen, while only slightly more original than "get ball to hole", having a space theme with no real 3D or more exciting gameplay cripples the game a bit for me. There is some tight programming in there, the graphics are nice, it all works well and feels good, but there isn't much more here to offer non-fans of similar, casual bus games. So all-in-all, not for me, but recommended to try it if you enjoy maze games or are stuck on a 12 hour bus journey.

One of my favorite Free 2 Play games ever, and honestly one of my favorite shooters ever. Not really p2w(and they're preparing to drop an update to make it even less pay2win), easy to get into, and generally well balanced.
Pros
+ Well optimised.
+ Can easily play without ever spending money.
+ Decent playerbase, can be hard to find a server way outside of peak hours but once you start getting even close to peak hours there's people everywhere.
+ Good, fast paced shooter mechanics like walljumping and strafing.
+ Generally good balance.
+ High skill ceiling
Neutral:
~ Menus run like trash. Even at 60 FPS they feel like they're running at about 15. This is under neutral because it's not a huge deal in the end and doesn't affect gameplay, but it is an issue.
~ Toxicity. This is an issue in any competitive shooter, but DB has some notable issues with it.
~ Decently high skill floor. This isn't a good idea for your first shooter unless you're comfortable doing very poorly until you get a good grasp on the mechanics and on general FPS mechanics and aiming. It has beginner-only servers to help you out, but you'll hit level 7 faster than you'd think.
Cons:
- Terrible team balancing. Games tend to be stomps most of the time. When you do finally get a decently balanced game it's incredibly fun but be ready to stomp and be stompred.
- Very little in the way of community servers, there's a couple but they're usually unpopulated.

Let me just say that this game is amazing. It has depth, complexity, immersion. It is worth every penny spent.
The characters that you control, pawns, are funny as hell. If left to their own devices, they can accomplish a bit provided you build the necessities for them. Although, they can't handle enemies in a decent manner without your input. But their traits, backstories, skills, and mental quirks give each one flavor. Even in a colony of 20, you probably won't have two of the exact same colonist running around.
The game's overall mechanics are fairly easy to grasp. From the UI to the tech tree, it's not hard at all to get started. Learning to get into Rimworld is something that only should take a few hours. Of course, there is a lot more once your experience certain events and disasters. But overall, it's just install and go ham. The challenge comes from what happens to your colonists and what the world throws at you. Depends on the difficulty level, not much can happen. Or you can hate your life. There is a peaceful mode for just a base bulding simulator. And there is Extreme, which tests your skills and base management. You can also choose from several variants of how events spawn, from random to smoothe sailing.
From the images shown, it may not look like much in today's gaming market, but the detail is there. When a substantial fire has started, the brightness of the center glows like a star. The grass sways in the wind. Blood, vomit, and dirt are visible on the ground. It may not be high fidelity, but that doesn't detract from how you can TELL what every effect is. It's even hard to get pawns to look exactly the same, and they're simplistic representations of humans.
I've sunk way too many hours into this game for me to just sit here and not want to point people in the right direction. If you have the money to spare on it, absolutely get this game. Do not let the fact that it's in "Early Access" scare you off. Even several updates ago, this game would have been more complete than most AAA titles that get released. So every update now is just a minor bug fix or just plain icing on the cake. If you like management sims, base builders, or god games, this is right up your alley. Go on, give it a shot.

This is a true - and long - story about a brewery, a narcissistic alcoholic and a sneaky bottle-thief. This is my first colony.
It begins - crash-landing into a temperate forest, Snow, a fat oaf with green thumbs and an artistic vision; his future wife, Nina a fellow farmer and passionate architect; and their brainy, hard-to-please de-facto leader, Samantha, born into a now-ancient nobility (having spent the vast majority of her life in cryosleep). A small 8-year-old Yorkshire Terrier named Cassidy is also along for the ride.
Snow quickly puts axe to wood, providing Nina with the materials to build a simple homestead under Samantha's watchful eye.
A nearby swathe of fertile soil in a swampy woodland soon becomes host to a huge number of crops, as Snow and Nina plant hops together, and enjoy their deep conversations. Samantha does not stoop to such work, preferring to sit and research new technologies to improve their meagre life, or hunt the smaller animals nearby for Nina to butcher and cook.
It's not long before Snow and Nina are hand-in-hand, moving into their own separate room and beginning to fall in love. Cassidy the Yorkshire Terrier seems to prefer the company of others, quickly bonding to Nina.
Spring is almost over. The hops begin to flourish, and with the brewing table that Samantha had spent days designing, the trio quickly begin pouring buckets of fresh wort, ready for fermentation. Nina carves local oak into large casks - Samantha helps too - which they fill and leave to ferment at room-temperature.
As Summer begins, a new face joins the flock - Colt, an explorer who worked his way up from humble beginnings to buy a ticket on a starship. He quickly integrates, sharing Samantha's thrill of the hunt and Nina's love of hammer and nail. Snow and Nina become engaged to marry. Life is good... but not for long.
A freak heat-wave seems easy to regulate - ensuring that their stores of rice and meat do not perish in the heat by fashioning coolers out of nearby scrap metal. In the delirious heat, and their absense of practice, the gang neglect to check their casks - their first beer is spoiled in the heat. They empty the casks and watch as their hops struggle through the summer.
They use this time to build a fermentation room - its heat regulated to a steady 19 degrees - and eventually fill it with casks of their second crop. Snow and Nina marry, a humble ceremony amongst the roses and daylilies they had sewn together.
Fall is mostly uneventful. Much of it is spent indoors - hiding from a rampaging Rhinoceros and surviving on the ample food-stocks they had gathered. The beer ferments steadily, away from the eyes of the waiting brewers.
The beast eventually wanders off, just as a blight decimates the crops toward the end of Fall. They finally reap the reward of their efforts, filling an entire room with brown bottles of liquid gold. They allow themselves a single bottle once every three days, to remind themselves of their victory.
Samantha put the most effort in, of course, having designed the brewing table, the coolers, the heaters (and even the casks, a bit!) and so she ignores this mediation, deciding to binge instead. She spends an entire day retreiving bottles from the beer cellar, drinking them at the dinner table. She becomes too drunk to walk, and Nina puts her to bed. Samantha appears to stick to the once-every-three-days rule after this embarrassing moment.
Winter has only just begun when a cold-snap completely eradicates their crops. The earth is too solid to plant more seeds, and their few heaters barely provide any warmth. There are many cold nights. To keep their spirits up, they allow themselves a bottle of beer once a day - even allowing Cassidy a sip every now and then, when it's particularly chilly. Their fermentation room stays at a steady 19 degrees, and they suffer uncomfortable working conditions for it.
They choose to drink to keep themselves warm as they begin work each day. The bottles slowly deplete - a little too fast. Something is wrong.
As the winter passes, the bottles continue to disappear too quickly - Samantha appears sober.
Cassidy the Yorkshire Terrier, now 9-years-old, is secretly drinking multiple bottles of beer every day. She has built a massive tolerance to alcohol, and must drink three-times as much to keep herself happy.
This can't last forever, though. It's only a matter of time before traders arrive and all of the beer is sold to them, allowing the group to purchase the materials necessary to move on to higher-things.

Game Tycoon is a very unique tycoon game to the point it could be considered a point and click adventure / tycoon game. Nothing is laid out with menus, its all places and locations. You have a university, office plaza, media plaza and your home (which seems pointless). In these locations they are like city streets, you need to scroll your mouse left and right and click on doors. One click will have your player character enter, two clicks will automatically enter. When inside a building, you see a room and need to find what you want to do. It makes the controls needlessly cumbersome. To see how many copies you have in stock, you need to go across town. To see your finances, you need to go back across town. It is crazy.
The game is very click base as if it could be a mobile game, you won't find hot keys or even menus. Right mouse clicking exits you out of an area. Stats and charts need to be found in rooms and areas. Even then, there's no depth. There is no way to see how well games are selling, you just need to hope they sell well that month at the price you've set. You can visit a university magazine stand to find out the most popular games and genres for $4 each time. You can visit a game store in the media plaza to see where your games rank. You can visit an advertising executive to publicize your games, your company and see how you stack compared to the two other companies you're competing against. You can even visit a banker, take out a loan, buy and sell stocks of your company and the other three. Those are nice features, but when you visit the banker and executive, you need to talk with them. Click something to say and listen for them to say it before you can continue. If you dare click on something else it could cause a glitch that will loop the speech if not crash a menu 10 seconds later. It is stunning.
When you play, there is no hand holding. I needed to figure out to visit my office, create a game engine (or license one), then click and drag the 'print out' into my inventory. Then go next door to the development office? Once there, I need to click and drag the 'print out' into the project list. After that, since I had no employees, I had to go to the university and figure out that I needed to click a bulletin board in order to find employees. The hiring system is nice, it shows you the quality in stars, and their tempo to complete the job. You hire programmers, artists and composers. Some you can hire and others that are independent. So they can get better jobs and come back to you when you need them most, but they don't get paid when they're not working. Then its back to the development studio with my employees. I need to click the project, then assign programmers to the engine and click start project.
After you wait a few in game days, weeks or months, its time to take that game engine project, click and drag it back into your inventory, then go next door to your office and make a new game after clicking and dragging the engine into the proper position. Creating a new game project is easy. You'll get to chose things like what languages and what platforms. By platforms I mean, PC, arcade and console. There are no specific consoles. Just those three. Then when that is all 'printed out,' its back over to next door to click and drag the 'print out' from my inventory into the project window. Once there, I need to click on the project, then sift through my employees to assign programmers, artists and composers. The more people I have working, the faster they'll get done. The higher quality they are, the better the game.
From there, you don't just release the game. Once you click and drag the finished project into your inventory of course. Its off to the manufacturing facility where you click on the design table to include everything that will come with your game. By design, I mean pack the box with stuff and raise the manufacturing cost. Shirts, buttons, stickers, black and white instruction manuals, color instructions, an insert. Its all up to you! With some click and dragging. With that done you'll visit the manufacturing machine that will churn out the copies of your game. The more copies, the cheaper they become to manufacture. Click and drag the finished product into the machine. Then start manufacturing! After a few game days, all of the copies will arrive.
Do they just sell themselves? Nope. Time to find a publisher! So you need to visit a publisher's office and select a publishing deal from books on the wall. They all have minimum quality ratings, so your 45% quality game can't be published with a 53% quality deal. There is a punishment for failing to release the game by the allowed time and for your trouble of making a game, you'll get 6% of the profits depending on the deal. Some deals are far better than others.
After that, its back to the factory that has your copies. You need to click on the pallet with the finished copies and click and drag your publishing deal from your inventory into the game's slot and flip the checkmark switch to officially release it! Wasn't that easy? No hand holding at all!
Of course 5 hours into the game, I finally discovered the tutorial was in the campaign, but wasn't marked as a 'tutorial.' I thought it was just another scenario in the campaign. The tutorial explains what to do, but it gets caught on itself and could explain things better, such as flipping through a gaming magazine had me clicking all over before I figured out to click a game title. The voice over will talk over other voice overs. Not just that, but if you go to a different location than you should be in, the tutorial narration will tell you what to do as if you're in the correct place, instead of saying no this is the office, go to the university.
As soon as you get the hang of the 1,000 step process, it becomes an insane juggle of going between locations since there is no menu. Waiting to pan the street to the right or left. Waiting for your character to walk to the building before you realize double clicking enters the door instantly. Even though there's a game speed, that doesn't speed up the character. It doesn't speed up every time I need to hear 'I would like a bank loan,' then hear the banker's rebuttal.
There are visual errors here like text not disappearing when the dialog boxes do. Text overlapping out of windows. Sometimes the ticker PDA doesn't show anything when it should have a message. The PDA (ticker) is nice, it pops up useless information like you need to pay $3,000 for golf clubs or you're having a bad hair day. Its all random things that might as well be Chance cards from Monopoly. The PDA pop up changes the game from fast to slow, which is good, but the problem is that a lot of what the PDA shows is useless moments to make you laugh. You didn't sleep well, because your bed broke. Stealing MP3s is bad. Visit the gametycoon website. Your employees will get sick and will be unable to work for 12 days.
The only way to get a game over is if you go into debt for more than 90 days. You can get loans and sell stock to stay a float, but even on normal, it seems difficult. Your games only make money at the start of every month. You have full control over the price of your games at the factory, but to put publicity into the games, you need to go to a different area down the street.
The game itself is difficult even on normal. Luckily there is an easy mode. To top everything off, it has crashed or permafroze a few times, so you'll need to keep saving frequently, since there is no auto save feature. With all of that being said, there are some interesting elements in the game, but the juggle and struggle of going location to location over and over again is unfun and begging people to not play it. If only there was a menu and no traveling. The time it takes to hear people talk is just too long with no way to skip it.

With lots of attention and upgrades since its original launch, this has become a very good sci-fi RTS.  For example, originally it did not have the capability to do replays of your battles that you could watch and learn from, and now it does.  It also now has a more extensive campaign.  Credit to Stardock for supporting its product. This game is Stardock's test ground for developing the next generation RTS.  It also has many levels of difficulty to choose from in the campaign and skirmish, so new players can learn the game starting on the less difficult levels and progress up.  That also means that if a campaign mission is hard for you, you can lower the difficulty to complete it if you wish (and then try playing that mission again at the next level of difficulty).  There is much to master in this game, including orbital abilities.
The game has more features than I've seen in any other RTS. For example, here's a useful feature not even found in Starcraft 2: game speed control during the game.  In Starcraft 2, you can set the starting game speed to faster, fast, etc, but only at the starting conditions of the game.  In this game, you can change the speed in-game.  I like that because there's more happening in late game, so slowing down the speed in the late game allows more time for thinking and controlling all those units.  This game also has 'free pause', so you can also pause in late game to assess the situation and issue orders.

Aerofly RC7 is an RC aircraft simulation game/training tool from simulation developer IPACS. In Aerofly you learn how to fly a wide variety of RC aircraft ranging from small quadcopters to giant military jets in a number of different locations mainly across the US and Germany. With a huge amount of customisation and realistic physics this is a must have for anyone interested in RC aircraft.
While you read my review please take two things into consideration. Firstly, I played entirely with an Xbox 360 controller throughout my time with it. Secondly, I own the ultimate edition so some of the things I will talk about may not apply to the version of the game you're interested in.
+Great flight models, they all look very realistic especially on ultra graphics settings
+The physics are very realistic and from my little experience with real life RC aircraft the aricraft look like they behave as they should
+Super simple interface that's easy to navigate and stays out of your way when you're flying
+Lots of optional instruments and displays to make flying easier
+Over 50 different locations to fly at most of which are photrealistic while others are fully rendered 3D locations which allow you to use different camera views
+All locations have a number of different starting positions
+Before takeoff you're free to move the aircraft around
+Over 200 different aircraft which have a good variety of size and type of aircraft
+Some cool 1:1 scale aircraft
+For the most part it runs fantastically, I'm running it all just below max settings at around 120FPS
+Lots of customisation options for aircraft including their size and mass
+Can be played using KB&M, a controller, a flightstick or an actual RC controller all of which are easy to configure
+Smooth controls, the aircraft all feel very responsive
+You can play it splitscreen
+/-Sound effects are hit and miss, some are excellent while others don't sound real at all
-As has been said by other reviewers it's a bit too forgiving when it comes to stall recovery
-You can't zoom in on the stationary camera (the only one available for most locations) so it can be very easy to lose site of your aircraft
-The in-game smoke system available on some aircraft has a huge hit on performance, when the aircraft was close to the camera with smoke on I noticed a drop of up to 100 frames
-Helis and gliders show very little to no visual damage when they crash apart from their rotors looking crushed or damaged
Verdict:
9
If you have any interest in RC aircraft then this is a must buy piece of software with a wide variety of great looking models and great physics. Whether you're new to RC aircraft like myself or a veteran RC pilot you're gonna like this a lot.
***This review was written using a key provided by the Developer for review purposes***

The aim of this review is to inform the reader of whether this game is ideal for beginner RTS (Real time strategy) players.
In my opinion, as a fan of RTS games - Age of empires 1 was if not my first, definitely one of the few PC games I played that I remember being destroyed at as an infant. But this concerns the sequel, for which AOE 2 improved upon the original.
The goal of the game is to conquer (this is the most popular game mode) the enemy player; starting with a town center and a few villagers - the player has to build an army to do so; this is done by spawning more and more villagers to collect resources (wood, food, gold, stone - food being the most valuable) and constantly expanding his kingdom because resources run out and it is necessary to find more, while it is in the enemy's interest to stop him. Now some RTS have the mechanic where the resources are sustainable; for example, "Supreme Commander" and "Rise of Nations", however, while those games are relatively heavily strategic, they are strategic in different ways: for instance, Rise of Nations is more of an economically strategic game as more depth can be found within that element than AOE. Moreover, Supreme Commander's difficulty lies in the sheer abundance of units available and allowed to exist in a single game. However, this is where I stress the success of AOE - there are so many games that add more complexity to AOE's mechanics that one would question why bother playing it? Well to answer that one must think where did the love of RTS spawn from? Where was the match that struck the box? Where was the key that turned the ignition?
The reason for such a short review is not to praise the game but to enlighten: if one seeks to learn to play complex RTS such as Total war, supreme commander, even turn based strategic games like EU4 then allow the mind to be touched gently, not punched or pinched but carressed like a baby and soothingly let one's mind be developed into a machine capable of domination over others in whatever arena the opponent chooses.
If one can play AOE, he has the tools necessary to pick up any game of his choosing in a matter of minutes.

Titan Souls is definitely an indie game, as most people use the term nowadays. It's akin to Cave Story in that they're both good examples of short but otherwise worthwhile experiences. Allow me to explain step by step.
Let's start with the Gameplay. We'll break it down between controls and mechanics.
As far as controls go, this game is very simple. You move your character with the arrow keys or control stick, you can shoot your solitary arrow if you have it stocked or call it back after shooting with the same button. While aiming to shoot, the arrow keys/control stick become your method of aiming instead of moving. Along with movement and arrow play, you also get a dodge button that can be held to make your character run. I highly recommend using a gamepad, some bosses are near-to-outright impossible with only 8 directions to move and shoot in.
In contrast to the simple controls, the gameplay mechanics are more in depth than one would expect. The entire game can be boiled down to a glorified boss rush. Every titan encounter is in the typical "boss room" structure, whereas upon finding the titan in its room and engaging in it only victory or death will allow you to leave. Every boss has a weak point, but is otherwise invincible unless you hit this one spot with your own arrow. This makes each boss feel more like a battle of wits rather than strength, where solving the question of 'what' the weak point is and 'how' to hit it is as important as not being hit yourself. Learning a titan's pattern through trial and error and finding the perfect moment to attack is what this game's combat is at its core. It’s best not to get too worked up as death will happen in this game, again and again and again.
Outside of battles with the various titans of this world, the player is left to explore an unexplained and quite desolate world in search of the aforementioned titans. There are little rewards for exploration if you were looking for more than another titan to fight, and none if finding vague hints of the lore doesn't interest you. There are no mobs to find, and no enemies to deal with and level up against. This is a world of titans and decisive actions.
Now let's talk about Narration. This topic covers story as well as the level of engagement the game is capable of putting you into.
As far as the story goes, you're a chosen hero on a mission to kill all the titans and obtain the ultimate power, and learn the truth. Although, none of this is told to you in the game. Going off just the game, and not the game's description on this store page, you're a guy (or girl...?) with an magic arrow searching for and killing titans to collect their souls. There are murals that vaguely depict events or prophecies, but nothing is exactly obvious. The designers seemed to have taken a page of From Software's book of 'finding the story' design, without actually putting much story to find though.
Despite having such a paper thin plot, I found myself immersed during my gameplay all the way through. The engagement factor comes from the gameplay I mentioned before. Such an in-depth game of solving the boss' puzzle coupled with the sense of true satisfaction every time I figure it out and earn victory coaxed me into taking the next step and finding the next boss to fight. In some cases, yes I thought it impossible to defeat a boss, and ended up skipping it for another fight. Though that didn't deter me from playing nor detach me from the immersion, in fact it forced me to rethink how I approached the boss and lead to victory once I learned how to really fight each boss.
Now we'll finish off with the Aesthetics. This'll cover the art, which includes both sound and visual, the setting of the game, and how everything ties together into one experience.
Titan Souls uses a pixelated style mixed with simple three-dimensional graphics snuck in with a pixelated dress on to look more like all the other sprites in the party. Though it isn't 'anime with 3D CGI' levels of cringe worthy obviousness, in fact they're done quite well that I'm unsure whether the game was actually pixelated and not one big 3D graphic to begin with. The way some bosses can look like beautifully intricate sprites while others appear as pixel-textured models, and all of them fit without anything looking too far out of place is a feat on its own.
Speaking of fitting aesthetics, I found the music to be amazing in quality and purpose. The music is there to set a tone or invoke a feeling. With each area of the world came a theme that played the trope as straight as the typical lava area and snow area would in any adventure game, however that doesn’t mean to diminish how well it was produced. The feeling of first finding a new themed area coupled with the sudden shift in tone for the background music gave me a warm feeling of accomplishment, as if all that exploring actually wasn’t all for waste.
Don’t even get me started on the boss themes. I absolutely adore the boss themes of this game. From what I could notice, every boss has its own theme. Some even move to their theme, at least in the beginning. Every theme came off as fitting for the titan at hand, and made that fight all the more memorable or even fear inducing when their theme would come in at the start of the fight.
On the topic of themes though, I found the settings of Titan Souls to play most of the usual tropes. You start in a simple temple area, than branch out into the forest, volcanic caves, snowy peak, and even a small graveyard, all linked back to the main temple and its own little gardens. The areas are large, giving the sense that you’re actually in a world and not some corridor leading to the next boss. That same size also plays into the general theme of the world. It’s empty. It almost feels dead, abandoned, apart from the titans you’re there to defeat. It gives an odd sense of wonder, like something else is going on. Your mission isn’t some fanfare’d prophecy about saving the world, there isn’t seem to be right or wrong here. Just titans, and you who have come to slay them for your own goals.
Altogether, Titan Souls becomes an experience more than a walk from boss to boss. If you take the time to look around and get a sense of the world, and think about what’s going on, a whole story built on speculation opens up. The same book players would write for themselves when playing one of the notorious ‘Souls’ games by From Software, this game builds a world using only aesthetics and gameplay and doesn’t tell you anything at all outright. Each battle is a challenge on its own, forcing you to master the simple controls and the mechanics of the game alike as they’re presented to you within each fight. Death will happen, but it’s not the end. It’s only a means to grow and try again. Just you, your arrow, and a dozen titans to slay.

A great FPS game with lack of content
I like the fast-paced mechanics of the game. Walljumping will change the way you play each map, because there are a lot of variations to get over different obstacles. There are a lot of characters to chose from (22 at the moment). You can pick 3 before each match, and you can decide which one to use each time you respawn. The only downsides of the game are the lack of character/weapon customization and gamemodes:
You have to open lootboxes to get different weapons and skills for your charecters. The problem is not the existence of lootboxes, but the way they are designed. Your character skills and weapons are on the same card that you open, so you have to be VERY lucky to get the card with the weapons and skills that you want. In my opinion it would be much better if we could open different lootboxes for weapons and skills. Also it would be great to customize our characters with some clothes or skins. The weapons that are in the game can become boring after a while, so it would be amazing to customize them with attachments like grips, barrels, supressors, scopes, stocks etc.
There are only three modes in the game:
- 6vs6 casual: Objective and Stopwatch
- 5vs5 ranked: Execution
There should be more gamemodes like Team Deathmatch, Free For All or Gun Game (a free-for-all-style game where players receive different weapons after each kill)
In conclusion, the game is extremely addictive and fun, but you can get bored with the same gamemodes and weapons.

Hero Siege is a decent timekiller as it stands, but at this point it's not worth buying outside of a sale IMO.
The visuals are cluttered, it's always hard to see what's going on. Projectiles are often covered by vegetation, enemies or gore. Combined with unbalanced audio volumes, incorrect tooltips and vague patch notes, this makes the game appear very unpolished. Speaking of audio, I'm pretty sure they nicked some voice clips from DotA.
Combat is okay as far as hack and slay goes - sort of repetitive but skill is involved - but the graphical mess is a problem.
The balancing has gotten much better since I bought it, but it's still odd. Upgrades used to be irrelevant, but they fixed it and now there's actual progression.
The random level generation isn't worth mentioning, since most of the game happens in wide open areas outside.
Thanks to the varying power of random item drops and enchanted enemies, Hero Siege is luck-based to some extent.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

This was a fun and short game that was intriguing enough to keep me playing until I beat it (took about 3 hours). It is largely an interactive story, but it has plenty of gameplay (solving puzzles) that allows progression through the story. For instance, finding items to get you through a locked door. I felt the ending could have been better, but it worked. I suggest buying this game on sale considering how short it is. Pay whatever you think 3 hours of entertainment is worth if you like mystery/sci-fi and point-and-click adventures.
For the achievements, if you click on everything until it begins repeating dialogue, and try most items on everything, you should get all of your achievements the first time. Otherwise, just play through the game to enjoy it, and look up an achievement guide after. Once you beat the game you can easily go back to previous chapters to get achievements you missed, and there are great guides online to tell you how to get them. As is, I got all but four achievements my first time through without trying to get them, and going back only took a few minutes for completion. Enjoy! :]

I have mixed feelings about very certain aspects of this game. I cannot stress enough that I am in fact recommending it but it is EXTREMELY frustrating at times. I'm playing on the "I Am Death Encarnate" difficulty which is the second highest, and I was prepared to get my♥♥♥♥♥whooped on a Dark Souls scale. BOY was I underestimating just how hard this game would beat me. I've died at least thirty times on almost every checkpoint. I don't mind this fact alone. I'm fine with trying again and again because that makes the time I succeed even more gratifying. But there are some balance issues in this high difficulty that make the experience very inconsistent SOMETIMES. Enemy health, especially that of the mech type enemies with chainguns, seems to be completely ♥♥♥♥ing random. In most games, you'll learn the most efficient ways to kill enemies pretty quick. "These guys take two headshots with the dmr, a throwing knife will take down lightly armoured enemies instantly, but do nothing to anyone with substantial protection." That kind of thing. So I learned early on that these big mech guys take exactly two rockets to take down. Otherwise you'll be wasting all of your ammo on them. So I get into a room with two of them, and a rocket pickup right next to me. I grab it, and have 6 in total. I drop one of the guys with two as normal. The second takes 4 to the face and then kills me. All direct hits. This kind of thing happens a decent amount, most often with the special type enemies which, granted are supposed to be difficult but I'd like them to be consistent in their difficulty. Little things like this that break the flow of the otherwise very consistently designed game are what frustrate me. Not bugs which there are very few of, just enemies soaking up damage that they haven't been able to throughout the whole campaign. And for all I know these could just be balance issues due to playing on a high difficulty. Or I could just be bad at the game. But regardless of these infuriating little inconsistencies, this game has captivated me. The guns all feel and sound punchy, with the throwing knives being my favourite along with akimbo assault rifles. The gameplay is fast and the sprawling massive level design cators to plenty of different playstyles, whether its run and gun, picking people off from cover, or sneaking around, knifing people or picking people off with the supressed pistol. One incredibly enjoyable aspect that I really didn't expect was the writing of all the characters. Even the supporting roles had tons of personalitiy and had me worrying about them whenever they got in sticky situations, and the romance between B.J. Blazkowicz, the protagonist, and Anya Olyvia, your partner from near the beginning of the story, doesn't feel forced or like it was placed into the story to fill the minimum amount of sex scenes. The performances of the actors portraying them were genuine and sweet which caught me off guard in a modern fps game. Overall I'd definitely recommend this, but the higher difficulties will definitely test your skill and probably your patience. If you can stick it out though you're in for an intense and unique story and fast energetic gameplay. In all honesty there are many parallels with Half-Life 2, mainly in tone and plot but some levels gave me a distinct City 17 feel. So if you enjoyed that game, and let's face it who didn't, you'll probably get more than a couple kicks out of this game too.

Well as you know there are 3 top RC simulators (RealFlight, Phoenix and Aerofly RC) in the market and this simulator is one of them. I have both RealFlight and Phoenix RC simulators and I just bought ultimate edition of Aerofly RC to compare with them.
To be honest, It is very hard to compare all those 3 top rc simulators with each other, they are all good and they have all pros and cons. However,instead of comparing all those 3 games, I will try to explain my opinion about Aerofly RC.
The Graphics are really good and it will probably satisfy rc sim fans.
The Gameplay mechanics are really good and this simulator will really help you in real life if you are beginner. Especially, I have some of the in-game plane models in real life and game really gave me feeling that I am flying in real life. By the way, I am using Art-tech 6ch simulator transmitter which is cheap and easy to use on your computer.
Sounds are good enough for you to feel realism and sucks you in the game.
The aircraft details are fine and realistic
The weather is good. Especially if you fly your rc models at noon you can set up the time of the day and practice not to fly in to the sun.
The wind is effective and normally in my city its rare to see weather without wind, so in the game I am using wind settings to be better rc pilot in real life.
Summary:
Best part; In my opinion, the hardest part of the rc plane is landing and this game will really help me to increase my skill about landings
I wish; there are some kind of missions which can add more playable options with friends, the game is a bit expansive and you really need to buy ultimate edition if you want more and you will want more... In some sceneries you can not change the views. There can be more planes, especially some electric motored planes are not enough for me because in real life I am just flying with electric motored rc planes.
In conclusion: this simulator is really great and it will give you both pleasure and training for RC models. I insist that you should use simulator controller (with cable if you can) instead of xbox or other type of controller. The other simulators are also great. However, this one is enough for you if you are searching for a really good simulator which will train you for real life or just enjoy multiplayer with friends.

If you're looking for a realistic shooter, then Squad is the game for you. The game punishes you for every mistake you make, which can be very fustrating to new players. If you give the game enough time, and learn how and when to use your utilities then the game feels very rewarding. I never felt so much reward when cordinating with a team and flanking and wiping out enemy squads. This 1st person shooter has one of the most intense gun action I've seen, as sometimes your getting shot from all sort of directions, or you and your enemy both are in the same room just waiting for someone to lose patience and push. If you're tired of the run and gun 1st person shooter genre, than I suggest this game as it requires teamwork and actual tactics to asure victory. I give it a 9/10.

Titan Souls is definitely an indie game, as most people use the term nowadays. It's akin to Cave Story in that they're both good examples of short but otherwise worthwhile experiences. Allow me to explain step by step.
Let's start with the Gameplay. We'll break it down between controls and mechanics.
As far as controls go, this game is very simple. You move your character with the arrow keys or control stick, you can shoot your solitary arrow if you have it stocked or call it back after shooting with the same button. While aiming to shoot, the arrow keys/control stick become your method of aiming instead of moving. Along with movement and arrow play, you also get a dodge button that can be held to make your character run. I highly recommend using a gamepad, some bosses are near-to-outright impossible with only 8 directions to move and shoot in.
In contrast to the simple controls, the gameplay mechanics are more in depth than one would expect. The entire game can be boiled down to a glorified boss rush. Every titan encounter is in the typical "boss room" structure, whereas upon finding the titan in its room and engaging in it only victory or death will allow you to leave. Every boss has a weak point, but is otherwise invincible unless you hit this one spot with your own arrow. This makes each boss feel more like a battle of wits rather than strength, where solving the question of 'what' the weak point is and 'how' to hit it is as important as not being hit yourself. Learning a titan's pattern through trial and error and finding the perfect moment to attack is what this game's combat is at its core. It’s best not to get too worked up as death will happen in this game, again and again and again.
Outside of battles with the various titans of this world, the player is left to explore an unexplained and quite desolate world in search of the aforementioned titans. There are little rewards for exploration if you were looking for more than another titan to fight, and none if finding vague hints of the lore doesn't interest you. There are no mobs to find, and no enemies to deal with and level up against. This is a world of titans and decisive actions.
Now let's talk about Narration. This topic covers story as well as the level of engagement the game is capable of putting you into.
As far as the story goes, you're a chosen hero on a mission to kill all the titans and obtain the ultimate power, and learn the truth. Although, none of this is told to you in the game. Going off just the game, and not the game's description on this store page, you're a guy (or girl...?) with an magic arrow searching for and killing titans to collect their souls. There are murals that vaguely depict events or prophecies, but nothing is exactly obvious. The designers seemed to have taken a page of From Software's book of 'finding the story' design, without actually putting much story to find though.
Despite having such a paper thin plot, I found myself immersed during my gameplay all the way through. The engagement factor comes from the gameplay I mentioned before. Such an in-depth game of solving the boss' puzzle coupled with the sense of true satisfaction every time I figure it out and earn victory coaxed me into taking the next step and finding the next boss to fight. In some cases, yes I thought it impossible to defeat a boss, and ended up skipping it for another fight. Though that didn't deter me from playing nor detach me from the immersion, in fact it forced me to rethink how I approached the boss and lead to victory once I learned how to really fight each boss.
Now we'll finish off with the Aesthetics. This'll cover the art, which includes both sound and visual, the setting of the game, and how everything ties together into one experience.
Titan Souls uses a pixelated style mixed with simple three-dimensional graphics snuck in with a pixelated dress on to look more like all the other sprites in the party. Though it isn't 'anime with 3D CGI' levels of cringe worthy obviousness, in fact they're done quite well that I'm unsure whether the game was actually pixelated and not one big 3D graphic to begin with. The way some bosses can look like beautifully intricate sprites while others appear as pixel-textured models, and all of them fit without anything looking too far out of place is a feat on its own.
Speaking of fitting aesthetics, I found the music to be amazing in quality and purpose. The music is there to set a tone or invoke a feeling. With each area of the world came a theme that played the trope as straight as the typical lava area and snow area would in any adventure game, however that doesn’t mean to diminish how well it was produced. The feeling of first finding a new themed area coupled with the sudden shift in tone for the background music gave me a warm feeling of accomplishment, as if all that exploring actually wasn’t all for waste.
Don’t even get me started on the boss themes. I absolutely adore the boss themes of this game. From what I could notice, every boss has its own theme. Some even move to their theme, at least in the beginning. Every theme came off as fitting for the titan at hand, and made that fight all the more memorable or even fear inducing when their theme would come in at the start of the fight.
On the topic of themes though, I found the settings of Titan Souls to play most of the usual tropes. You start in a simple temple area, than branch out into the forest, volcanic caves, snowy peak, and even a small graveyard, all linked back to the main temple and its own little gardens. The areas are large, giving the sense that you’re actually in a world and not some corridor leading to the next boss. That same size also plays into the general theme of the world. It’s empty. It almost feels dead, abandoned, apart from the titans you’re there to defeat. It gives an odd sense of wonder, like something else is going on. Your mission isn’t some fanfare’d prophecy about saving the world, there isn’t seem to be right or wrong here. Just titans, and you who have come to slay them for your own goals.
Altogether, Titan Souls becomes an experience more than a walk from boss to boss. If you take the time to look around and get a sense of the world, and think about what’s going on, a whole story built on speculation opens up. The same book players would write for themselves when playing one of the notorious ‘Souls’ games by From Software, this game builds a world using only aesthetics and gameplay and doesn’t tell you anything at all outright. Each battle is a challenge on its own, forcing you to master the simple controls and the mechanics of the game alike as they’re presented to you within each fight. Death will happen, but it’s not the end. It’s only a means to grow and try again. Just you, your arrow, and a dozen titans to slay.

Despite trying to be a good game at heart. Titan Souls falls short in many aspects, game length being one of those especially. It took me barely 2 hours to beat the initial game, and even with 3 extra modes added on, this is simply laughable for a 15$ game.
Some could say that Titan Souls is "Inspired" by SotC, while I'd rather say that it's just a blatant 2-D ripoff with a much duller boss design. The fact that everything except for the final boss dies in one hit completely rules out the possibility of multiple form fight, which was amazing to look at in SotC, seeing how you were actually weakening the gargantuan enemies. In Titan Soul's it's just:
-Look for a giant glowing spot.
-Plink it with an arrow.
-Dead.
Absolutely underwhelming gameplay.
The story, again, ripped off of SotC with minor changes which only make Titan Souls looks simplistic and evoke the classic "2deep4u" trope. The fact that the game is going for the "butchered indie retro" look only reinforces this, sadly.
The only redeeming quality was the soundtrack, which was unexpectedly great. I would absolutely listen to something like that in my spare time, especially the overworld music.
At the current price, I would strongly recommend against buying this game. It's more like a well-made demo, if anything.

TL;DR: Highly reccomend Squad for anyone looking for a realistic military sim game, but still want to feel like they are playing a video game.
A truly incredible game, even in its current alpha state. Squad feels different from any other game I have ever played right down to its core. The visuals, the sounds, the teamplay, the comradery, the firefights; all perfectly crafted and relatively realistic. Realistic is the key word here, though. While each match typically offers you plenty of action, there is down time where you'll be just travelling to the next objective, or waiting to be a potential ambush for the enemy team. Squad is a game of patience, you can't go in running-and-gunning your way though it most of the time. You have to think critically and tactically, and when you die you might have to wait a few minutes before you can be back into the fray. Though, this added layer of higher stakes only draws me into learning this game even better, because I know that the same stakes apply to the enemy. I've fallen in love with this game, and I can't wait to see what the future holds for it.
