Although the gameplay may not be that exciting (expect lots of quick time events), the dialogue and choices are really what this game is about. There is a nice balance of nostalgic references/cameos from the original games as well as plenty of original and fleshed out characters and locations. The writing for Tales from the Borderlands extremely refreshing, hilarious, and in many ways better than that of the actual Borderlands games. I haven't laughed so hard playing a game - let alone a movie - in a long time. Compared to the Telltale Game of thrones or the Walking Dead games, I find that I never regret any of my decisions and can actually enjoy the entire experience without hating myself afterwards. My only real criticism is that I wish that some of the decisions had more tangible impact on the story. A lot of the results appear to be the same but with different (albeit entertaining) banter to accompany them.

Best Dragonball game ever. Inventive story, great visuals and lots of easter eggs all over the place. The combat feels as true to the source material that you could probably get and the created character campaign portion is inventive (written by Toriyama, expect nothing less than great). The new MMO-esque social hub has replaced a traditional menu system and I can understand how it can bother someone who doesn't want to run for 10 seconds to get to a certain menu but I appreciate what they've done with it. Ultimately it all helps add to the emersion into the DBZ universe and make you feel like a character in the series and not just a videogame player. It might get more annoying later, but for now I like it. But that is not the game...that's just a social system and the game is awesome. A succinct little game that deeply explores what most AAA titles tack on as an afterthought - the moral choice system.
Starting with KOTOR (as far as my memory goes) and getting built into virtually every Bioware title I've played as well as half-hearted attempts in games such as Red Dead Redemption or Bioshock (which I hold in very high esteem, otherwise), accumulating "good/bad" points in these games has felt little different from accumulating cash-back rewards on my credit card. In most of these games the only incentive to do anything you may find immoral is simply to role-play as a sociopath. Enter Beholder.
Beholder drops the player into the role of a landlord, Carl, whose role is to manage his apartment complex as well as enforce the draconian mandates of the totalitarian regime under which all the characters live. Difficult moral decisions are forced upon the player through the elegant lense of simple economics - "my daughter is sick and needs medicine immediatly, but I can't afford it, so what do I do?" The clock is always ticking. You cannot decide to revisit the issue later after you've looted a few bandit caves. And the only the reliable source of income in this nightmarish setting is to victimize the very people you call neighbors.
This is the only game I have ever played that truly asks the player "do the ends justify the means?" Whatever your answer to that question may be, the fact that it is asked at all makes this game worth playing.

First and foremost, I hate Diablo.  Diablo was  game that was a chore at the fourth level and I stopped playing, except in multiplayer and even then that didn't last beyond 10.  The fact that Hero Siege had Diablo elements at all was a real turn-off for me, but it was on sale and I liked the retro look so I got it anyway.
Thankfully, Hero Siege plays more like classic Gauntlet -- it knows nobody cares about the story and doesn't bother with it.   The game isn't punishingly difficult but death can come suddenly and unexpectedly if the wrong combination of things hit you at once, but being rogue-light instead of rogue-like means that while you can't keep your cash or power-ups to the next play through, you do keep your gear and levels.
The action is continual and your characters -- if they survive -- ramp up their power considerably and pretty soon you're going from just trying to survive to seeing how fast you can wipe out the wave.  Make no mistake though -- while mechanically you can survive everything in one go, realistically that's not going to happen as early on one mistake can be your last.  As you get the hang of each character you can start to dominate everything -- and the better gear and levels helps a lot.
The Negatives
==========
On the negative side, the characterizations are terrible; as much as I enjoy the style of the characters I wish the default would have them mute like Link.  None of them are interesting, and it's hard to pick what's worse -- the voice acting or the dialogue.  But that's the only real negative, aside from some minor bugs.
The Verdict
========
While it takes a bit to get the feel or flow, it's a good game and well worth the asking price.  Going from barely surviving to complete domination is satisfying.

Alright, so this is a special review, and I'm gonna ask you guys to read it to the end before dropping any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on me. A good friend of mine gifted me this game like 2 days ago, and I actually like the game. It has some flaws, like the random nature of Roguelike games for example, but it's not a terrible experience. So, why do I NOT recommend it? Easy.
The game is a rip-off. And I'm not saying that like "it copies the concept and gameplay of other games". That would been aceptable IF the game is good. What I mean, is that the game quite literally uses assets from other games. I can accept using the Diablo font, for example, since the game IS a parody of Diablo. What I CAN'T accept, is that the game uses an INSANE amount of sprites taken directly from games such as The Binding of Isaac. And unless it's proven otherwise, they did NOT ask for permission, because that would be like asking the Bank manager for the keys of his Safe-lock.
I usually ♥♥♥♥♥ about games having ♥♥♥♥♥♥ bugs, glitches or being lazy, but taking assets from other games and using them in your own TO THEN SELL A GAME WITH THEM, is STEALING the effort of other people, and getting paid for it.
And it's sad, really. I was going to give the game a positive review, but then I noticed all the stolen sprites. I'm still gonna play it, don't get me wrong... But why they stole all of that, is a mystery that goes beyond my mind right now.
EDIT: I discovered some extra stuff yesterday, and I also forgot some others. I'll keep it short:
-Controller support seems to be random. I have a Xbox360 controller, a PS4 controller, and a random other controller that was cheap as hell and works at times. Weird enough, you have to select what kind of controlls you want in the Controls option screen, but the game doesn't recognize ANY of them.
-The game has just too many grinding. I can understand that in games such as Disgaea, but here it gets boring quite fast.
-Remember that I talked about the randomness of Roguelike games before? Well, screw that. This game goes beyond. What do I mean? I've faced multiple times already some unfair stuff, 2 of the 4 times, I had a LVL3-5 character on the first stage, and for no reason an enemy with arround 60k HP appears, and kills me in one hit. Difficulty should not mean "Of 9001 tries, you might win a stage once".
-While the controls with a keyboard are okay, it feels weird. You attack with the arrows, while moving with WASD. Why not making your character face somewhere with the mouse, and attacking with it? Would been better, on my oppinion.
-The game kind of drops you into it without any explanation at all. You have to select a character from 10 or so, and it doesn't tell you what each one does, you have to look it up on the Internet. The game doesn't then tell you where you have to go. At first I though I had to talk with NPC's for quests, but turns out ALL of the NPC's in town just trade some stuff on crystals, an ingame currency. I don't like tutorials, but the game should at least give some indications of what you're supposed to do.
-Tried the multiplayer once, and I will never do it again. Why? Tried it 10 times in a row, NOONE of them ever worked.
I'm kind of glad I didn't buy the game, it was a gift... But I feel bad for the friend who bought it to me. He though I would fall in love with it. Kind of sad to see potential go to waste. I hope tough, that they make a sequel at some point, with all of this stuff fixed. And please, don't "take" so much inspiration from other sources next time, try to make it more original. Diablo parodies are nice, but I rather play something refreshing, with some innovation.

This review was previously posted on the "Ashes of the Singularity" storepage - following the merging of "Ashes of the Singularity" and its "Escalation" expandalone I thought it would be best to post this review here as well, since the original game is unavailable for purchase. Notice that my playtime may appear lower than stated in the review - this is due to most of my time being logged on the original title. If you would like to check, accurate hours played can still be found in my community profile. With that out of the way - here is my review:
I am obsessed with this and I'm not even halfway in.
Let me open this by saying that this game is hard. Perhaps frustrating for the less patient of you; games can last upwards of two hours and, online, there's no way to speed through that, however, if you're willing to wait longer for gratification, and if you enjoy spending time thinking through, formulating, and refining strategies: this game is for you you.
Put simply, if you think chess needs more lasers, this game is for you.
The gameplay itself is meaty. The units are quite limited in comparison to, say, Planetary Annihilation, but this means that there is more of a focus on what you do with your units than which ones you make, something that is sadly lacking in the RTS world. Resource management is critical, and it therefore helps that resource flow is simple and well shown in the HUD. The AI is refined, with enough difficulty settings to feed Africa - even going so far as to allow the player to choose the preferred game plan for each individual AI.
My favorite thing about Ashes of The Singularity is that it forces you to think, no one strategy fits all: with more than one way to win any game (either by elimination or by critical holding points for a certain time), a stupid number of maps, the aforementioned AI systems, anywhere between 2 and 6 contestants, team systems, and finally, preset scenarios, allowing limitation of the buildings and units buildable, Ashes is far from being so simple.
There are two playable factions in Ashes, PHC and Substrate, Only one of which I have ever played, quick reminder, I've got in excess of 100 hours at this point.
The competitive multiplayer is well designed - ranked matches, custom matches, profiles for all players and many many leaderboards, even going so far as to host competitive leaderbards for player hardware benchmarks (did I mention this game has some great benchmarking tools for framerate junkies?) however, it appears occasionally buggy and disconnections are known to occur.
For modders, included with Ashes is one of the best damn Map editors I've seen in my life (accessible by setting the -modding launch option) and, on moddb, you can find an exceptional modding guide written by the developers themselves. I've spent a significant time messing with these, and I'm confident you will too.
In terms of graphics. Well. The menu screen takes me aback, and the game doesn't exactly disappoint.
There are so many things I havent touched on here, the campaign, the quanta system, the control group system etc. etc. etc. But if you're feeling at all convinced, although, again, I recieved this for free, I will tell you, the £30.00 price tag is worth it. I hope to see you in game soon.

SP review only (Multiplayer not considered, no DLC)
My favourite RTS is Supreme Commander Forged Alliance and this game feels in a similar vein, albeit not nearly as

What's good:?
The game is mostly fun to play and I do recommend.  The graphics are pleasant, and the UI is well considered.  I am delighted the devs included an ingame speed option for SP.  This seems obvious to me, but I can't seem to remember any of the other RTS titles doing this, so hats off to StarDock (SD) for simple things.
It is true that a well designed RTS does not need a SP campaign (e.g.SOOSE), but in my opinion it is better to have one than not to (despite my complaints regarding ashes campaigns, see "whats not so good" below), and the missions objectives in the campaign are varied enough to keep it interesting, and long and plentiful enough for probably around 50 hours of gameplay depending on your play style.
-------------------------------------------------------------
What's not so good?:
Still unstable.
Can sometimes play for hours without issue, yet will crash within 30 secs at other times.. Seems totally random and is still frustrating.
The army reinforcement tool is only sort of useful, in that its handy when it isn't really needed, and more trouble than its worth when it is.  it's handy but not remotely needed at the beginning of a mission where there are few units and few if any armies, yet when army macro is becoming an issue and it's now needed, its too clunky to rely on.
In mid to late game, and especially on larger maps, because you can't specify which factory does the building, it takes too long for reinforcements to arrive at the front lines to be viable. Also, having little streams of individual units heading to an army at the other side of the map makes them vulnerable to attack.  Now the argument here is secure supply lines but securing supply lines on some campaign maps isn't always possible and by the time it is and you have a large enough force to make this tool worthwhile, you've probably already won and don't need it now.  For this reason I barely use it, relying on managing it myself.
This is a regrettable criticism as I feel the SD are trying hard here to come up with a way to reduce army management micro, which I fully appreciate and encourage, but at present without some way to designate which factory any given army is reinforced from, the loss of control hurts more than the micro. However, I think trying to implement such control with the present system might murder many CPU's.
The campaign plot seems to be attempting to take a strange and compelling viewpoint of humanities possible future with regards to accelerating technological development, but because the voice acting is at best mediocre (looking at you Halee) and the dialogues are groan inducingly painful (all of them), it takes a fair amount of effort to care about it.  By the third mission on the second campaign ( I did try to give it a chance), I was spam clicking through every dialogue box without reading or listening to the text because my face was sore from all the palming i'd been giving it.
Convincing dialogue has never been SD's strong point though (I still♥♥♥♥♥♥myself laughing at the intro movie for SOOSE diplomacy,  it is  not possible to say the word diplomacy, and make it sound menacing, but SD would not be deterred...ah bless), so it is not that suprising that this is one of the weaker area's of the game.
On mission completion, the typical reward expected of a cool cutscene with some exciting plot exposition is quickly replaced by the creeping feeling of apathy as each cutscene eats away at any enthusiasm you may have had regarding the plot.
The game has a nasty habit of hijacking the camera for scripted cutscenes while battles are ongoing.   It's very rare I lose my temper at a game, but when you lose your frontline dreadnought in a battle you felt you would have won because Mac (or Halee or Samuel) decided to muscle in with more tedious dialogue, pulling the camera away to the far end of the map again at the most inopportune moment, it serves only to make my blood boil and reduce the lifetime of my mouse and keyboard.  This also happens on a mission were you periodically get free reinforcements and for some reason the camera jumps to the spawn point every time they arrive, which becomes infuriating fast.
These issues mean I've grown to loathe all the main characters because they insist on speaking, especially Mac. (grits teeth), but a positive spin might be that the campaign
Though if Halle says "We need more logistics!" one more time I think I might scream.  I know I need Logistics, tere a big flashing number in the corner to remind me and you've been saying it every 20 seconds for the last 5 minutes now.   Strangely, muting voice does not stop this. I really hate Halee now.
Unfortunately I have not yet managed to complete the Genisis campaign due to constant crashing and what appears to be an issue with the Griffenclaw mission (not confirmed).  The Juggernaught (JN) seems to suicide itself when off camera.  It would go from 100% health to < 10% in a matter of seconds when not in view even though it was still sitting in my base, far from the front lines with no enemies to be seen.
At first I thought the AI was spamming quanta attacks but parking the JN next to a quantum jammer had no effect, the JN still exploded for no reason I could discern.  To keep it alive I had to keep it out of battle with about 20 repair units constantly sitting next to it meaning it is useless and I would be better served destroying it to free up the logistics for units that can actually do some fighting.
My experience of stardock supporting their games (SOOSE, GALCIV 1 & 2) has been excellent so far,  so I am optimistic the game will improve with most issues ironed out.  At present I would describe this as a solid RTS with promise and score it at 7/10.
With a bit more love and polish this might one day rival the mighty supcom, here's hoping.
TL/DR
7/10

This is a nice, simple point and click adventure game.  The items you need to progess are used in ways that actually make sense, meaning that you essentially know what you need and how to use your items at any given time.  Most games like this force you to analyze every bit of you surroundings for some obscure object that makes absolutely no sense when used, but not this game!  Oh, I found a crowbar?  I'll use it on that door!  Oh, a lighter?  I'll use it to make a fire.  Just very simple, straight forward puzzles like that.  There's also a time mechanic where you can jump into the future and to the present on a whim, which opens up a whole new level of exploration and puzzle solving.  Overall, a very good casual adventure game and I would recommend it to anyone!

Games in the point-n-click genre, the master of the 90's, especially the ones developed by Lucas Arts, some of them have some appeal - mainly the story, but also the style of the graphics. Those are at least the things I like in games such as this. So when the story in 'The Silent Age' was really lackluster - you never really care about any character and what their objectives are - it made me a little disappointed and gave me the feeling of "I'm just playing this to finish it and get it over with". A feeling you don't want your game to radiate, so to speak.
But even though the major point of the game is a con, there's also some pros to bring up. The first one is the short length, it never overstays its welcome. The second one being in two parts, one being the graphics, second being the games overall simple style. Graphically it's not much details in characters and such, but the developers made it look really good. In the sound department, the music is decent but the main point is that the main character says very few lines, which should bring you more into the game, which it doesn't, but it contributes to the overall simpleness (is that a word?).
In the end, I'd like to recommend it, but I don't think I can. Only if it was really cheap, like when I bought it during the Steam Summer Sale - €2.99. Decent price for a short game. Other than that, you'd have to be a fan of this type of games for it to be worth it.

Nice little gem here, definitely pick it up if you're into this kind of thing. Aerofly RC7 is a flight simulator of RC aircraft and can also be used as a training tool for those interested in the real hobby. Aircraft range from miniature indoor helicopters to full scale, fuel-guzzling beasts, every one is easy to fly yet tough to master! The sim includes beautiful photo-realistic scenery from real locations all over the world with many different airparks to fly from, which all have their differences, my favourite being the variation in runways (gradient, length, width etc). Every one makes for a challenging flight without even considering the wind yet!
The hud is great and easy to interpret, it includes vital instruments in a simple easy to read format which can all be adjusted to your liking from the dropdown menus, everything works very smoothly and everything feels like how it should feel. From the menus you can also customize each aircraft to your liking e.g. throws and whatnot. I've found nothing annoying about this sim yet but If I do I'll be sure to come back and update this review.
To sum it up;
Pros:
Great physics
Awesome interface
Stunning photorealistic scenery
Smooth running, high fps on ultra settings
Easy super simple control setup(Regular Joystick, Keyboard or RC transmitter of the simulator type)
Plenty of great aircraft
TrackIR compatible
Very customizable (Aircraft flight surfaces, throws etc..)
Cons:
None other than the cost aspect, I got the regular edition yet moved to ultimate as I noticed a few of my favourite birds were in it. Ended up costing me well over $100 all up.
I guess in the end if you really are into flight in general, flight simming or RC aircraft the enjoyment had is definitely worth it. Like all flight sims especially those with payware they are not cheap, I'd honestly say this one is worth every penny, and I personally love it!
A must have for any AVGeek!

I have mixed feelings about very certain aspects of this game. I cannot stress enough that I am in fact recommending it but it is EXTREMELY frustrating at times. I'm playing on the "I Am Death Encarnate" difficulty which is the second highest, and I was prepared to get my♥♥♥♥♥whooped on a Dark Souls scale. BOY was I underestimating just how hard this game would beat me. I've died at least thirty times on almost every checkpoint. I don't mind this fact alone. I'm fine with trying again and again because that makes the time I succeed even more gratifying. But there are some balance issues in this high difficulty that make the experience very inconsistent SOMETIMES. Enemy health, especially that of the mech type enemies with chainguns, seems to be completely ♥♥♥♥ing random. In most games, you'll learn the most efficient ways to kill enemies pretty quick. "These guys take two headshots with the dmr, a throwing knife will take down lightly armoured enemies instantly, but do nothing to anyone with substantial protection." That kind of thing. So I learned early on that these big mech guys take exactly two rockets to take down. Otherwise you'll be wasting all of your ammo on them. So I get into a room with two of them, and a rocket pickup right next to me. I grab it, and have 6 in total. I drop one of the guys with two as normal. The second takes 4 to the face and then kills me. All direct hits. This kind of thing happens a decent amount, most often with the special type enemies which, granted are supposed to be difficult but I'd like them to be consistent in their difficulty. Little things like this that break the flow of the otherwise very consistently designed game are what frustrate me. Not bugs which there are very few of, just enemies soaking up damage that they haven't been able to throughout the whole campaign. And for all I know these could just be balance issues due to playing on a high difficulty. Or I could just be bad at the game. But regardless of these infuriating little inconsistencies, this game has captivated me. The guns all feel and sound punchy, with the throwing knives being my favourite along with akimbo assault rifles. The gameplay is fast and the sprawling massive level design cators to plenty of different playstyles, whether its run and gun, picking people off from cover, or sneaking around, knifing people or picking people off with the supressed pistol. One incredibly enjoyable aspect that I really didn't expect was the writing of all the characters. Even the supporting roles had tons of personalitiy and had me worrying about them whenever they got in sticky situations, and the romance between B.J. Blazkowicz, the protagonist, and Anya Olyvia, your partner from near the beginning of the story, doesn't feel forced or like it was placed into the story to fill the minimum amount of sex scenes. The performances of the actors portraying them were genuine and sweet which caught me off guard in a modern fps game. Overall I'd definitely recommend this, but the higher difficulties will definitely test your skill and probably your patience. If you can stick it out though you're in for an intense and unique story and fast energetic gameplay. In all honesty there are many parallels with Half-Life 2, mainly in tone and plot but some levels gave me a distinct City 17 feel. So if you enjoyed that game, and let's face it who didn't, you'll probably get more than a couple kicks out of this game too.

As the media called out that there’s now a Shadow of Colossus and Dark Souls mixed into one game, I got sceptical. The games name was Titan Souls and started of as a game jam project, started from three guys named Mark Foster, David Fenn and Andrew Gleeson.
The basic gameplay is that you are a Titan hunter and are on the mission to kill all titans you can find and absorb their souls. Your weapon of choice is bow and arrow. One arrow to be exactly because this one arrow can be shot and pulled back to your player via telekinesis.
On your way to become the next legendary Titan slayer you face up to 17 Titans and the final boss, which is the Titan Soul itself. There are 6 parts of the world where different elements of Titans are waiting for you. Heat or Lava types vs ice types, normal types and venomous types.
Each Titan can be killed with one hit to their weakspot, the problem is, that either this weakspot is hidden behind cover that you have to break or you have to act really fast to get a shot at it.
The gameplay is a big challenge and sometimes really annoying as you have to run a few seconds to get from your savepoint to Titan that you’re trying to fight. These few seconds are not that much alone, but if you fail multiple times again and again, you’re really annoyed that some Titans are that far away from your savepoint. I’d love to see a improvement so you are respawning right at the door to the Titan again.
The graphics of this game is a fantastic 2D world mixed with some 3D elements from time to time. The world is filled with small details like small piles of snow, that you can roll through, a dead Titan lying on the corner of the map and overall the style of the game has a reminiscing touch from FEZ, which I really liked.
The soundtrack is really awesome and in fact I’m listening to it right now as I’m writing this review. Each area has it’s own music and every Titan again too. The thing is that you will probably not hear much of the Titan music, as you are first, concentrating on not dieing and shooting your arrow in the right moment, second you probably die or kill so fast, that you won’t have a chance to listen to the soundtrack until the end. But don’t worry, if you bought the game, you can find the music and all sounds in the games directive as .ogg file.
In fact, you could mod this game easily with photoshop and a sound programm to exchange some data, but that’s a different story.
For you out there, who really want a challenging and simple game, Titan Souls is your first choice if you’re not that much against using a gamepad on PC. The game is just designed for a controller because you need the accuracy of a joystick to target with the right angle on screen.
[SPOILER WARNING]
But there’s also a hidden 19th enemy, called the truth, which has a slightly different challenge for you. You can beat him in three different steps, because he is changing is form in 3 variations. The thing is, that once you got to know the pattern or system behind the movement, you can do the first two steps without a problem. The third step again is a real challenge and considering the fact that three steps of random events like chasing eyeballs might be too hard to manage, it is probably for the better.
After you beat the game you get a nice screen presented which tells you how many Titans you slaughtered and how many times they did. My playtime of my first full run was about 4 hours and 20 minutes, with over 200 deaths.
The game presents you also the possibilty of 4 savegames to start different runs with different modifications such as Hard mode, Iron mode, Truth mode and No Roll, which means no rolls OR running.
To be honest, the first normal run was difficult and stressful enough for me, so I have not played the game on harder modes yet. I can only guess that these modes really stress you out and I think that the gamedesign for your player might be too difficult at that point.
[END SPOILER WARNING]
So this game is a big challenge and if you are the type of person that likes to struggle and seek for the one perfect shot-moment, you’re definitely the type of gamer that should check out Titan Souls.
My biggest problem is, that there’s no real point of doing all this. You’re just the kid running around and absorbing souls. You will only get a small hint of a lore, but that’s all about it. To me, this game is more arcarde style, which is not bad, but could have been a little bit more.
So my final thought on Titan souls is, that it’s the perfect small game to test your skills and nerves, but if you are looking for something with real depth, there’s not much to it except for the beautiful graphics and music.
But you can download a Demo on Steam, so go and find out for yourself if this game is worth your money or not.

I went in expecting the game to be challenging, and got a game that was just frustrating.
Firstly, the controls are simple, in fact too simple. Putting two functions (roll and run) on the same button makes it very difficult to survive bosses because I was constantly messing up, forgetting to keep holding down X because I just had to press it to roll. Also, why isn't running the default movement pattern? The world is too large to just stroll around in, because then you'll just get bored. Back to the controls, aiming is a b**ch since you can only use the arrow keys, which is incredibly inprecise. It'd be easier if there was real mouse support.
Secondly, the map is confusing. Bosses are not easy to find beyond the first set of 4, and there are plenty of branching paths from the spawnpoints that lead you RIGHT BACK to the spawnpoint. If these paths don't lead anywhere, why are they here? Just to give an example, there are two bosses in the forest/swamp area. To reach the one to your right, you have to take the right path, then when you get to the next area, immediately turn back around. When you get back to the spawn area, it's no longer the spawn area and it leads you to the second boss. How is that sound design? And how was I supposed to know that? The game is already challenging enough with the bosses, making it harder and take longer to reach them (because it does those bosses are sooo far off) only takes away from the game.
The bosses are difficult, and if you can overlook controls and map and want a challenge then this is for you. If you don't like what I've written, don't buy the game.

DBX is a fun and engaging arena fighter with enough content to keep you playing for hours. Above average visuals and near flawless performance (I have not encountered any bugs or FPS drops). Character creation is not the deepest but there are plenty of other options for you to get creative with for your look, your gear and even the moves you use during a fight.
The Combat: Single-player this combat system is near flawless in execution and makes for some really exciting fights, the only issue being the camera due to the lock on function. Co-op the combat system remains flawless in execution unless you and a player controlled partner are attacking the same target in which case you will often find your target being knocked away multiple times and your big attacks end up missing.
Visuals: If you've played the Budokai series of games then you know what to expect here, it's the same cell-shaded style only a lot more crisp and defined. though that definition only pertains to the character models themselcves, environments are not so crisp and detailed.
Audio: Sound effects and music are all top-notch here, what you would expect. The only "Audio" issue i have is that some of the enemies are not voiced by their original VO's, it's not game breaking and is more of a personal preference (Cell and Frieza stand out the most and i swear to god it sounds like the dude voicing Ginyu is the guy that voices Nappa in DBZA)
Content: there is plenty of content to be had here. First off you have the story, taking you to key places of key events within the DBZ universe to set history back on the correct path, this is single player (As far as i know). Outside of that you have the Paralell quests which can be either taken on solo or taken on co-operatively with up to two team mates.
PQ's see you taking quests that seem to run along the same lines as the story, events ripped from the DBZ universe, each battle has bonus condition which will unlock a bonus fight within that mission, PQ's are where you will get the bulk of your gear and items.
Outside of PQ's you have the battle mode, these go from 1v1 to 3v3 and can be highly entertaining, there are both Online and Offline options for this, There is a world tournament mode though right now it is locked.
Honestly the game is deep, a lot deeper than i expected it to be, what i have listed is the bulk of the experience. There is a lot more, skill shops, item shops, clothing shops, mix your own capsule (potions) shops, mentors and so on. It's a must have for any DBZ fan and even if you're not a DBZ it's still an all around good game to play.

Having knocked up a couple of hours, I think I'd share some information and feedback about this game. In part, to counter many of the negative reviews that don't give the game the credit it deserves, but also to give an honest perspective.
To start with, let me say that it doesn't necessarily deserve the negative feedback that it's getting. The problem here, that I see, is that some are experiencing issues with the game and the software tutorial itself doesn't give a whole lot of help to resolve it. That said, there are some issues that deserve mentioning and some interesting features that also deserve a few words.
Graphically, the game is pretty nice and certainly well laid out. There are different areas to head to for specific intentions and it works well. The controls are well thought out and it's effortless to shift between each area. Use of the right mouse button to transition between areas is an boon - since many of this sort of game neglect the use of said button. The music, too, isn't too annoying and blends nicely in the background, with an easy to find method of turning it off and on. It's smooth and not too demanding on modern systems (meaning pretty much any system from the last 5-8 years) but that's to be expected in an older title.
The game itself seems to borrow some ideas from other games, which isn't unheard of. There's a few places where I immediately thought of Airline Tycoon/AT: First class. Again, not a bad thing but hardly innovative either. There's lots of clickables in the world, though there's no real explaination of what they do, if anything and I did notice on the official forums/website for the game that there's very limited support for English speaking individuals, whereas there's a wealth of support for German speakers. Hardly the end of the world, but considering the planet is more English speaking than German, maybe something to look at down the line.
On to the negatives.
To start with, I have to make mention of the lack of subtitles. Many of the spoken lines can be hard to hear through any form of background music, be it ingame or otherwise and with no means to read that spoken word, rather than listen to it, it's a little annoying.
Also, the method the game uses to publish your titles. You have to have a contract with a publisher - there's no method of self-publishing (at least, not as far as I got - which was into the early 90s) and promotion of your titles doesn't really seem to fit. This is one of the game-killers for me. I can earn money - make some top notch games but without a method of publishing, I'm limited to the contracts on offer and that, to me, makes little sense. If you're sitting on a few million and you have the means to buy a publishing company, you would if it was financially viable.
Also, there's a lack of polishing to this game and, again, I recognise that the game is ancient in PC gaming standards ( 8 years or so). Nevertheless, a little extra work could have made the game more enjoyable. There's a great start here, but it needs more, especially as the tycoon market seems to be pickiing up again and competition is starting to hit the shelves again (Game Dev Tycoon immediately comes to mind).
Speaking of which. Another of the features this game is really missing is R+D and this is something that goes right back to the dawn of computer gaming. Without R+D, there would be no innovation, nothing to set the big companies aside from the little. Also, when you take over a competitor, it would be nice if you could keep the name and use it for, say, publishing or research or whatever else your mind fancies, rather than the name disappearing. There's little to stop you from taking over and becoming an umberella company that publishes games from your child-companies.
The game, on the whole, is good, though it has little replay value because it ends up being a chore to rinse, lather, repeat. Adding more staff options would help and delegating some of the more mundane tasks to AI workers would allow you to manage the areas you want to, without having to keep doing the same thing over and over.
All in all, if you're looking for a distraction and want a few hours of game play here and there, it's worth the investment. It's the sort of game I, personally, would keep going back to while deciding what main project I want to start (Mount fo Blade, Tropico 4, whatever) and it has some value there. However, if you want something more meaningful, either look at Game Dev Tycoon (also an indie title and a demo is available) or wait and see what happens with Game Tycoon 2.

Tonight I got through Unepic. This game is big and unlike most games out there. The sidescrolling exploration RPG genre, if there is such a thing, is pretty much limited to the Castlevania series, and even then, depending on the title you get more or less RPG out of it. Unepic allows you to specialize in several weapon types, armor or robes, health and several schools of magic, all of which have obvious gameplay benefits. Only a few of them feel like "must haves" giving room for quite a bit of player choice.
The Hard++ mode is very, very difficult, somewhat to the point of feeling a little unfair at times, but like all good and difficult games, it required me to change my strategy, rather than just "do better," an essential quality.
The story is irreverent, and at a few places early in the game, even a little insensitive or perhaps offensive depending on the individual. However, it takes what seems like a throw-away premise and turns it into a story that actually develops in surprising ways.
Ultimately it took me a supposed 22 hours to get through it, but I wouldn't be surprised if it was quite a bit longer considering the amount of hours not accounted for with all my repeated deaths. The quantity and breadth of content here is surprising. Rarely do I play an indie game where I think to myself "Wow, they really couldn't have done anything more." They really have a ton of varied content here and was surprised at the variety of enemies, level scenarios, bosses, tactics I was required to learn and master, and ultimately a huge ending that uses just about every skill you know, and requires you to learn new ones, in order to beat it.
I really can't think of the last time I played a game with this much breadth in its mechanics, and if you like complexity in your action games, you're probably going to love Unepic. If you're not so much into that kind of complexity, I recommend Unepic anyway, just play on an easier difficulty than I did.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Grade: C-
Almost like Castlevania, but with it's set of flaws.
Pros:
1. Intersting story.
2.  It's nice if you play it for the multiplayer.
Cons (mainly when playing this game solo):
1. The customization may seem great at first, but at one point you'd realize weapon balancing is funky in different areas/boss battles, and by that point either you'd want to roll a new character or have to respec.
2. Pets are hard to manage for no good reason, and there's no way to level them up. In Castlevania, pets are either invincible or they cannot be targeted by mobs... not in Unepic. Your pet will die in later stages, and they cannot be unsummoned/summoned on the fly because then they lose their energy charge.
3. The game suffers a fundamental problem in character actions - too many actions for a simple game. For example, instead of setting an AI behavior for heal potions (i.e. heal with lowest/highest quality), the game requires you to map one button to one function only. That may seems fine in the beginning... at one point you'd have so many items and weapons and spells that you can use it starts to look stupid. Castlevania's Symphony of the Night and later series features tons of characters action... all being performed on a game pad. Do we really need 20+ hot keys for a 2D action game?
4. So areas gets harder after you "open up the gates." It's meant to be part of the story progression, right? But some areas would get a lot more harder because all the mobs can aggro you once the gates are lifted... and they stay that way.
5. Some boss moves you cannot dodge with skill, it's almost luck based, i.e. raining down magic randomly.

Unit 4 is a retro platformer developed and published by Gamera Interactive
Upon first look, Unit 4 may appear to be a simple Megaman clone, but there's actually quite a bit more to it than that. Unit 4 is about an evil alien army that has stolen a sacred artifact from your home planet. Rumors swirl of other planets having the same thing happening to them. Your team (Unit 4) will embark on a journey to try and discover what is going on.
Unit 4 plays like an old school NES platformer. You control a single player on the screen with the ability to change into one of your Unit 4 brethern with a push of a button. Each person in your team has a different ability to help bypass obstacles and enemies in your way. Blue has the ability of mega jump which allows him to jump extremely high, Red has a super dash which is very useful smashing through enemies, Green has the justic hook which allows him to latch onto walls, and Yellow has ghost flight which allows him to glide through their air and through enemies. This game also supports 4 player locally allowing all 4 Unit 4 members to be on the screen at the same time.
This game is very reminiscent to unforgiving old school NES games. It may take 15 minutes just to get past one section of a level due to the intricacy of the levels. This game also has a few mini games such as racing in it which if you win can give you items to allow you to customize your Unit 4 hero, or your ship, these changes are sticly aestetic though and don't actually change anything else.
The level select screen is laid out like a Galactic map allowing you to pick levels. The more levels you finish, the move planets you are able to visit. Despite the game sporting an old school appearance, the graphics are very sharp, and the developer did a fantastic job of making the game appear to be modern while sporting an 8-bit look.  The game has 15 different planets, and 3 different worlds to fight for. Each planet contains about 10 levels and a mega boss at the end that will test your patience and skills.
This game is a lot of fun to play, but can be extremely frustrating due to the difficulty of some of the bosses (as shown above). I have not tried the 4 player local version yet, but part of me thinks that with the exception of the bosses, it would make the game a lot harder trying to move from left to right without leaving your team members behind.

This is game is an historical classic.  One only needs to know the historical games history to know this is a fact.
This game is approaching 2 decades old and has an active growing community of players. The original game was released in an era when RTS were frequently anticipated AA titles and this is one of the only games from that time period that truely stood the test of time. It has seen success over its rivals, predacessor and successors and is one of the only true contenders (along with starcraft) for greatest rts of all time. So what  makes this game so good?
Age of Empires 2 is a game that is simple goal and easy to understand mechanics, many layers of complexity. This makes it a fun game for a wide variety of skil levels. At the simplest level you have a city building RTS where you expand your town and kill an enemy. This is a common setting, but age of empires 2 really perfected it. The game features a great set of single player campaigns which you follow the tales of historical figures such as Ghengis Kahn, Atilla the Hun, Jean De Arc etc.
The game also features a mutliplayer which rewards players at every skil level. Beginning players may take their time to build cities and large armies. Advanced players learn different strategies to engage in early game skirmishes. This is a game where the more you give to the game  the more you get from the game.
Other fun elements of the game is the game has both indepth campaign editor, easy ai scripting  and allows users to view recorded games. This allows people to create their maps, study past games and really take their time to learn the game.

Even with all its little shortcomings (many of which will be resolved in an upcoming patch, the game director assured me), one can't help but see what a nice little game this is.
The pixel art is very cute, and the level design is full of ideas: I've completed the first world so far and I've never encountered the same kind of obstacle twice.
The character-switching mechanic is nice, and between all of them, the four protagonists of Unit 4 represent all the gimmicks we've seen in indie platformers in the last 10 years: from the classic double jump and triangle jump, to a warioland-like dash, to the ever present grappling hook, to the ability of de-materializing yourself to pass through obstacles and float gently while falling down.
My big gripe with Unit 4 is that having to switch your character using the LB/RB pad bumps it can be quite tricky to do the more complex maneuvers, ie to do a double jump and then a dash you have to start with the blue character, press A for the first jump, X for the double jump, LB to switch to the red character, then X again for the dash.
Definitely takes some time to get used to it. I would've preferred to have the four front pad buttons assigned to the four different powers, so that you could ie. dash just by pressing (let's say) B, while also switching to the red character if you haven't already. So the aforementioned example would've been just A/A/B, but most of all the levels could've been traversed in a much more dynamic and spectacular fashion, even if I guess with enough practice you can do it anyway, even with the current control scheme.
"Practice" being the keyword here since, while not being a full-blown punisher (many of the most difficult parts are optional), Unit 4 can be quite tough, and some passages will require you memorizing patterns and carefully choosing the best character for the job.
In the end it's a very neat little game, not perfect, but enjoyable on its own right. The price is a bit steep right now, but whenever you see it in a bundle it'll be worth a shot.
Give yourself enough time to get used to its control scheme, and you'll be surprised at how inventive this title can be!

Your experience with this game will boil down to four stages, which conveniently reflect your first encounters with the major facets of the game.
1) Character creation: Wow this is huge, it's stunning how much variety there is between any two random individuals. Asthetics, clothing, and of course move sets, stats, and equipment are all customizable so the charcter you're playing as is tailored to your play style.
2) Gameplay: At first movement feels stiff. You're bombarded with a ton of inputs and only a couple special attacks. It takes a couple hours to really get the hang of things, and ultimately most of the characters feel remarkably similar. The mechanics are tailored to allow for 3 vs 3 matches, which the game employs frequently. One on one battles aren't as concrete or intricate as Budakai Tenkaichi 3 but then again that game didn't have six man simultaneous free for alls. Native English speakers may not have translated this game.
3) Online: This unlocks once you finish fighting Vegeta and Nappa, so maybe a couple hours after starting you'll get online. It's for your protection since before that point you'll have no idea what you're doing.You remember when tf2 implimented taunts? The world hub is a party, it's super satisfying to see all your OC's posing with one another, gallavanting in an ocean of wildly different people. I haven't seen any green and purple themed characters other than my own. People need to make more or I'm calling a doctor.
4) The Hellish Difficulty Spike: It sure was nice of you to kill three majin buus with SSJ3 Goku's help. Now we're taking Goku away and giving you 4 more Majin buus to fight bringing the total to seven in a row, which in itself wouldn't be so bad if you weren't being teamed up by them constantly. Even the side missions are out to get you, as you soon find they consist of you fighting against multiple enemies who just love to chain stun you ala Dark Souls. Just two bots combined can whilttle your hp in half if one relentlessly spams basic ki blasts leaving you vulnerable to the otherwise very-easily-dodgable-super-damaging special ki attacks.

Guys, this is the solution for the stuttering of the game. Go to the config file (WillowEngine.ini). Search for "bSmoothFrameRate" by press and hold Control + F, and search for it. Change "bSmoothFrameRate=True" to "bSmoothFrameRate=False" and search for "UseVsync". Change "UseVsync=False" to "UseVsync=True". It will solve the lag/stuttering issue. :)

I really like the basics of the game - solid economy system linked strongly to map control, having units behave automatically in the (mostly) best possible way allowing players to focus on strategy rather than tactics. Gamepace starts slow but increases through the game to satisfying levels.
Single Player AI is surprisingly adequate opponent.
The not so good:
The game went through a lot of balancing and people playing since the start went through a many up and downs with glitches, bugs and glaring imbalances. The balance and resource collection tend to force certain unit compositions rather than allow variation.The units in the game are mostly bland. There are dominant strategies that ideally should have good counters but presently do not. Aircraft behavior is weird - permanent flying in circle - and makes for plenty of accidents.
The Bad:
Multiplayer community is barely existing. Rarely there are more than 15 players online and queing for a match often means waiting 15 minutes for a quick, one-sided slaughter... you see, cant really implement a match-making system with so few players. Really poor solution was placing AI bots in multiplayer to "fix" that.
Whatever the positives of this game I can't stomach the total lack of effort on the developer side to increase multiplayer player pool and have mostly given up on playing.
TL:DR:
If you are looking for multiplayer experience - stay away for now.
If you are looking for single player experience - it is good, get it.

Borderlands was a very fun game that I have now completed three times. I really like looters, and this game did a great job with tons of interesting guns to use. The story is interesting but is missing something to make you care more. The side quests are mostly just tons of fetch quests that get boring quick. Occasionally there will be one fun side quest that is quite memorable, but most are just rehashed version of go there, kill this, come back.
My biggest complaint is with enemy variety. After the first 15 minutes of playing, you will see the things you will be fighting for the rest of the game. The bandits and rakks just level scale and become more challenging. If you can get past this problem and the dull "fetch" quests, this game is really fun. For an FPS, this game moves fluent and leveling is great. Multi-player is where this game shines. Those dull fetch quests and same mobs don't bother you near as much when you are playing with a friend. The boss fights are also fun, but nothing too special. You will also find the characters you meet are not very memorable. Finally money is near useless. You will get money everywhere but never really need it.
My first run through, I had no complaints. The game is often fun, but never really so compelling that you can't turn away. You will even get a few laughs out of it. I myself really liked The Zombie Island of Dr. Ned. Generally by the end of Borderlands, I had fun, but I had no urge to keep going. Here is my take away in a pro con chart.
Pros
Lots of guns with lots of effects
Tons of looting, making it worth checking around for hidden chests
Multi-player is really fun
Story line is fairly interesting
Fluid game play
Lots of little goals to accomplish (such as 1,000 SMG kills, ect.)
Good for some laughs
Cons
Very boring side quests
Almost no mob variety
Very little voiced lines, meaning you will be reading a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton.
Money is almost completly useless
All in all, this game is worth your time to play it. So if you are wondering where in the series to start, I would recommend here if you got a friend or two to run it through with. I'd give the game an 8/10.

Almost like Castlevania, but with it's set of flaws.
Pros:
1. Intersting story.
2.  It's nice if you play it for the multiplayer.
Cons (mainly when playing this game solo):
1. The customization may seem great at first, but at one point you'd realize weapon balancing is funky in different areas/boss battles, and by that point either you'd want to roll a new character or have to respec.

That may seems fine in the beginning... at one point you'd have so many items and weapons and spells that you can use it starts to look stupid. Castlevania's Symphony of the Night and later series features tons of characters action... all being performed on a game pad. Do we really need 20+ hot keys for a 2D action game?
4. So areas gets harder after you "open up the gates." It's meant to be part of the story progression, right? But some areas would get a lot more harder because all the mobs can aggro you once the gates are lifted... and they stay that way.

This is an EPIC future based mass warfare game. Starts on the principles of Total Annihilation but instead of Commander you have a command hub. You gather iron and radioactive materials and start building your army to conquer the enemy.
The maps vary in size, resources, theme and number of players although I personally love doing a 6v6 map size and only a 1v1 with me and the computer.
On skirmish mode you have many options to choose from to keep the game interesting like the ability do disable orbital abilities, or set that the air is too thin to fly aircraft. The AI is extremely intelligent but doesn't cheat like other games I find and it doesn't take the same actions every game either, changing its strategy to force you to change yours. At times I can find myself in huge fights on several points in the map, and sometimes it can be overwhelming. The strategic map modes make this easy to manage though.

You can see thousands of units you spent 45 minutes building, get ripped apart because you decided not to invest in a unit that can counter what is ripping your units to shreds. I have had 10,000 units on the field at once. And the opponent puts up a hell of a good fight. My favorite part though.... No nukes. It is so nice. I hate nukes.

EDIT: 15/01/2015
So, it's come to my attention that this review, which initially began as a joke, has become tremendously popular on the store page (huge thanks to all who voted so positively!) so I decided I should actually include something in this review to keep it helpful to newcomers or fans coming off of Borderlands 2 and The Pre-Sequel.
What is it that keeps Borderlands so good to come back to, and compulsively play on a consistent basis? If you were to ask me this question, there would be no way I would know how to respond simply. But, I can at least try to break it down.
Gameplay-wise, Borderlands has all the fundamentals of an FPS, shooting feels good and there's a wide range of guns with a unique feel to all of them (more on that later) without sacrificing movement. FPS makes up the core gameplay and how you interact with the world and NPCs in terms of combat, and it feels fantastic. However, the RPG elements are what give this game that extra depth that stops it from being 'just another' shooter. Every character has unique perks and skill trees that can be customised in different ways to alter general combat and your unique action skill. It keeps combat fresh and skills balance across characters really well. You might not see trees as unique as Zer0 or Krieg from Borderlands 2 but you can expect deep customisation nonetheless. No one character defines a playstyle, any of the four can be decked out with the according loot to keep you tanky, but the action skills and trees prevent the protagonists from feeling same-y.
Storyline wise don't expect a deep tale, or even a sweeping adventurous romp like Borderlands 2. Instead, Borderlands goes for a strong atmosphere communicated through mission structure and world design, and yet I have no complaints about this lack of story. Gearbox balanced innumerable quests with a consistent world to combine for a truly unique experience. This is a game that, thanks to an RPG quest system, lets you get out there in the game world and get lost in it doing missions for insane amounts of time but lets you stay immersed in the storyline and world at the same time.
Now, the meat of Borderlands. Let's be honest, RPGs have had shooter elements before, but, in my opinion, never has an inventory system in an RPG felt this good. Borderlands has my favourite inventory/loot system because it cuts the crap and gets right to the stuff you care about: guns, guns, guns! Don't expect to be picking up some arbitrary "Lord Generic's Gold Coin #74 with Blue Palette" to sell later. Borderlands gives you gear you use practically, and can sell for money. Expect to pick up grenade modifications, shields, class modifications which power up your skill trees even further and of course, guns.
Perhaps what keeps the loot so good in Borderlands 1 as compared to 2 and Pre-Sequel is how they function relative to your character's level. I love Borderlands 2 and Pre-Sequel, but I found myself selling guns a lot more than in BL1, because Gearbox opted for a more balanced weapon system. Borderlands 1 has a different experience to opening loot chests. You could open something and still have the same giddy eagerness as when you first opened one in your early hours with the game because genuinely powerful and versatile weapons can be found. This is due to levelling and some manufacturers having incredibly unique traits that set them far above other manufacturers. Take, for example, the fact I own a Hyperion shotgun with a level 15 requirement that I still use on my level 44 Mordecai and you get an incredible idea of what this game can offer you. Not to mention the amount of guns outnumbers Borderlands 2 by around 3 million (5 mil vs 8 mil) and this game keeps a lot to see in it. Like the other Borderlands games there's a lot to see in the way of second playthroughs, offering more quests, even better loot and more challenging enemies.
I feel as though my review barely scratches the surface even after typing all of this, but overall, I highly recommend you purchase this game if you want to get lost and spend countless hours in one of the deepest shooters I've played this past decade.

Wolfenstein : The New Order takes place in an alternate history where the Nazi Germany won WW2. You control the protagonist, B.J.Blazkowicz in the game.
The game's prologue mission is set in 1946, where B.J is part of an Allied mission to kill General Deathshead, the man responsible for the technological superiority of the Nazis. The mission fails and B.J passes into a coma and remains in that state for 14 years. He comes out of his coma in 1960 to see a world ruled by the Nazis. The rest of the game is about B.J joining the Resistance and trying to kill General Deathshead.
The game offers you a wide variety of weapons, an assault rifle(which can be upgraded with a rocket launcher later in the game), a sniper rifle(they call it marksman's rifle), a shotgun, a pistol, a knife and ofcourse the LaserKraftWerk. The assault rifle and the LaserKraftWerk feels really nice to use. Oh, you can also dual-wield any two weapons of your choice.
Generally, the game offers you two approach a level stealthily(especially where there are commanders present) or guns blazing. Both the options are equally enjoyable.
The game's story is decent, with adequate attention given to developing B.J's character, though it could have been a bit more angaging. The side characters are also good, especially the musician J. Dialogues are also a strong point of this game.
The locations you get to play in are quite diverse, ranging from a lunar base(though surprisingly there was no weightlessness inside it) to underneath the Atlantic Ocean.
The enemies you encounter are pretty varied, from ordinary soliers to mechanized hounds to huge robots and super soldiers. I found the last bossfight to be a bit too tedious, though it was enjoyable for the most part.
Now, the things I did not like about the game.
1. The lip syncing was really not there in this game(atleast with the copy I had).
2. Some of the collectibles are really hard to find.
3. Sometimes the fight gets frustrating.(Though this is not much of a major issue)
Overall, I found this game to be amazing. It is totally worth it. Looking forward to the New Colossus.
P.S : Since I played this game in offline mode, the correct gameplay time is not shown.

As for the plot, I at first assumed that this game was going to be about Deathshead the time traveller, because aesthetically this game looks like if TimeShift had bothered to do any worldbuilding. Instead, they took a different tack entirely. You know how in a lot of games, they make the Nazis be right about something that, in the real world, they were wrong about? Usually necromancy. The Jewish character is literally responsible for the rotten foundations of modern civilization, and later on tricks the hero into killing hundreds of civilians.

Many are recommending this to people who like Papers, Please.
Beholder gives you all the tools of a long term, open-ended game like Papers, Please and then fritters it away trying to create drama and tension unnecessarily. You will likely have just gotten settled into the game and the controls before realizing you've been playing it all wrong and need to restart - indeed, it is entirely possible to put yourself in an unwinnable state by buying some items and then not having enough to repair apartment 2 after you evict Jacob Manishek, the Very Obvious Tutorial Tenant. I had a perfectly good apartment 4 that I'd repaired too that I couldn't use even though all the game actually wants you to do is move in one of two new tenants.
Having learned your lesson and your way around the controls and game mechanics, you start again, get a little bit further, and are suddenly presented with two sheer cliff faces of dilemmas involving your family. This is not just a vertical wall but one that actually overhangs you by a significant distance. You need forewarning to even be prepared to deal with these in the time allotted. And then, even if you do, you are thrown a second huge curveball in one of them before the situation is resolved, almost as large as the first.
I have been reading walkthroughs trying to even figure out the first one, and when I saw the second one, I realized this simply wasn't for me. It is the difficulty spike to end all difficulty spikes. I speak as someone who played Dead Rising on the 360 a dozen times to get all the endings, items, survivors and achievements and say that this is worse. You need an absolutely perfect setup to get these things done; essentially, there is A Correct Way to play through the game and anything less will leave you feeling like you've failed or have somehow come up short. It isn't even that you failed as a player, you simply lacked a crystal ball to see exactly what was expected of you and were therefore unable to guide Carl to act with prescience, completely removing any tension or investment you would have otherwise had in the very intriguing scenario and story.
For that reason, I can't recommend the game. If it's meant to be an arty piece where you basically get everything thrown back in your face with a "ha ha, that's what living in a real dystopia would be like!" message then it succeeds. As a game where we expect to have the power to influence our own course and make a difference in the outcome based on quick thinking and skill, it fails.
With respect to Papers, Please, then: that game gave you obvious and logical clues as to what taking certain courses of action would have with respect to the storyline. Here you are suddenly thrown an unhittable curveball and told you're out if you don't somehow knock it out of the park.

This is game is an historical classic.  One only needs to know the historical games history to know this is a fact.
This game is approaching 2 decades old and has an active growing community of players. The original game was released in an era when RTS were frequently anticipated AA titles and this is one of the only games from that time period that truely stood the test of time. It has seen success over its rivals, predacessor and successors and is one of the only true contenders (along with starcraft) for greatest rts of all time. So what  makes this game so good?
Age of Empires 2 is a game that is simple goal and easy to understand mechanics, many layers of complexity. This makes it a fun game for a wide variety of skil levels. At the simplest level you have a city building RTS where you expand your town and kill an enemy. This is a common setting, but age of empires 2 really perfected it. The game features a great set of single player campaigns which you follow the tales of historical figures such as Ghengis Kahn, Atilla the Hun, Jean De Arc etc.
The game also features a mutliplayer which rewards players at every skil level. Beginning players may take their time to build cities and large armies. Advanced players learn different strategies to engage in early game skirmishes. This is a game where the more you give to the game  the more you get from the game.
Other fun elements of the game is the game has both indepth campaign editor, easy ai scripting  and allows users to view recorded games. This allows people to create their maps, study past games and really take their time to learn the game.

Giving a review of this game for me is pretty hard at this point. On one hand, it's not bad per se. It's got very nice pixel art graphics which are pretty much how Diablo II would have looked like had it been an 8-bit game. It's smooth and fast-paced and the gameplay is overall fun. Music is nice, classes are diverse and original, and enemies and items aplenty.
HOWEVER.
I really feel like Hero Siege is a textbook example of how to get the general picture right and then ruin everything by screwing up the details. The main problem the game has is: it's hard in an unfair way. It's not like Binding of Isaac, where difficulty feels like a progression. No, here you can become a powerhouse, slaughtering enemies with so much ease it gets boring - and then still die because THAT ONE enemy is able to deliver insane amounts of damage in one hit, despite it being an utter weakling under all other respects. This means you'll get stuck repeating the same levels over and over, getting more and more powerful thanks to the leveling up system, so that the 99% of the time you spend fighting manageable enemies becomes utterly uneventful - but then something happens and you still die. It's an addictive mechanism but it doesn't work because it's fun, only because it makes you come back in rage and frustration.
Another really annoying thing is how the updates work. Despite being nominally a released game, Hero Siege keeps getting major changes on a regular basis. This isn't limited to small balancing tweaks. Entire classes are nerfed or powered up. Skills are taken out, then put back in, or their effect is changed. I've leveled up a character disregarding its close-range skills only to find them transformed into ranged attacks the next update. One class had its entire appearance changed for no reason. Rules change on a daily basis sometimes - money doesn't persist after death? Well now it does. Got used to that? TOO BAD NOW IT DOESN'T AGAIN. And no matter how broken it gets, you still manage to die in stupid ways because of that one deadly bullet with one pixel wide hitbox.
The third problem is input bugs. Press a button too long, it will be taken in twice. This is especially jarring since in some instances this can lead to stuff like you losing a legendary item just because you wanted to check out an alternative on the ground (items, once discarded, are lost forever, and the button to look at the drop and to equip it is the same). There's stuff like using events that only fire when a key is pressed for a reason, people.
Overall, it's a rather unpolished game, and one that changes way too often to offer a consistent playing experience. I got it in a Humble Bundle so it wasn't a big deal, but full price, I'd seriously suggest you give this a pass and play Binding of Isaac: Rebirth instead.

On first start-up things were off to a bad start. The opening cinematic had the audio playing twice with a slight gap between, so it sounded completely chaotic. Skipping to the main menu didn't even stop it. Bugs already?  After restarting the game it didn't happen again though so perhaps it was a one-time thing?
With the settings cranked to Ultra the game is extremely beautiful with the beams, plasma shots (or whatever those are) and explosions dazzling the eye while the ships swarm in incredible numbers. The command view is neat as well as when zoomed out it shows a copy of the mini-map with units represented by simple icons and numbers indicating their strength. This can be jumped to in real-time so makes commanding large groups of units or watching the movements of the enemy a snap.
The amazing visuals took a toll however – the 1080 could keep a consistent frame-rate but it began to rev up louder than on anything else I've played yet which surprised me as even Doom 2016 on the higher settings didn't seem to tax the system so hard which I had thought to be more demanding. After a quick check online I'm not the only one who observed this and this owes to the game using high amounts of VRAM and me using DirectX 11 (as DirectX 12 provides more efficient use of system resources).
While the effects are pretty as are the units themselves, there is a black mark on this and that is in the overall design. At a quick glance it is difficult to tell units apart from each other. Coming from games like Starcraft and Command & Conquer – the units lack personality and while them sharing hull shapes and having a cohesive design is realistic it makes it aggravating to try and identify units quickly. Even the noises they make when clicked on are too similar from one unit to the next.
Any difficulty with learning to play ends there as much of what is expected from a traditional RTS is still there so it wasn't as different as I was expecting it to be. Anyone who has played an RTS game in recent years will be instantly familiar with how to control units and the camera and there is the traditional 'two' resources – metal and gas in this case with a third (quanta) providing special upgrades and unique abilities. There are only four main construction buildings and there isn't a complex tech tree to ascend.
Overall the game is fun and is awe-inspiring visually but just doesn't have the personality to make it as memorable as others in the genre. 7/10

I wanted to love this game. Played the original game jam version when it came out, and loved it. I am a big fan of difficult games, and I enjoy a bit of rage-inducing challenge and the subsequent payoff. The art and music is beautiful, and the bosses are imaginative.
However, there's something just off about the mixture in Titan Souls that keeps me from enjoying it. In a game relying on split-second decisions, your character needs to feel responsive and movement skillful. Instead, we are given a just-slightly-too-slow protagonist and a just-shy-of-tight set of feedback. I didn't come away from a successful titan kill feeling skillful, or that I had finally got it right - I felt like I finally got lucky. I had figured out what I needed to do many lives before, but was constantly frustrated that I couldn't make my character do what I was trying to make him do. I didn't overcome the boss, I overcame the controls.
The game is also extremely short given the price point. This i can forgive - the level of detail in each boss fight, and the unique aspects of each one justify an unusual development effort to game length ratio.
Most games that give me difficulty also keep me going. I want to reach the end, and the more angry I get, the more I can't wait for just one more shot. Titan Souls had those moments, but as it went on... I wasn't angry, or excited; finishing the game was an obligation, and I was just glad to be done with it.
