Unepic is quite an interesting game, it is a side-scrolling platformer, an RPG, a dungeon crawler and a riot to play with your friends!
In order for me to properly write a review for this game though, I must go over the basics; in the single player adventure campaign, you play as Daniel, an ordinary gamer who decides to play a game of Dungeons and Dragons with his friends, now what Daniel doesn't realize that he's in for the RPG of his life! But you must be wondering; What method do they use to transistion from this to that? Quite simple actually, they do it in the exact same way as the book "Narnia: The Lion, The Witch and the Wardrobe" did it, but being transported there while being in the bathroom (Okay, maybe not 1:1 like them)!
As I understand, the single player adventure is like your standard dungeon crawler meets RPG with quests and challenges. This part of the game focuses on writing alongside the gameplay as you would expect. To be completely honest, I didn't play very far into it to realize where Unepic's magic truly becomes Epic for me.
That magic I refer to is Unepic's Multiplayer.
As you would expect, this portion of the game isn't going to be really story centric like the single player campaign was made to be, this is where you play to just enjoy the sheer fun of the game that is Unepic.
Unepic's Multiplayer has to be probably be one of the most intriguing online experiences I've experienced with friends in quite some time. You can play the multiplayer with up to 3 other players, which any of you can build your characters in anyway you can imagine with the skills provided in the old school RPG level/skill-up system through as I write this up to seven dungeons of well designed deceptive hell for any newcomer to the game or the type of game Unepic is and that's only the "Unepic Maps", there are going to be more in that section and more in the Official Maps section that get made by the players themselves as well!
Mind you this game isn't exactly perfect either, it does hold some particular quirks and bugs as well, but nothing game breaking, such as in-session trading for items found in a dungeon level, meaning any items you wish to possess or trade to your allies has to be done right then and there, otherwise those items will become bound to your character.
If you're a fan of games such as Dungeons and Dragons, Baldur's Gate and Maze of Galious, then you will feel right at home with the way this game is played, provided you can handle the platforming on top of the already challenging dungeons just filled to the brim with stone blocks, boulders, fireball, spike and monster traps all waiting to turn you into a bloody pile of flesh on the floor. This game does not hold your hand by any means, you must figure out what will do what, works with what and how you can overcome the challenges up ahead, for if you don't, then the game will complete you instead in how difficult the actual boss fights can be.
Just to provide perspective to someone wishing to potentially buy this game.
I bought this game during the 2013 Steam Winter Sale and I've easily played on and off for around 70+ hours on just multiplayer alone as I've gathered friends to play the game with.
I probably should've mentioned this much sooner, but even if you complete through all the official multiplayer maps (Unepic and "Official" Official maps), you can then design your very own dungeons for you and your friends to play, maybe if you're lucky, you'll even have your masterpiece of a map turned into an official map for all to play and be ravaged by your devilish designs! There are even more ways to play the game, there are modes for Deathmatch(PVP), Capture the Flag, Survival (Not Complete yet, but imagine an endless gauntlet) and even good ol fashioned Racing.
The game truly proves in its own gameplay that it is inherently fun to the audience it's made for.
My only true complaint is that the actual online multiplayer for the singular adventurer is going to be rather held back comparably to that of someone who can bring friends along in a quiet, private session as the online multiplayer does suffer from most players sticking to their usual clicks and playing privately, leaving little room for public play as an available option.
I recommend this game for the price it runs, if you truly feel unsure even after all of what I've said, then wait until it is finished, imo the game is worth it as it is at its current content featured.

Pros:
- Shooting is satisfying as heck as you get a variety of weapons + duelwield, and you get to blow enemies' limbs off in an over-the-top fashion.

Cons:

- Characters are very forgettable, especially the antagonist - no joke, he only appears twice, at the start and at the end of the game.

Wolfenstein: The New Order differs from Return to Castle Wolfenstein. Rather than divulging more into the occult science fiction aspect of the Nazi Regime that was on display in Return to Castle Wolfenstein, the New Order explores the notion that what if the Nazis won WW2 and took over the world in an alternate 1960s. In doing this we learn about how the Nazis expanded on the advancement in their twisted technological experimentation. You again reprise the role of B.J. Blazcowvicj. Unlike in Return to Castle Wolfenstein where B.J had no personality and was just a one man army meathead. In the New Order he has a personality and a backstory. Speaking of story, The New Order does have a story/plot that is worth following. The gameplay is a balls to the wall/adrenaline rush in a totally awesome way in terms of the weapons and chaos you can ensue. This is mostly due to the amount of weapons you can use at your disposal, and for thew first time ever......dual wielding guns which takes some getting used to but totally fun. This game made me emotional in terms of how much I hated the Nazis and what they did to people and the damage they caused. I can't remember a game where I felt such an animosity to an antagonist in awhile. The New Order is a linear game that should take you 20 something hours to complete depending how fast you progress through the game and the difficulty your playing on. Overall Wolfenstein: The New Order is a great game to play not only becasue it's relatively short and keeps your attention, but also due to the story and gameplay.

So with this game, I would say I liked it overall, but I have some major gripes with a variety of the game design aspects within. My first is with its core identity. It plays like a cover shooter, but wants you to go out to collect ammunition and health whilst fighting, instead of setting up a good place to take cover and slowly advance. And if you run and gun, you often find yourself getting absolutely crushed, especially later on into the game. But not only is there that, but picking up resources manually often slows the game down, and further encourages the cover mechanics, so I still don't understand a majority of their resource placement.
Next gripe I had was with the final boss fight. I won't give away too much, except that there was a lack of information provided, which made it a nuisance to play. It was hard to spot the objectives in the fight, and hard to tell if you were progressing, and it was hard to even see anything. This is what I call cheap difficulty. Unfun difficulty. Games often give you this kind of information in a boss fight so that way it all comes down to skill. You learn what you must do quickly, adapt, and fight. But with this, there is no clear direction, which causes unneccessary confusion, and is a flaw in the overall game design.

With that aside, the other problems I had were too minor to really mention. I thoroughly enjoyed the story, the themes, the characters, the graphics, the mechanics and the emotions. Playing DOOM before this, I often found myself comparing it to DOOM. They are different in many ways, but I still feel like it falls short of DOOM's campaign in every way. The gripes I had with this game were non-existent with DOOM due to its overall design being of a higher quality. I do feel like this may be simply a difference in developer, with id being known as a company that revolutionised the games industry, and machinegames just picking up. Hopefully the sequel will iron out a lot of these issues.

Played on the free weekend and I'd have bought it then and there if I wasn't so broke. This game rather than enabling milsim roleplay, all but demands it in order to be effective. It is possible to do CQB without stupid things like magically waving barrels, but you'd have to get that close first. Odds are you get lit up at 50m by a well set enemy squad.
If you don't have buddies to bring to the table, the game has voip you can use to coordinate with squadmates. So don't worry about not having coordination unless you're the one staying quiet!

Normally I am not inclined to recommend shootemups - it's an old tired genre, there's little to no value in rehashing it.
However, the developers of Galak-Z put in an extraordinary amount of work to make the genre breathe again (in an iron lung kind of way).
Gameplay isn't anything special, unfortunately, but if you're going to play a ripoff of Space War from the 1960's, this is arguably the best rendition we're likely to ever see.
3D assets, wide support for controllers and M+KB, modest storyline, and specifically effort to make the game not only work in 4K, but look good at contempory resolutions - the game carries the hallmarks of high quality.
If you must play a shootemup, this is the one.

All my thoughts and feelings about this game summed up into one sentence:
If you are looking for a modern RTS that has a traditional feel to it and countless hours of fun to be had with nice graphics and huge armies, there isn't a better choice on the market right now than Ashes of the Singularity: Escalation.
A couple things to note:
- If you have an epic graphics card/processor and a good cooling setup and you are already thinking about getting this game, get it!
- If you are wondering if this game will run on a budget PC or something that can't really be considered a "high end gaming PC" you probably won't be able to run it at max settings, especially in bigger battles. However if you plan on getting a high end gaming PC in the future having Ashes of the Singularity: Escalation in your library isn't a bad idea.
For clarification, when I first started playing this game I had 2 way SLI with 2x GTX 970's. They would get pretty hot when I tried playing with high settings, like over 80C and only stayed at 80C or lower after I toned down some of the settings. After switching to a single GTX 1080ti my graphics card never goes above 65C, even with DirectX 12 and maxed out settings. While I know the maximum temperature for the 970's is 98C and for the 1080ti its 90c, the 1080ti was much farther from it's maximum temperature than the 970's were.
Basically other than the things I mentioned, this game is awesome and a lot of fun, especially to me as someone who enjoyed a lot of other, older RTS games.

This game kind of had a rough launch, mostly due to lack of content, but has come a long way with numerous free DLC releases.
Strengths:
-Even at massive scales (larger even than SupCom:Forged Alliance), I haven't generally noticed significant performance degradation. One of the best optimized RTS's around.
-Good skirmish AI, which is competitive against causal players without needing to cheat. Furthermore, it doesn't fall off late game so much,  where as most RTS's have AI's that are good at rushing and that's about it.
-At this point there are fairly broad and interesting unit rosters, although it still lags behind SupCom in this regard.
-Devs appear to be interested in implementing full modding support. At this point this is limited to maps scenarios.
Weaknesses:
-Somewhat buggy still, but I've encountered few game breaking bugs or crashes.
-No naval units or water terrain
-I'm not a big fan of the implementation of the orbital abilities. The devs have moved in the right direction with rebalancing these since the game was originally released, however.
Overall, it's a great game for those who like large scale RTS's in the vein of SupCom, and doesn't come with SupCom's terrible AI and lack of optimization.

EDITING THIS REVIEW Now that I've had plenty of experience with the game, I can give a full on review.
The Good
-Custom characters! In a game worth playing! DBZ fans can rejoice because it's finally happened and you aren't really restricted on your character. You can choose between 5 different races for your character, each with it's ups and downs. The personalization options feel just enough so you'll be happy with your dude but you'd wish there was a bit more stuff to choose from. In addition, you can build your characters skills. Not gonna lie you start out with some pretty bad skills other than the melee rush one, but after playing for a bit you'll get some decent moves and you'll have a blast Kamehameha'ing Raspberries and Appules all day erry day. There's also a fair bit of clothing that you can get and really customize your person, but there's problems with this that ill talk about in a bit.
-Simple yet fun combat mechanics. This game's not a button masher and if you play it as such you'll get rekt'd. You have to learn to combo with not only your basic and heavy attacks but your supers. Dodging is a huge part of the game and you'll have to rely on it on the tougher bosses (at least so far against Frieza, he was a pain in the butt to deal with). While you won't get the satisfaction of memorizing huge input combos, there's just enough so that you'll feel yourself get better the more you play it.
-Graphics are great in this game. I'd argue this is the best looking DBZ game yet (Just barely above Raging Blast 2 for me) because of the true to the anime cutscenes and beautiful animations. It's also low end friendly apparently because I'm pretty sure, but not entirely sure that my video card is below the minimal reccomendations and I still get 60 fps on max settings, so that's a plus for people who don't have a 1000 dolla mega pc that they can have a nice looking next gen game that'll run good. Also, THOSE ANIME CUTSCENES.
-The DBZ game series has finally produced a game with an original plot! Instead of it just being a loose version of the regular anime or it being word for word you take the role of a Time Patrol person who has to go fix goofs in the timeline of the universe before everything goes to crap. Unforunately, early on you're introduced to Blue skinned jessica rabbit and totes not Android 16 smurf edition, and it's up to you to stop these cretins from trashing the universe of our favorite anime! If you're a long time player of DBZ games like myself you might have liked the 'What-if' scenarios that were present in some of the games, and that's basically the whole game here, and it's a really nice cherry on top to a decent game.
-The sound design here is pretty great. The music is pretty good and the sound effects here are really pronounced and gutteral, and this combines with the awesome visuals to make a really authentic DBZ Experience. The voice acting has lip syncing issues occasionally and the voices are occasionally a bit too hammy, but it's what you'd expect from DBZ, so there's not alot wrong to love.
-Game is hard. Not often unfair, it feels like a game from your childhood that understood a good strong enemy vs an unfair one. IT's satisfying to beat a level you've been struggling against and it rewards you for learning your race's combos rather than blind button mashing, or running away and spamming ki blasts at people. I feel like this is a game from the ps2 era of games in terms of difficulty but aged way better and feels more modern, it's weird but totally something I'm behind.
THE BAD
-The roster is a bit strange. No android 16, uub or majinn vegeta but we get freaking RASPBERRY AND APPULE? And the complete lack of movie characters besides Broly and the two Gods feels a bit bizarre but it makes sense since they were trying to remain in the series established canon. Regardless, this is really excusable because of the custom characters and the game's emphasis on playing as them regardless.
-Sometimes the game feels incredibly unfair in certain places and the missions can sometimes be a repetitive and boring. When you go into the side quests you have no idea if the mission you're about to play is going to be a really fun one or a dull, boring and stupidly hard mission. The Story mode is unforunately the worst offender with the infamous Beerus vs Whis fight, but the secret saga kicks that up a notch, and although you are not required to play through it you most likely will to unlock all the characters and parallel quests.
-No way to see how a piece of clothing will look on your character. What the hell? I know this is a problem in alot of games but money while easy to obtain and plentiful usually means you have to go spend 10-15 minutes in a mission getting it, so wasting money on a fugly piece of clothing is always a bummer. Not a problem for the iconic stuff like the goku gi's, the saiyan armor or the scouters but everything else can be a pain to figure out.
-Planned DLC. This doesn't bother me as much as some people might be bothered, but it still feels uncessesary. Dimps if you're going to throw pan and kid goku from GT at us to be released just a month later, why not have them in the game now? While the game has alot of content in it right now unlike a game like Destiny, I still don't think it's kosher to wave your DLC around like that while the roster is missing a few key characters as it is.
Verdict:
This is a really awesome DBZ game and a pretty good game as a whole. If you want a good PC fighter this may be it, but it plays more like an action mmo than a traditional fighter. So if you want to try something a bit out of the box go ahead and you won't be dissapointed, but if you're a DBZ fan there's no reason to miss out on this game. It's really Budokai 3/Legacy of Goku 2 levels of good!

游戏界最近似乎起了一股反乌托帮的热朝，这游戏也是这股热潮中的一款，也是以我们的先知奥威尔笔下小说1984为制作原型的游戏。
小说中，人们生活在一个独裁统治的世界，所有人都受到政府的严密监视和控制，而在游戏中我们则是扮演政府手下的一名间碟，去监视人们的一举一动。游玩的方式相当有创意，公寓管理加上监视，不过着眼点还是在监视上，在经营公寓上做了很大的简化，我们只用把人找过来住即可，还有就是偶尔修修坏掉的家具。
游戏一开始，是要我们去监视房客并把得数据卖给情报局。不过游戏并没有强制我们去完成这些，所以我们也可以帮房客做点任务，或去反抗政府，全凭个人选择，因为任务都是可选和限时，完没完成，都会带来不一样的结局。
每个人都想当好人，可是现实并不允许。我们伸张正义，然后等着筹不出家里的生活费，儿子的学费。甚至女儿的医药费。不如率性一点，当个坏人，偷窃，倒卖，插赃，勒索等等。去骗那些相信我们的朋友，为的也只是可以多活一年。
看似自由，其实体验到更多的，是身不由己。是人在国家机器前的无力感。
制作组将我们置身于一个人吃人的环境下，让我们去做出选择，去重新思考道德与人性，这一点相当成功。
为了让我们融入游戏当中，游戏极力塑造出阴暗压抑而且充满黑色恐怖的世界，游戏画面一片灰和黑，人物也只用简单的黑白基本线条来刻画，符号化的人物形像，给人一种不信任感，这种演出效果相当出色。在发生重大事件时，还会有专门的CG动画过渡，完全超乎预期，真的感受到制作组在这方面的用心。
值得称赞的还有游戏的中文配音和中文翻译，不过这个翻译相当粗糙，基本是机翻的水平，这方面制作组也保证会有后续更新去改善。但就诚意来看，首发中文是绝对大赞。
要咎病的是糟糕的任务引导，到后期发生多线剧情时，人物数量多，任务又复杂，很多任务容易做到一半，找不关键道具，卡着完成不了。
而另外一点就是游戏一开始的摄像头，本还期待它的发挥，结果在完成新手任务后，再也没有实际作用，基本就是个摆设。
当然游戏本身的质量还是相当不错，作为独立游戏，完成度也十分高，游戏内容札实题材新颖，趁着打折，机不可失，各位赶紧+1吧。

Fun and Easy to get into for anyone who knows the basics of a fighting game.
I'll be sinking a lot of time into this one...
However, there are a lot of pros and cons:
The Good:
- Combat system is fun and easy to learn.
- No complicated combo strings that require 15+ button presses.
- No Directional inputs.
- Silly, wacky storyline that fits the DBZ universe perfectly.
- Diverse array of skills, stat choices and gear.
The Bad:
- Currently the servers are god awful. If you can even log in, you'll be kicked after doing a few missions.
- Convoluded stats. No explanation for what any stat does, and the only way to redo your stats is by gathering the Dragon Balls, which can take 2-5 hours to farm all 7 of (Because RNG is amazing).
- RNG. All I really need to say here. It ruins games.
- While there ARE a lot of moves, most of them don't scale linearly with your damage stat, so you'll find yourself using a much smaller pool of abilities for maximum damage.
- AIs are wonky. Your allies as AIs are borderline braindamaged, even in the storyline, and your enemies spam evasive/recovery moves like crack addicts. The only big challenge is actually landing a combo on an enemy AI.
- Unflinchable boss fights. In a fighting game about combos and locking down an enemy, it completely defeats the purpose to add enemies that cannot be flinched in an easy way. Not only do enemies become bullet sponges, but they become unflinchable and a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to solo unless you abuse Z-Souls or items, BOTH of which form bad habits.
The Ugly:
- PvP is a mess of hackers, abusive Z-Souls and glitch exploits. I'm staying clear of this until they fix it. Like, to give you an accurate image of how BAD the hacking is right now: 1 in  3 players you meet will be a hacker in PvP. Unlimited energy. Unlimited Stamina. Unlimited Health. Because who buys a game to NOT HACK, am I right?
- The final boss in the storyline is such a huge letdown of a fight. Instead of adding meaningful or cool mechanics, they simply made him a huge, unflinchable waste of time.
10/10 GOTY

Admittedly an oddball in my Steam game library - one filled with gory shooters, slaughterfests, and other such M-rated material. Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is like the stray hippie amongst a population consisting of shizophrenic sociopaths! If you don't like long reviews, just skip to the last paragraph, where I summarize everything!
I quite honestly don't remember just how exactly this game ended up in my library, but I recently decided to play it anyway.  Because while I may have many games I still need to play out of my library, I've been desiring a decent racing game for quite some time. Did I expect this game to actually fulfill that desire by being anything close to what could be considered a quality racing game that brought me some great amount of entertainment? Honestly, no, I did not.
But alas, I was surprised! What I expected to be nothing more than a dumbed down racing experience with unbalanced items and cheesy banter between characters that would make me want to turn this into one of those M-rated shooters I own so that I may claim unsavory vengeance upon them for their horrible forced personalities, turned out to actually be one of the few good racing games I've seen on Steam!
How is it good? Well, allow me to explain! Wait... Oh, right, that's what reviews are about... Um... Moving on!
From the screenshots, and the involvement of Sonic and co, in a bright and cheerful-looking environment, one may be brought to the understandable conclusion that this game would only be enjoyable if you were young, or the stereotypical "hardcore" 50-year old Sonic Fan with no friends, who yells "You're too slow!" at every car he drives by on his way to his minimum wage job at the local McDonald's. You would be wrong.
Amazingly enough, this game is actually enjoyable regardless of age, and you really don't have to be a fan of Sonic at all to enjoy the gameplay. I'd recommend this game regardless of the age of the player, as it's obviously safe for young kids to play, but definitely offers an enjoyable experience for older players as well (For reference, I'm almost 19).
Is it for the "filthy casuals"? No, not at all! While a casual could definitely get into the game on the lower difficulties that take nearly no skill whatsoever, a pro gamer could easily find a good challenge on the hard, and expert difficulties!
My only complaint would be how few tracks there are. A total of 16 new tracks, with an additional 4 classic tracks, plus mirrored versions of all the tracks, and +1 new track with a mirrored version if you get the DLC. Thankfully, the game offers a variety of modes to make this small number of tracks less bothersome. Nonetheless, it is a small amount, and new DLCs with additional tracks are unlikely.
Speaking of the DLC, it's not bad, but I certainly wish it offered more than just one single new track. A full circuit of four new tracks would certainly be more appealing. The DLC track isn't really worth it in all honesty, since it's not nearly as interesting as the tracks originally in the game, and there's also a few bugs in it that can be accidentally triggered from time to time (nothing too frequent, so don't worry). Buy it if you
want a new character, and desperately want an extra track. Otherwise, skip it.
So, in summary, a great game for all ages (children or adults), and offers a challenge for both casuals and hardcore gamers, providing a small number of tracks, but a fair number of characters, and overall one of the few
racing games on Steam right now.

There are usually only a couple games a year that I get extremely excited about - the last being the Binding of Isaac: Rebirth - and Titan Souls was the first game this year I needed to play. After my first playthrough of the game, I can tell you that getting that final titan kill was one of the most exhilarating feelings I've ever experienced. Just working out the patterns and  mechanics of each battle is engaging enough, but the ultimate reward and satisfaction of finally taking down the beast you've been dissecting for the last half an hour is a feeling like nothing else. I'm sure you know by now if Titan Souls is your type of game or not: challenging, analytical, and precise. It is not for everyone; this game weeds out the impotent and incompetent. But, if you're a masochist with an eye for reconnoitering, I promise you will enjoy every little bit  of this game.

I dislike this game more, rather than less, after seeing more bosses.
In addition to the notes below, I'll add the following.
Boss fights feel like games of random chance far too often. The underwater worm boss, the ice guy with the teeth, the mushroom boss, etc, etc. Hitting them is way more about lucky timing than skill.
Where's the epicness in this game? Run around like a mad man, avoiding pretty obvious obstacles, then try to stand in the perfect spot while powering up your arrow. It's just not all that engaging.
Some bosses are just annoying. Hitting the Yeti is frustrating. I landed many strikes that should have been hits but just bounce off. While other bosses seem too easy to hit. What gives?
Yes, there are some puzzles, but man they are really weak. The reentrant maze for the mushroom forest guys, lighting the fires, very very light weight.
As a thot exercise, imagine Mega Man with no jumping, just a dash move, one bullet and one hit bosses, nothing else. But, with loads of running, and running, and running. Would that be fun? I really don't think so.
At first blush it seems like an interesting idea, but upon further reflection it just isn't.
The whole concept is just too darn minimal. That adrenaline rush I normally feel when fighting a boss in say Dark Souls, Mario, Zelda, Metroid, Ninja Gaiden, etc., just isn't there, and the satifaction I normally feel when defeating a boss isn't there either. I have yet to feel like I really figured out a boss, because their mechanics are so darn obvious I know how to defeat them in the first few seconds (there's nothing to figure out). Forcing the player to run around isn't epic, it's frustrating. The depth of the gameplay is far too shallow to ever be more engaging than a long drawn out checklist.
Sorry, still a big thumbs down for me.
5/10 (for the graphics, score and atmoshphere)
(Killed the first 4 bosses, about 20 mins in. Decided to leave some early impressions.)
Titan Souls is a very interesting thought exercise. What if an adventure game just had bosses? Big world to run around, lots of stuff to look at, but nothing else in the way of challenging adventure style gameplay. No enemies, no items, no locked "doors" that need a certain "key". Just bosses. Interesting yes, but is it actually enjoyable?
Overall the game is well crafted, great score, sound fx, animations, art style, and I don't mind the controls (some people seem to hate them).
What I can't seem to get over is just how much better this would have been if there were challenges along the way to the bosses. The world is just screaming for little puzzles, things I can collect, enemies to overcome. The adventure to the boss, I've come to realize, actually makes the boss fight better. It’s not just a fight with a monster, it's the final crescendo after all your hard work. A chance to show off your skills by having them pushed to the max by a worthy opponent.
This "missed opportunity" is so palpable that it's actually distracting me (really really distracting me) from enjoying the  game. When I climb down a vine into a pool of water, I want to feel smart for noticing that you can climb on vines. Maybe I get an item that opens up new gameplay possibilities, or some kind of upgrade for my hero, or I get to face off against a rare mini boss, or the game tells me why the heck these Titans are here. Something, anything, to feel like exploration is something more that a gigantic ball of catnip.
Instead of making me feel smart and engaged, the game feels like one big tease. It's as if I'm running around Disney land, but only a few rides are working, there's no Mickey, no Goofy, nothing, the entire bloody park is absolutely deserted. Sure fighting a boss is kind of fun, but afterwards I have to go back to deserted-Disney only to be teased yet again by places  I want to explore (but known there isn’t a point), places I’d love to encounter a puzzle (but soon realize I never will), places I’d love to battle some enemies (but come to the crushing realization that they’re all on strike, or eaten by titans, or sick, or who the heck knows).
Clearly the game is inspired by Shadow of the Colossus. I think SotC got away with the “boss only” model because (1) it was stunningly presented, (2) it was extremely novel for its time, and (3) the bosses felt alive in addition to effectively being a big level with unique challenges, puzzles to figure out, multiple weakness points, etc.
The hyper minimalism of TS has just been pushed too far. It’s just too bloody empty!
I knew going in that it was all about bosses, and although they are fairly challenging, they're just not enough to carry an entire game. In order to "just have bosses" they need to be of the same class as say a Punch-out! opponent. Super rich mechanics, tons of personality, lots of different ways to defeat them. The bosses in TS don't even come close to that bar. They’re extremely flat, - a gimicky mechanic wrapped in some decent pixels. You don't get carried away by them, deeply want to beat them, they don't taunt or mock you, or drive you to be faster, smarter, better. It’s sad, but they actually feel more like items on your todo list, then the Titans they're supposed to embody.
For $15 dollars, with very minimal production values, that just not good enough.
I'll probably give it another go, and update this review after taking down a few more "Titans", but for now I leave feeling let down, and actually kind of ripped off :|.

I do recommend Galak-Z, but it is brutally difficult.
Positives:
The art and snippets of story are good, and the characters and enemies say some fun lines (though there's a limited number, so you Will rehear them multiple times)
It is satisfying to pilot your ship/mech: Throwing asteroids into groups of enemies, and filling tight corridors with your laser and missile fire. It is also fun to find upgrades for your ship and collect salvage to buy more.
The core gameplay is great, but the larger systems surrounding it can be frustrating.
Negatives:
To make the game more "rogue-like", dying means losing all progress on the current level, including all the money and upgrades you collected. Losing progress is never fun, but death can sometimes feel unfair when a while into the game, sword-wielding mechs appear that can easily just shrug off your damage and chase you down for the kill. Spending so long and getting so close to the end of a mission just to die and be forced to restart several times can be really irritating.
The tough penalty for defeat wouldn't be so bad if the game was wholeheartedly training players to improve their gunplay and mobility in combat, but instead it almost always provides a much faster and easier way out. Rather than overcome tough encounters the game usually encourages players to just find and exploit "cheese" tactics to get through. When blind shooting from off-screen, running
far away spamming shots at whatever is following, or just skipping a tough encounter entirely, is rewarded so much more than overcoming it the traditional way, players dig a hole for themselves later when they can't skip a fight and they get abused by the hefty defeat penalty.
The progression system is another controversial topic. Upgrading your ship is crucial to the game, but after every set of ~5 levels the story will continue but all of your upgrades are taken away. The progression system feels a lot less deep when half the time you're just re-earning the upgrades you had not long ago.
(At first I was really annoyed, but after playing Galak-Z over many separate playsessions this stopped being a big deal, I just worried about my current set of upgrades and getting more, not dwelling on what I had lost)
The last critique I have from my experience with Galak-Z is its underdeveloped (or at least under-explained) stealth system.
You can see the "field of vision" cones for nearby enemies, and a glowing aura around your ship to represent the distance away you can be detected. Yet I still didn’t feel like stealth was a very viable option. Enemies seemed to notice me randomly on occasion, and most mission finale areas aren't large enough to provide stealthy options. I'd also love to see some ship upgrades related to stealth, but I don't think there are any.
Overall:
Galak-Z has a lot of room for improvement, but it is still a very fun spaceship shooting, action game. The exploration and upgrading is fun, the combat is intense (because you really don't want to die
haha.) And if you have patience and like skillful games, Galak-Z can be very satisfying.

Basically it's "Total Annihilation". If you never played that old school RTS, it's a game of scale. Big scale. Not the crazy scale the newer Planetary Annihilation tries to encompass, but it also doesn't feel as trite or as over whelming as PA. Graphics are ok, even on max though there's nothing particularlly impressive visually other than how many on screen units you can get. Everything is old school, resource node grabbing, resource management, upgrading units and creating armies of varied units to be able to manage and combat other armies. To some people it must seem very tactical, to me it seems very simple and a battle of mix n match numbers. Build a bunch of meat shields, a good amount of basic range units and then try to cram in as many special elite heavy units as you can based on your current oppositions weaknesses (I.e- Do you want units that are strong against armies with many units, air units or heavy elite units?) And then right clic to watch the fire works. You can build structures to add in some 'commander' style abilities like radar scan, the good ol' orbital strike and even a 'plasma storm'. They're basically 'ace in the hole' abilities that can soften an enemy before your primary forces arrive on site. The basic concept is each resource node gives you either Metal or Radioactive materials, you want to always be building, either structures or units, the goal is to manage your usage of your resources to be just below your income of them at all times. It's pretty decent, fun to play, though the voice acting for the campaign is just painful. Within the first 10 minutes the term "Something else" was used to refer to the unknown enemy 'we' were facing probably 10 times, talk about forced mystery. Also, and this is a personal thing, Total Annihilation offered structural weapons like the 'Big Bertha' long range artillery. It wasn't a mobile unit, you simply built it like a building and it lobbed high powered rounds an absurd distance. Things like that seem to be missing, I say seem because no, I didn't dump a lot of time into this and it's possible that later in the game such a thing comes around. However, I've done this all before. It is that similar to Total Annihilation for me. It's worth a play, depending on how big of an RTS fan you are. However, my personal preference is Dawn of War 2 (NOT 3), that is spectacular and in my opinion far better of a RTS. I got this from Humble Bundle myself, so I'm not sure what it retails for normally. If you are a big RTS fan, I'd say it's worth between $15~$20. If you aren't such a big fan maybe wait for it to drop to around $10.

I wish I could recommend this game. The gameplay is tight, the style, graphics and theme are an absolute treat. However, this game fails on a fundamental level by doing several incredibly big taboos.
First: This game doesn't have an ending. That's right, it just...stops. The developer's stated reason is that they saw only a few hundred players reached the end of the latest released "season" so they stopped and didn't make a final ending to the game. Cool.
Second: The game is divided into 5 "seasons" which basically boils down to 5  "randomly" generated missions (always one of two map types recycled to be slightly different) with one of them being a bit more scripted, like finding an npc or w/e with a boss encounter (usually a slightly buffed normal big baddie). But the kicker that makes this infuriating is that you LOSE ALL YOUR PROGRESS WHEN REACHING THE NEXT SEASON.
These two things alone made me stop playing. The gameplay, looks and theme are great, but that's not enough if you're going to make the game punishingly hard, and then on top of that, arbitrarily take away everything I earned (which is also random, not guaranteed you'll earn the upgrades you like) and then the cherry on the cake of "hey, the game doesn't have an ending...cuz...reasons".
No way, no thanks. Such a shame, I REALLY wanted to like this game. Maybe the devs will learn lessons from this game, I hope they will anyway. The game is trying to hard to be two different things at once.
It wants to be hardcore roguelike, but doesn't have the enemy, environment or gameplay variety to justify that.
It also wants to be this dynamic story experience with full voice acting (which is pretty great) but then doesn't actually give you any story beats and doesn't even FINISH THE ****** GAME. ffs
I wish the devs luck and hope the next game doesn't have these same problems and mistakes, so I would suggest getting this game if you REALLY love space shooters/anime/mecha but only when it's on sale.

Large scale RTS gameplay especially suited for those that don't enjoy APM focused strategy games. Unit variety can be seen as lacking compared to its direct Peers, such as Total Annihilation and Supreme Commander, but it's it's well enough for engaging counterplays and variety between matches. Battles on large maps can get
massive (without much of a slowdown if you bring the hardware) with multi-frontal engagements between several large armies but quick 1v1 matches of 15-30 minutes are just as doable. The map pool is of decent size covering from 1v1 all they way up to 16 players. The first campaign (there are three at the time of this writing) is perfectly functional while unremarkable.
What really drives me to recommend this title, though, is the very active (and
) developer. Regular updates, providing user-feedback-driven balancing, bugfix and QoL improvements, are the norm. The average unit variety mentioned earlier is already better than at release with new units filling in certain tactical holes and a completely new end-game focused "experimental" unit type has recently been added for both factions. I've been involved as a player in this project since before it was alpha. Buying in at that point and buying other copies for my kids and friends as the game matured.
I have really enjoyed my time with Escalation, and while I didn't mind Ashes and Escalation turning into separate projects, I also don't mind them being combined. The RTS community needed the next big thing since SupCom, and while folks want modern SupCom, it isn't happening.
But what AotS Escalation does offer is a fresh look on an old genre, with a new engine capable of excellent graphics, scope, features, support, core usage, graphics technology support, etc. It is clear that a lot of work has gone into the Oxide engine, and I want to give all parties major props for continuing to push this engine. Sure lower spec PC's will struggle, consider this the Crysis of RTS games for 2016/17 and beyond. We NEED games like this to push hardware and drivers harder, so that technology can improve meaningfully. This game accomplishes that beyond the built-in benchmark.
Onto the strategy aspect, I appreciate the constant tuning and adjustments based on community feedback. I appreciate the constant communiation with the community that StarDock has maintained throughout the development of AotS, and I feel that has done them a lot of favors, and provided good and bad feedback they needed to read and hear. To me it seems clear they're listening and working hard to make Ashes amazing, I feel it has been great for a long time now...1.3 in original Ashes of the Singularity was where things really improved IMHO. The game pace was increased, the effects and graphics were improved as was performance.
Is this game for everyone? NO, but I'd wager to say most RTS gamers would enjoy it, even those that didn't like the originally released Ashes a year ago. I will suggest any RTS fans play it. If you're looking for sci-fi, hover tanks, lasers, great graphics, and large scope...this game has it in spades. If you have a beefy system, you can really take advantage with what the game has to offer with effects and visuals. It is simply the best looking RTS I've ever played.
The AI kicks♥♥♥♥♥ or at least kicks my♥♥♥♥♥all the time...and I enjoy playing against it, whether solo or with my kids. We have a lot of fun and it keeps us on our toes. The recently added units are a bonus and Brad's statement to keep developing the game, adding more campaigns (there are several already!), maps, units (water units and maps), more DLC, and also making the game a "modding platform" are all excellent news.
Brad himself said that he wants Ashes to be a modding platform with Steam Workshop support as well, so that folks can mod the game any way they see fit, be it a huge mod, total conversion, small mod, texture pack, etc. He even suggested that folks might go as-far-as to create their own versions of a modern SupCom, Total Annihilation, Sins of a Solar Empire, etc. as mods to Ashes. The fact they're supporting and working towards that goal should put other developers on notice, this is the kind of support we SHOULD see for other large games.
Considering StarDock has released patches for GalCiv 2 (not 3 mind you) recently and more recently the 5-year old Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion (to 1.9) means long-term support is excellent here...industry leading I would have to say for the kind of games SD is developing or involved in. I still play GalCiv and SoaSE, and am very happy with those as well and have plenty of hours into all of the games mentioned here.
In the end, I feel the current Ashes experience is worth full price, let alone the frequent sale prices you can get it for. My kids are able to play it at 1080P on medium/high settings with no AA using an i3-4160, 8GB DDR3, and a GTX750Ti 2G or GTX 1050 2G and achieve great visual results and smooth gaming. I can go beyond that to Extreme on my main rig, i7-4790K OC'd, 16GB DDR3 2400, GTX980Ti 6G.
Yes the game is a beast, yes it responds better to more GPU, CPU and memory horsepower. It should, it is 2017 and we need to be pushing the envelope. Having a core neutral game engine is a huge plus for keeping the game going strong well into the future.
I have played mostly single player, between skirmishes and campaigns and have greatly enjoyed it. StarDock did do a subpar job on the first released campaign before Escalation was released, but they've not only redeemed themselves but also added more campaigns, remastered original campaigns and release new content on an almost monthly basis some free, some DLC. It all seems priced fair and I have had no issues buying multiple copies as gifts to introduce folks to. Some have laughed this game off as nothing but a DX12 benchmark, well get ready to add Vulkan to that, Linux support too...and I invite you to come back and try Escalations today, it is a lotta fun to play and watch.
The large battles in this game with all the effects is still awe inspiring. The lighting, shading, angles, smoothness, AI control, unit coordination, and just pure action is so fun to watch that I care less about individual unit micromanagement than I thought I would. Frankly I like the army system they have here, it works well, and makes the meta unit approach a smooth operation that is easily managed. Changing to WASD panning also makes things nice for usability, as I never use keyboard shortcuts for build orders.
I gotta say this game has worked hard to earn its 9/10, and overall the experience has been very good, there's been some bad too. More in the EA and just past release than now. This past year has been just amazing with so much improvements and promise that one cannot help but be excited and entertained. I have to say that I believe I've gotten every penny's worth out of this investment and its still got such a ways to go and so much happening in the future, that the party's just begun really. StarDock is excellent, and Ashes of the Singularity: Escalation is equally excellent.
If you're an RTS fan, you owe it to yourself to have this game in your library! There's SOOOOOOOO much more here than a benchmark, and as Escalation matures it is only getting better and better and really it started off quite good. Good job StarDock! Thanks for your support and thanks for making this excellent RTS. We needed a large scope RTS to replace the aching hole of SupComFA being so old, single threaded, limited and tired. Don't get me wrong, SupCom is badass, I still play SupCom FA and SupCom2 (with my sons), but my go-to RTS is and has been AotS Escalation for quite some time now and that doesn't appear to be changing anytime soon.
Check it out and see what all the fuss is about, if you don't like it refund! I bet you'll like it. :)
If I were stuck on a deserted island with one RTS game, it would be this. Trust me I had to fight with considering Tiberian Sun, Tiberian Dawn, Red Alert, TA, StarCraft 1 + Brood Wars, Dawn of War 1, and SupCom/FA. In the end, Ashes wins where many of those classics now lose. Modern graphics and performance due to scalability, future mod-ability could lead it to compete more against FA Forever, PA Titans, StarCraft 2, etc.
If you're an RTS fan, BUY THIS NOW! Thank me later!

One time I played a demo of the first Age of Empires while staying the night at a friend's house. I stayed up all night on the Syracuse scenario. It was really bad because that was all I wanted to do when I would go over there. So I decided to ask my parents for a real copy of the game for my birthday. I told them very carefully: "Age of Empires. It's a game where you build stuff from the Stone Age to the Iron Age."
My birthday came around and I they got me Age of Empires II. I didn't really understand sequels back then so I was perplexed and wondered if it was the same game as I couldn't recall any kings, vikings or samurais in what I had played. Then I installed it and sure enough it was the wrong game. I was very sad, but I wanted to be polite to my parents.
But then I played it. The pathing was much better, the villagers didn't get stuck on rocks and trees, the civilizations were much more different from one another with unique units, castles, cannons, and knights! Then I played and played and played and played. It was the best mistake my parents ever made, besides making me of course. :)

As with all Telltale games, you don't necessarily play a "game" so much as watch a movie and add your own input every now and again. It's a refreshing pace from the typical fast and loose action or FPS games of late and really allows you to get into the Borderlands lore with an entirely new story. Except in this story all of the important choices are left up to you and you might not always have enough time to make an important decision. Oh, and there's quicktime events too. Some of which may end up leaving you dead if you fail.
The graphics are very nice and play quite smoothly on my old Macbook Pro. Even though it says my particular graphics card isn't recommended (Intel HD 3000), the game looks great and plays smooth with only a few barely noticeable stutters. I'm able to play it nicely with the graphics on High and the resolution set to 800x600 though I also tested it any my native 1280x800 and it looked just as good that way too. As with all Borderlands games, the graphics are in the typical cell-shaded, comic book style of the main series and with the slower pace, the style really shines, giving characters a charming yet gritty quality that is somewhat lost in the rough and tumble of the main series games such as Borderlands 2 and Pre-Sequel.
The music is top-notch as well, featuring a catchy opening song ("Busy Earnin'" by Jungle) that makes you feel right at home on Pandora once more. In this game you don't get to play as a Vault Hunter. Instead you play through two paralell stories as Rhys, the Hyperion worker and Fiona, the con-artist. By playing through both sides of the same story, you get to make unique choices that affect the overall narrative... and end up meeting a very familiar face or two along the way. I won't spoil who you get to meet for those who have yet to play... but it will certaintly incite some fangirling (or fanboying as the case may be).
What makes this game different from the other Telltale works is that you are given a bit more freedom to move about and explore. There are portions in which you can walk around and interact with various people and objects in the environment but the twist involves Rhys and his ECHOEye implant. With this you can scan certain items and people in the game, revealing little tidbits of Pandoran lore and the like. It's an added touch that immerses you further into the world of the game (and if you interact with a certain someone enough, the scanning changes accordingly - with often hilarious results!). When you aren't walking or interacting with the characters/environment, you are able to sit back and watch the story unfold, while also making dialogue choices which affect the narrative as the game goes on. Some choices are better than others.
However there are a few negatives to point out. One is the small window of time to make dialogue choices. You are given a mere few seconds to choose your dialogue from a list of 3-4 options and sometimes can end up clicking the wrong thing in your haste to pick the dialogue of choice. It would have been nice to have a bit more time to ruminate over choices. The other is the noticeable lag in places, particularly during intense fight scenes or during character movements on ocassion. It isn't enough to totally disrupt gameplay, but its there. Other than those two things, there really isn't much else wrong about the game.
So, would I recommend this game despite the minor issues? You bet I would, kiddo. Tales from the Borderlands is more than a worthy entry into the series and I cannot wait to play more. The story, the memorable characters, and the thrill of returning to Pandora once more makes this Telltale's best game series yet and acts as a great way to pass the time until the eventual release of Borderlands 3.

UnEpic starts with you sitting with some friends playing some D&D, when you announce that you need to use the restroom.  While in the bathroom, the lights go out, and upon lighting your lighter, you find yourself in a dark castle corridor.  Thus is the setting of UnEpic's story;  an ongoing question of whether this is all going on in your character's head (he assume's his friends slipped drugs in his beer) or if you've actually been teleported somewhere else.  How that story resolves, however, shall likely remain a mystery to this writer, as sadly, UnEpic is exactly that.
The gameplay uses the tried-and-true "Metroidvania" formula to present you with a side-scrolling Action/RPG where you can choose to be any number of character "classes" by way of which weapons, armor and spells you prefer to upgrade; though if you chose anything other than a potion-making Warrior with only a slight dabbling of magic, you chose poorly and will likely have a very hard game ahead of you.  And thus enters the very first problem with UnEpic, even if you know how you want to play the game, it doesn't matter unless your choice meshes with the design of the game.  The game sort of makes-up for this by offering a quest that gives you a reset of your spent skill points roughly halfway through the game, but even that reeks of too little, too late in this pseudo-difficulty-based game.
Just what do I mean by that?  When I say "pseudo-difficulty" I'm generally referring to the practice of making a game artificially harder by testing the player's patience rather than by testing the player's skill.  In this game, it comes in the form of every section of the dungeon having it's own hurdle to deal with.  Whether you're in the Catacombs where the game floods you with enemies (of whom you can only hit one at a time while the others are free to swing at you freely), or in the Halls where the majority of enemies take zero recoil and deal massive damage with their attacks, there isn't a single area in UnEpic that was a joy to explore and conquer.  Rather the game felt more like a slog.
The only reason I made it as far as I did in the game is because I wanted to at LEAST beat the game; but I can't do it.  It's not for anything actually "hard", so-much as I just got sick of dealing with all the hurdles.  There's a fun game buried somewhere in all of that code, but sadly the developers don't know how to bring it out.  They were so hell-bent on making the game "harder", without actually knowing how to make a game challenging, that they've buried whatever fun might be had with UnEpic under a landslide of bothersome gameplay and bosses that often feel more like battles of attrition than actual tests of skill.

Honestly wasn't expecting much from this game. Definitely didn't expect it to become likely my favorite kart racer out there... But it did. It's fast-paced and chaotic as any good kart racer should be, items have plenty of variety but nothing really feels overpowered, tracks are well designed with plenty of little hidden shortcuts or alternate paths, and the karts are very well balanced, even allowing you to make small alterations to the stats of drivers you invest time into to fit better to your style. Really like driving a huge tank but find it a bit slow; use the speed mod and get a little boost while sacrificing some handling. Brilliant! Allows you to keep your favorite driver even if their standard stats arn't quite your style.
Only downside is the standard world tour system is how you get to unlock more tracks, karts, and mods; earning stars that allow you to get through locked checkpoints along the way. Put simply, you will -not- see the final track variations or unlock the last couple drivers just playing on easy or medium. Only way to amass the numbers of stars it's wanting is to compete and win on the upper difficulties. Even having cleared the better portion of the game with A and S class ranks (hard and expert) I'm finding I'm still short on stars for the very last few unlocks.
That said, most of the late game content is the same tracks you've been racing on just with altered courses, events, or mirrored, so you don't ever feel like you are really being left out. If you liked the old Diddy Kong Racing, but found it a little clunky compared to the Mario Karts of the same era, this is the game for you. I do wish there were more tracks that were solely for car-form racing, but still great fun anyways.

Alright, let me clear something up. I do like this game. I think it can be fun at times. Unfortunatly, those times have HUGE time gaps. Let me list the things I like and the things that I don't.
Pros:
-character customization (pretty darn cool)
-move list (pretty darn big)
-fights (sometimes pretty intense)
Cons:
-character customization (can only make a second character AFTER beating the game, which is dumb)
-move list (made up mostly of ki blasts, is lacking in any awesome strike specials, and there are few transformations to pick from, going from kaioken as a human, to super saiyan as saiyan. pretty sure thats all you can do.)
-fights (often times are really boring and can be exploited easily, or are mind-bogglingly hard. Also there are mechanics that I still haven't figured out yet (like the fist-clashy-thingie).)
-boss fights (two words you will grow to hate: SUPER ARMOR)
-clothing (you can't preview the clothes that you buy, and you only get half of the money you pay for selling it, so you better hope that you choose wisely.)
-Multiplayer parallel quests( Don't bother. There are never any lobbies and it takes a billion years for anyone to join you.)
-Beam clashes (remember those cool beam clashes from games like dbz budokai tenkaichi 3? Yeah. None of those here.)
-Cool strike supers (remember stardust breaker or final revenger from budokai tenkaichi 3? Yeah. None of those here.)
Aaaaaaand...yeah. I think that's about it. Oh, wait, I forgot a big one.
- Super repetetive (This game starts out being fun. It really does. Then you start to realize that you really aren't changing the formula for the fights at all. Everything is about the same.)
So yeah. It starts off being good, but it gets really boring over time. Don't waste your money on it, of on the dlc (DONT EVEN GET ME STARTED).

This game has insane potential, I could see myself having a lot of fun in this game specially if I play it with friends but as it stands now the game is in a very messy clumsy place.
The thing that kept me hooked in this game is that the character building and rpg aspects of the game are very well done, best attribute/character building I have seen in a while, it reminded me a bit of vampire the masquerade in the sense that if you build a certain type of character you suffer in other areas, example, you build with non-combat stats, you will suffer in combat and will most likely want to avoid combat until you make up for that or if you are forced to fight, this gives a sense of self in the game, you're just a person and every other player has different stats and different advantages, you can survive by yourself doing things your own way or you can complement yourself with other people.

All in all, if this game is treated well and given proper attention, it could be one of the best games ( in my opinion ) that I would have the pleasure of playing in a long time. All I can do now is wait and see where this goes but I really hope this game grows to realize it's full potential!

Aaah, bliss! This brings back the good ol memories!!
I remember Wolf 3D was one of the first games I ever played. Those days, the graphics were as good as it could ever be (pretty much rivaled Doom & Quake).
Many years later, out came Return to Castle Wolfenstein. Upgraded graphics, more weapons, cooler weapons, insane enemies and the (ahem) Elite Guards made the game extremely interesting and eye catching. Heck, my dad & I kept fighting over who would play the game. (We finally compromised and used different save files).
In 2009, the revamped Wolfenstein was released. As a revamp of the original Wolf (albeit a few modifications like the Thule Medallion, the Black Sun groups, etc.), the game was rivetting with very well designed levels, enemies and weapons. I figured Wolf could not be improved upon for a long, long time. To my surprise, yes, it could be, and it was sooner than I ever expected.
Wolfenstein: The New Order dishes out the fun like there's no tomorrow. Insanely cool weapons, amazing enemy AI (though the only thing I can't figure out is why some of the enemies spot you, make a noise, but remain in the same place until they keep staring at you (perv much?) for a few seconds. The game caters to 2 timelines, based on who you decide to sacrifice for the greater good. Each timeline is almost the same, except for a few power-ups, scenes and designs.
What captured my fancy was that you are not limited to 1 - 3 weapons like most games allow you too. Oh, Hell NO! You get to use almost every damn weapon in the game, saving it in your inventory for you to raise Hell later. And the icing on the cake: Dual wield. The toppings: Almost all the weapons have a secondary mode (rockets, silencers, laser cutter / energy pulse, etc.)
The levels are amazingly designed, the cut-scenes are excellent & the acting is perfect! Heck, I'm on my third tour of the game and it still is a bucketload of fun.
My biggest regret is waiting for ages to get this
. If I could go back in time, I would definitely buy this game regardless of the cost, just because it's just that good.

From what I can tell, the reviewers here don't really understand what's going on with the Always Sometimes Monsters Demo. I'm not going to make a full review, because I'm not entirely sure that this is worthy of it anyway (no bonus for the devs here (it's an in-joke)), but I'll try my best to explain.
Basically, this is a free game where you play as a video game reporter going to the launch event of Always Sometimes Monsters, where a demo is available for everyone to try. After that, you have to return to your office and write a review for the game based on the demo.
If you're looking for a demo for Vagabond Dog's Always Sometimes Monsters, where you're supposed to look is inside the actual demo at the launch event in this game. It's an Inception thing; the demo for ASM is inside this game, and then you make a review afterward as part of an alternate experience that has little relation to ASM anyway.
Personally, I loved this. It was the most unique way I've experienced a demo for a game, and it definitely peaked my interest as to the style that Vagabond is going for with ASM. I'm definitely going to get the game now.

STOP! This isnt some nasty CSGO garbage rip-off looking for a quick buck on a broken F2P system.
F2P:  The F2P system isnt completely broken like many new F2P games and I feel like I can get somewhere with a bit of grinding. It is largly crate based however, which I am not a huge fan of. Most loadout cards in the crates are trash and I find that I need to recycle the garbage to create what I want (Honestly a good decision by the devs to add that in, if you ask me). The loadout card/weapon/merc setup is unique to most FPS setups which keeps me interested.
The Game:  Dirty Bomb is also extremely fast paced for an FPS game and the short respawn timer helps me keep my insanity. That being said, the game seems to honor players who play with a level head and pace themselves according to their role. Engineers play objective, medics revive, and tanks just soak up every ♥♥♥♥ing bullet you throw at them. I havent felt like any merc is too OP and a good weapon & loadout card setup goes a long way.
The Dirty Community:  Pretty average community for an F2P....many players dont use mics and casual matches have a bit of banter between the two teams. Unless youre playing a ranked match, dont expect players to fill their roles. That being said, I have seen many good medics that throw a revive when they can.
Conclusion: Dirty Bomb is certainly better than any other ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AVA/Warmode/Free2PlayBrokenFPSGarbage game. I played Black Light Retrobution a bit and I would consider this game a more modern equivalent. If you are going to commit to a F2P game, Dirty Bomb is a good choice.

I wanted to like this game. I really really did. But the difficulty level, steep learning curve (even at the easiest setting) and dodgy controls are all irredeemably brutal. There is no point in this game (despite all cutscenes and insistence to the contrary) where you feel like you are piloting a formidable hybrid mecha fighter capable of taking on large swaths of enemes at once. At best you're awkwardly glissading through space in a fragile tea cup trying not to run into groups of enemies larger than two, as they can all easily flank, out-manuever and out-speed you. This game was marketed as an arcade-style space shoot-em-up, but in actuality, it's a plodding stealth game of the worst stripe. The much-vaunted mecha mode (which you never even get to see until Season 2) is a largely useless melee mode where you are given a weak beam sword, a woefully ineffective directional shield, and an only moderately useful grapple launcher depending entirely on what kind of debris and environmental hazards happen to be nearby in a fight.
One of the biggest sins this games commits is, as the game progresses and gets harder, you are rarely even given enough reasonable opportunities to repair your own ship!!! I spent much of the first season of the game with my ship in flames and on the verge of death because there were few if any means available to repair it between missions. And even after repetitively gritting and grinding my way through randomly generated missions in a near-dead ship, gathering whatever upgrades the game would allow me to get (but not keep if the mission failed) and defeating the gruelling end-season boss encounters (the only unique and genuinely fun parts of the whole game), I was "rewarded" by inexplicably having EVERY SINGLE ONE of my hard-earned upgrades stripped away and being forced to gather salvage to repurchase them all again in a ship that has been completely reset to default while still having to face bigger and tougher enemies. Worse, this happens at the beginning of EVERY season! Who the HELL decided this was a good idea???
The only good thing I can say is they really nailed the old-school anime VHS aesthetic they were going for (right down to the cheesy saturday morning cartoon voice-acting), but taken as a game in and of itself, minus all the costume frills, it's not a game I can really recommend to anyone other than a masochist.

Surprisingly addicting, this game definitely deserves a Choices Matter tag. Haven't seen anything with as much unexpected outcomes since Witcher 3, and that's saying a lot for a 2D game. It has kinda of This War of Mine/Papers Please vibe, so much so that it even has a reference to the latter, but this game has a lot more depth than either. Still, it zooms by pretty fast and ends rather abruply, which is both a strength and a weakness. The game's pace keeps you on your toes, but it can also prevent you from really digging into it and makes the conclusion a bit unsatisfying.
This swiftness can also be aggravated by gameplay mechanics, which can be incredibly frustrating. A lot of the surveillance mechanics happen in real time, so while you're fiddling around with every little tab in the "Filing a Report" screen, stuff's happening. Some of this stuff can include family members dying because of choices you made, some clear and some very much not. Ironically, I was submitting tenant profiles to earn the cash they give, and I had just gone on a run of snooping to earn the few thousand $$ needed to save said family member's life. Because I was rushing I ended up clicking on a few incorrect details, got fined for the erroneous reports, and then had to rush to steal my tenants' valuables to make up the extra cash, and well...long story short, I missed saving the aforementioned family member by a few minutes.
All that said, it was an entertaining, if dark, experience. It really straddles the line between humorous and grim, though maybe a bit too much of that humor comes from low-hanging fruit. It can also take away from the gravity of the situation at times, and if I had one other complaint, it's that it feels a little too easy to divorce yourself from the severity of your character's actions and their consequences. Once my family started dropping like flies (which, if I had one OTHER complaint...), it became easier not to care about either the urgency of the many dilemmas or of the moral complications in what I did to the tenants. I just sorta went with the flow. I probably make it all sound more serious than it is, and the final verdict is that it's a fun time waster and interesting look on totalitarianism

The idea of Beholder is that you have won the job lottery in [insert political joke] and have become a landlord. You are informed by the government that you must spy on your tenants and report them for crimes, which change based on daily promulgations.
The decisions you make are not always easy; balancing family crises and flexing limited power over other humans, and that is the real allure of this game, which I would have wholeheartedly recommended if it was not for a single fatal flaw.
You can ignore your family.
Just ignore them! Don't look at them. If you ignore them, time sensitive and expensive "quests" do not populate, so there's never any real danger. There is no threat. It is similar to Prison Architect, where you don't have to accept prisoners right away, you can deny access to the prison and sit and wait for your money to accumulate. The difference is that in PA, once you have money, you can still have a challenging game thereafter. When you have money in Beholder, you're good, you're golden. There is no challenge.
You could look at this as a player-regulating difficulty mechanic, but for my enjoyment I would have preferred a ticking clock that I had no ability to counter.
So, do I recommend it? Urghhhhh. Difficult question. I genuinely think it is a good game. I like how it plays and controls, I like the interactions between the characters, and the moral decision about whether or not to help people out in a terrible situation or report them to the authorities for harbouring apples that I planted in their dresser, but as soon as I twigged that (what I perceive to be a) flaw in the crisis system I lost my enjoyment of the game almost immediately. It was stripped of its challenge, and since the challenge drives the narrative it means that it strips the investment in the story and the characters.
I can recommend it if you're interested in reading dystopian fiction, as it performs its part superbly, but I cannot recommend it as a game at this time. I look forward to seeing more of the developer's work, and if the family quest aspect is altered, I'm sure to come back to it.

Borderlands, the ultimate loot and shoot fest.
While this game does not boast the most engaging narrative or memorable characters, it does somewhat succeed to entertain on the gameplay front. In an open world with an abundance of baddies out to kill you, there is virtually no end to the amount of mindless shooting that can be done. While that can quickly become repetitive, and perhaps even dull in the minds of some, others will never tire. As for myself, I had mixed feelings, which I will attempt to describe at some length without boring you as much as this game occasionally could.
I couldn't help but notice that one of the labels this game has garnered on Steam is "RPG". Hmm, to the slightest extent, I may agree, but hesitantly. Yes, you can pick from a number of different classes that each possess different skills. Aside from that however, there is very little customization. You can select a variety of colors for your character's appearance, but that's hardly relevant. There is no decision making in this game. You will not have the opportunity to respond to any NPC you may speak to, their primary purpose is to provide you with quests so you can shoot more things. But while we're on the topic of shooting things, I musn't forget that there are several ways to do so. I have no idea how many weapons are in this game, but I can assure you that there is enough to the point where you will not find them all. And that is something that I rather enjoyed, as you will never find yourself spending a monotonous length of time with the same gun. Superior weapons will be popping up left and right, and all of them will aid you in shooting things with more efficiency.
Now that we've thoroughly discussed shooting things, I believe it's time that we covered the other main activity in this game: looting things. For the sake of keeping things simple and concise, allow me to inform you now that everything you shoot, you can loot. You will also find an assortment of boxes, crates, garbage piles, and, I kid you not, toilets that can be looted. What sort of loot will you procure, you ask? Weapons, money, and ammunition. Weapons so you can shoot things in a slightly different fashion, money so you can buy more weapons to shoot things with, and ammunition so you can never stop shooting things. If it hasn't become apparent already, everything you do in this game serves so that you may never stop shooting things, and if you discontinue shooting things, it means you're not playing this game, because as long as you're playing Borderlands, you will always be shooting something.
So there you have it. Of course there are many other aspects of this game that I failed to divulge, however I feel that I did my duty and informed you of the two most important components. What does that mean? It means that if you are an avid fan of looting and shooting things, then this is the title you've been waiting to get your hands on. If not, you may want to avoid Borderlands.
7/10 for Borderlands, your impressions of this game will be entirely dependent on your preferences, I simply don't view this as the sort of game that is either bad or good.

This game is a lot of fun with a little bit of not. Class-based with roguelike elements, it has a few surprises up its sleeve to keep it interesting and enjoyable. Just when I think I'm pushing water uphill, I manage to pull myself out of a tight spot. Just when I feel like I'm cruising along too easily, I get my face pounded in with something spiky and mean. I've clocked almost 10 hours in three days, and I'm showing no signs of stopping anytime soon.
I have a few problems with the game, however.
While the blood of a roguelike is pumping fast through the heart of this game, it isn't passing through the brain as much as I'd like. Collecting a relic grants an effect, but very rarely does the description of the relic lend to an explanation of what that effect is. A mouse-over text would do wonders for telling the player what they've just gotten themselves into.
Also...there's no nice way to say it. The voice acting is a crime against nature. Thus far I've played five of the available eight classes: Viking, Marksman, Redneck, Pirate and Samurai. Only one of these five (the Viking) hasn't made me wish I knew more about modding, and that didn't seem as though it lacked the attempt.
How is it that the Marksman is more redneck than the Redneck? The Pirate is so obsessed with treasure (and climbing, for some reason) that it actually makes other pirates look charitable - seriously, we get it, you like gold and want it in your pockets. As for the Samurai...
If you can imagine Antonio Banderas doing an impersonation of Christopher Lambert's Raiden from Mortal Kombat who is himself doing an impression of Mickey Rooney's character from Breakfast At Tiffany's, you've about got it. Seriously, Kyle Kinane's bit about Trader Joe's Asian counterpart Trader Ming was less racially insensitive, and it was mimicking a man who was doing a terrible Oriental accent. "Trader Ming demand respect from forrorers!" It's that bad.
Oh, you don't want to buy the DLC and find out? That's okay, just whisper the following phrase in a very pensive, meaningful way: "Your rack of barance was your reakness." That's an actual line from the game, in all the glory it lacks. You get me? You get me.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who has a strong love for games similar to The Binding of Isaac (same control scheme, even) but who have long patience for dying unnecessary while cringing at terrible, just terrible voice acting.
Oh, and Akrea, the Lightning boss, talks like a six year old with a speech imediment. "Awe you scawed?" L2speak, then we'll talk.
...seriously with this voice acting...

Alright, let me clear something up. I do like this game. I think it can be fun at times. Unfortunatly, those times have HUGE time gaps. Let me list the things I like and the things that I don't.
Pros:
-character customization (pretty darn cool)
-move list (pretty darn big)
-fights (sometimes pretty intense)
Cons:
-character customization (can only make a second character AFTER beating the game, which is dumb)
-move list (made up mostly of ki blasts, is lacking in any awesome strike specials, and there are few transformations to pick from, going from kaioken as a human, to super saiyan as saiyan. pretty sure thats all you can do.)
-fights (often times are really boring and can be exploited easily, or are mind-bogglingly hard. Also there are mechanics that I still haven't figured out yet (like the fist-clashy-thingie).)
-boss fights (two words you will grow to hate: SUPER ARMOR)
-clothing (you can't preview the clothes that you buy, and you only get half of the money you pay for selling it, so you better hope that you choose wisely.)
-Multiplayer parallel quests( Don't bother. There are never any lobbies and it takes a billion years for anyone to join you.)
-Beam clashes (remember those cool beam clashes from games like dbz budokai tenkaichi 3? Yeah. None of those here.)
-Cool strike supers (remember stardust breaker or final revenger from budokai tenkaichi 3? Yeah. None of those here.)
Aaaaaaand...yeah. I think that's about it. Oh, wait, I forgot a big one.
- Super repetetive (This game starts out being fun. It really does. Then you start to realize that you really aren't changing the formula for the fights at all. Everything is about the same.)
So yeah. It starts off being good, but it gets really boring over time. Don't waste your money on it, of on the dlc (DONT EVEN GET ME STARTED).
