I liked this game and it was fun while it lasted, but a malfunction in the core won't allow me past the first part of the last mission. So I cannot recommend a game I'm not allowed to beat. Once the game gets to the Noah Colony it gets pretty good for a while. Then it tails off at the end leaving a mediocre taste in your mouth. If you want more you can continue reading.
At the end some problems become apparent. Your ships remain un-upgradable just stacking points on, the Angelwing was god-like at the end. While others wither to your backlines because of a real deficit. Then you get a few ships late in the game that never really live up to anykind of hype. Wonky AI that will take a ship attacking another behind an ally not allowing your ship to fire. Mission with the convoy after arriving at Noah Colony, I'm looking at you.
Some equipment is downright pointless. Seriously, lasers... never worked for me. Then you have the Cyborg units, I was like cool I'll land some heavily armed men on a ship (even a small one) then take it over from the inside, or destroy it at least. Nope they just go in and die, not from the counter unit batteries just infiltrate, be there for a bit, die, or return to the ship like nothing just happened. Aside from a few side missions that net next to nothing, there is no reason to waste points on them, except the Angelwing since you'll have nothing better to spend them on.
I was awaiting the ability to command an armada and thinking it was going to be glorious, but it really got rid of some of the intensity of the fights. I found most of my time trying to micro-manage the movements of the fleet to keep them in a battle formation that made any type of sense. Once conveyed into battle units twist and rotate at random, tending to push guns out of sighlines forcing them to stop shooting. So you need to manually move them with the shift key, which isn't explained in the tutorial. Then clicking and unclicking the modules that were once an awesome dynamic to the battlefield, now, a tedious chore that prolonged a battle for longer than it needed to be.
Yet, it does get it right throughout most of the game and for that I can say I enjoyed the game. It balances strategy and tactics with an emphasis on prioritizing targets and launching suicide runs with your fighters to occupy the anti-fighter guns while your bombers attempt to do strafing runs. The ability to adapt to ever changing circumstances in the constantly shifting battlefield will push your plans out of sync. Force you to improvise at times, and sacrifice the few to save the many.
So the modules are a cool little thing that lets you send battery power to boost the efficiency of weapons, engines, shields, etc. to over 9000. Which also opens a vast array of strategies to utilize against your opponents. Strike out with the Brutus, then full power to shields and engines to try and lure a few overzealous captains into range of the Angelwing. Which in turn strikes with a fury.
So there you have it. Like I said this game gets it right for most of it, but tails off at the end. There are few others that can match it in gameplay while "right" but the end just kinda made me happy it was over.

This often forces you, the player, to make shady decisions to earn money. It may mean stealing tenants stuff to hawk. It may mean blackmailing tenants for a cool grand. Things like this. The dwellers feel

There is no randomized sandbox mode where you can try to go forever. It's not a bad thing at all, but just know this is truly story-driven.
It would have been nice to have controller support, but you only really need the mouse to play (keyboard can be used, but is not mandatory). It is also apparent that the writer was not a native English speaker, either. It's fine, but makes for a few awkward moments.
+Does a fantastic job of simulating a real community; everyone has their own storyline and quirks and problems
+Artwork is outstanding
+There is definately some complexity, which is always welcome with a management sim
+Definately addicting
-Some QoL tweaks should be made, such as not having to fill in all the profile details each time you want to amend a dwellers profile report
-Controller support would be very welcome
-I wish you could click on the walls (and not just the floor) to move the character
-You should be able to click on either side of a door to interact with it
-It definately needs a sandbox mode with random encounters, where you could theoretically play forever

The good:
+ tight and quick, little less then ~3h to solve
+ fun and quick time travel mechanic
+ solid sci-fi plot
+ puzzles are logical and solve smoothly, albeit a bit stuck in weird adventure logic
+ neat shaded polygon look
The bad:
- the game blends object transitions instead of animating them, this looks a little weird in places (e.g. when opening doors)
- character thoughts are not voiced, only actual dialog is
- character can only walk left/right, but not up/down, looks a little weird when entering doors
- characters are rather flat and don't have much in terms of personality
- the inventory stays rather empty and there is little room for experimentation
- text is displayed above the scene as one or two long line (i.e. Maniac Mansion style) instead of integrated into the scene itself (i.e. Monkey Island style), makes it hard to read sometimes
- no way to highlight interactive objects
Conclusion:
A fun little sci-fi adventure without any major problems. It's simple to play and doesn't have any major frustrations, but lacks a bit in the length and depth department. Despite it's shortness however the story feels complete and comes to a satisfying conclusion.

Early Access Watcher Reviews The Skies
Update Version: Alpha Patch #4
Disclosure: It was free on download, used the free premium weekend for part of the review
Right of the bat, I cannot in good faith recommend this product. I usually go into detail about key aspect such as story and gameplay, but the bugs and micro transactions will take main focus. Story is scattered in loading screen panels and very awkward voice acting with quests hidden behind NPC interactions. Visually the game feels like it was made in 2009, but it is not awful. The music is rather forgetful with sound effects drowning the speakers in gun fire and scarab clicks. Combat works, but the enemy AI switches from charge happy to standing until killed. UI is rather clunky with simple tasks such as sorting the inventory and interacting with the environment becoming frustrating. Alright, now to the big killers: bugs.
This game could have the greatest story ever told, gameplay that produced liquid joy and visuals which blinded you from pure beauty, but it all means nothing if it can barely hold itself up. The sheer volume of bugs, glitches and errors in this game is staggering; most require the player to exit the game and log back in just to fix. Guns and gear do not equip properly, being overburdened does not hinder movement, some stats do not do what they are suppose to do (Dexterity and Oratory for instance), selling items does not register, and other action graphics can become stuck on your character (pick axe was always visible after a failed node). Terrain appears unfinished with invisible flooring, the few items in barren homes will float in the air, NPCs are seen stuck in objects or walking into walls, enemies will just stand still when hit or appear to be stuck in place with you taking melee damage from them 6 yards away and gathering can get you stuck in the animation. I even got trapped in a staircase and a doorframe on multiple occasions. It just screams of sloppy design and poor self-checking, especially with the stats that fail to work.
Crashes, disconnects, frame rate inconsistency: the trifecta of annoyance. Crashes can happen from simply changing zones to reviving after being killed. Disconnects are rather few and far between, but it happens when the server load starts to get high. Frame rate personally stuck around 20-30 on Ultra settings, but I know of other players dipping into single digits. Mix these problems in with the bugs and you can see how it would feel tiresome just to complete a simple fetch quest.
Now for the controversial topic: micro transactions. It is a well known fact many games depend on them for the revenue to continue updating, but the problem starts to arise when the service provided affects gameplay so much. Thanks to the free weekend, I have been able to see the difference. XP gain, currency gain, crafting slots, time required to craft, it all becomes easier in Premium. This could be seen as a pay to win set up, especially with the amount of coins you get compared to normal player. For a game still in alpha, it is rather interesting to have working micro transactions when so many areas still need basic work. Just an observation.
PvP is always an issue of grievers and balance, so when I discovered how many people decided to camp outside town before the recent update it was clear why the safe areas were constructed. The game just screams effort, but like this constant threat of player attacks the game feels too frustrating when you fear the next bug could get you killed outside your quest destination. I do not know how long it would take before this game could be considered reliable, but at this point it would be more effort than payoff to play it. There are plenty of other MMO style games out there with less pay to win influence to tied you over while this gets further down the programming line.
Pros
- Safe zones at least promise you won't be player killed
- Plenty to do if you can get far enough in
Cons
- It needs heavy optimization
- Open PvP halts most progress
- Micro Transactions (that feel pay to win)
- UI about as frustrating as enemy AI

Do you like RTS games? Do you like space games? Have you played FTL, and did you like it? Do you like Star Trek? If your answer to any of those questions is 'yes', you should pick this up. If your answer to ALL of those questions is 'yes', you'll probably love this game.
Yes, it's nearly 12 years old. Doesn't matter. The interface seems a little complicated, but it's actually fairly straightforward. Yes, the AI can be a bit dimwitted at times, but the game plays very well. For a 12 year old game, the graphics are fantastic when turned all the way up. I'm running everything at max, 1920x1080, and even with VSync enabled, I'm riding a constant, comfortable 144fps to go with my 144hz monitor and my GTX-970 is barely lifting a finger. Sound quality is pretty decent too, even if the voice acting is a bit overly dramatic. So far it's running fairly stable on Windows 10, about 5-6 missions in.
Is the game worth $10? Yes. Is it worth $2.49 on sale? Absolutely, no question. Pick it up.
Full disclosure: I also played this game when it was brand-new back in 2004. The game honestly feels like it plays better now than it did back then.

If you like variety in combat, then you'll love UnEpic. You'll distribute skill points to specialize in various aspects of combat, whether you're using standard ranges or melee weapons, scrolls, potions, familiars or whatever. Every so often, you'll happen upon a new enemy type that really throws you for a loop, especially given how numerous they can be at times. It's worth noting that the level design in this game really suits the enemy distribution well.

Despite its simple look Galak-Z is a quite complex game with surprising amounts of depth. It has a lot of things going on, that makes it feel very hectic and exhilirating. And encourages replayability by being very challenging in a way that always manages to feel fair. It wants you to get better and really make use of all its systems to really destroy the enemy. The AI, as the game so promptly promotes, is very good. Enemies don't just run at you like drones. They will retreat when low, lose track of you if you manage to get out of their sight and try to find close allies to help them make your life just a little harder. You also face multiple factions in most levels, and they will actually not only fight you but each other as well. Making strategic use of the enemy of your enemy a very valid proposition.
Other than that, the game has robust physics that coupled with your very nifty grapple arm allows you to throw rocks, explosives or other space junk into enemies. Or alternatively the enemies themselves into spikes and other hazards that litter the environment. Using what is around you to fight is a huge part of the game that allows each fight to feel very different from the previous one, depending on where you are.
The depth is furthered by you always having two forms available, mech or ship. At the click of a button you can morph in to the other. Both forms have different strengths and ways to play. The mech is all about sword and grappling. It forces you to really use your environments and getting close to your adversaries. While the ship has a laser and missiles to bombard your enemy from afar. What really makes it work is how the different enemy types really make you use them both. You have big enemies that will sweep you aside if you get too close, and smaller faster ships that try to evade you and keep their distance.
The variation of the enemies and just how strong their AI is, together with the depth of the gameplay, is what truly makes Galak-Z special. The structure is that of a "rogue-lite". You go through what the game calls seasons, which are just a collection of five levels tied together with some story beats. These have set objectives usually but randomly generated layout, which makes the replayability high. If you clear all five them without dying you move to the next season. If you die, its back to the start of the season. (Unless you play on the new lower difficulty in which case you get checkpoints between each of the five levels). 
There are also upgrades for your ship. Different lasers, missiles and attributes for each. Like lasers that bounce off walls, has a large spread or set your enemy on fire. These you can find and equip straight away. Or you can find blueprints that then unlock for you to buy between missions, or when you die or move onto a new season. So there is some persistence in between deaths that don't make unsuccessful runs feel completely pointless.
My only real gripe is that I don't love some of the 2D art. Specifically the character designs aren't super great. The gameplay visuals are good though, with nice explosions that really make themselves felt. I also feel that the controls take a while getting used to. I played with a controller and it uses almost every button on it. Which is positive, and really speaks for the depth it has but I did die a few times from input errors. When I got used to it, it feels very natural.

Galak-Z is an 80’s anime inspired twin-stick shooter? That’s not really an accurate description; it’s got action-y elements, platform-y elements, rogue-like elements… I’ve found it hard to give it a genre. It’s been out on the PS4 for about two months, but it comes to PC on the 29th of October, and it’s pretty good. It has it’s faults; and I think it needs rebalancing, though I know there’s a lot of people who don’t think that, and that’s fine,  but just for me, I felt the extremely punishing nature of the gameplay was just pushing me away. And I’m inclined to believe, as a massive Dark Souls fan, that this is the fault of the game, as opposed to just not falling within my tastes.
It looks pretty sweet though. The designs feel very 80s-90s anime, which is nice, although I felt the character design didn’t completely reflect that. I liked the design of the characters, but I felt they resembled a more “saturday morning cartoon” western style instead of anime. The anime feel mostly comes from the music, the setting, and, oh yeah, the mechs. I like the environments, I just wish there was a little more variety. The game is split into seasons with 5 episodes, or missions, each. I’m not really sure why they couldn’t have designed a new environment for each season, because that would have worked really well I think. But for the most part, it’s either biological area or mechanical area, and that’s it. It could have been a lot more, with each season having it’s own distinct atmosphere.
The actual gameplay itself is pretty solid. At first I found it finicky, but once I got the hang of it and began using the environment to fight the enemies I found it a lot more satisfying. It’s certainly difficult, but it’s pretty fair. The thing I had an issue with, was the buffer room you are given. For the most part, if you end up at the most heavily damaged possible; 1 health and, the default, 2 shields, is good enough to make it to the end of the level. However, there are some, relatively rare, enemies that can kill you in one hit, by taking two shields and one health per shot. I don’t think this was a good call; health is insanely valuable in this game, and I feel the point of the gameplay relies on being able to be risky, but still retaining your health. If there are shots that can just take your health no matter what, then I feel it compromises the rest of the experience. And it’s not just that, there are a couple of other minor gameplay annoyances that make the experience pretty frustrating in my opinion; and really make the game ridiculous on rogue mode. When you begin the game you have the choice between rogue and arcade mode, and I would recommend only the most extreme masochists ever play rogue mode. It’s insane to me that arcade mode is a new addition. The upgrading system is weird, because when you are finished with a season you lose all of your upgrades. This is compounded by the fact that game doesn’t have that many upgrades to choose from. It’s pretty lacklustre, and I wouldn’t buy the game expecting an RPG-like skill tree. In general, because of the way the game works, if you're not a masochist of any kind, probably avoid the game.
The plot, while retaining a lot of that anime feel, isn’t really here to blow your mind. It’s nothing particularly interesting in my opinion, though I don’t feel it was trying to be, necessarily. You start off stranded, and then end up with a super weapon that you can use to overthrow the imperials… or something. I thought the writing was pretty good though, a lot of what the characters say is groan-worthy, but in a charming way. I feel like it really captures a saturday morning cartoon vibe with corny jokes.
The thing is, I think this game is solid, but I don’t think it’s worth 20 bucks which is the launch price. There’s a 20% discount at launch which makes it $16, even then I’d wait. If you ever see the game for $5, it’s a complete steal, if you see it for 10$ I’d say that’s what it’s worth, $15 is the maximum I’d ever say someone should pay for it (and even then I’d advise them to maybe wait), so $20 is really hard to justify for… maybe 5 or 6 hours if your playing arcade mode? I mean, if you are really excited to play this game based on my review, go for it, but I think for most people it’s smart to hold off.

Galak-Z is a must play for all anime and mech fans :)
First, a brief anectode.
Robotech, that's where it all began for me.
Of course, behind the shrouded veil of conspiracy and deceit, there's the real star, Macross: The Super Dimensional Fortress. But for children like meself,  whose only language was English / French or both at the time; Robotech was the tv show that got me into the Real Mecha anime genre that Gundam originally started. The story, the characters, the mech designs, the j-pop songs, space tuna (R.I.P), minmei's plum butt as acknowledged by Cmdr. Focker (or was that Lt? whatever, R.I.P chappie) , and deadly pineapple salads (why I hate salads). Then of course, Gundam, I never got the plot when I was a wee kiddie, but there was this one character in it whose name I never could forgot, Saylah Mass, cuz my aunt shared the same awesome first name, Mobile Suit Gundam 0079!!! It was a glorious childhood.
It wasn't until I made it to college that the journey really began, and Gundam, Macross, Yamato, FMP and a lot other series got my attention.
Nuff about the pastly past, onto the present.
Adulthood is super awesoeme. As mech games became somewhat popular with the advent of indie development, and of course, the games readily available on the Japanese market (GvG: Extreme Versus, and games released by Artdink or From Software).
Galak-Z is an homage to the past two decades of mech animes. The developers clearly are fans of Japanese mech animes, and have somewhat created a game that's akin to the episodic nature of the shows we grew up with. The story is pretty much Yamato / Macross at this point. Your battleship is far away from earth, and is traveling back through enemy territory. You are an awesome pilot, A-Tak, who also happens to be the last surviving pilot, flying the last transformable "variable fighter" available on your "science" vessel helmed by a lady commander named ... Beam. A-Tak and Beam then meets Crash, the salvage dealer/merchant, and the journey begins.
The game is set around 5 episodes, essentially chapters, whereby A-Tak has to undertake about 5 missions per chapter before facing off a big baddie ... from evil space wurm to evil alien superpilot. Each mission are randomly generated whereby A-Tak has to go on salvage runs or destroy enemy equipments to allow your ship to continue it's journey onward to Earth. If you die, it's game-over, but you can start over at the beginning of each episode with a stack of crash (the merchant) coins earned in-game,  which allow you to purchase a few random upgrades for your ship when you begin anew.
The gameplay is unique, and physics-based as you have to balance between using your propulsion system in a Zero-G environment to navigate asteroids field and derelict space crafts or enemy installations to carry our your jub! A-Tak's piloting skills is very dependent on the player ability to use the in-game flight system to avoid incoming pewpewpew, sssshboomsticks, and dangerous space flora that take away your shield among other things (traps). Lose a health bar and it's permanent. You can either recover it by spending cash to buy +1 HP, or you may receive a temporary HP bonus in-game. And there's the mech ... which changes how you play the game. Equipped with a plasma sword and a shield, you can charge in recklessly for the kill, or grab enemies from afar and hold them as a shield or attack them while trapped in your death grip!
There's a also a stealth mechanics, but I came here for the pewpew.
The enemy varities are varied between weak scout units, to enemy fighter plane, mechs and I guess, corvettes and later on mini-battleships.
Each faction encountered are somewhat very different, raiders have better shielding systems while the antagonistic imperial alien race, have more pewpewpew. And there are space bugs who go squished and often leaves A-Tak to spend his free time cleaning his little fighter.
The music and game atmosphere is very soothing, and the voice acting is spot-on. Between corny and adorable. I love A-Tak interaction with the crew.
You read all of that junk? Good, buy it now! :)

I played this game for the first time and it only took an hour or so.  I was pleased with it but a little disappointed it wasn't longer.  Then I let it sit.  Three weeks later I'm back playing it through again, making different choices, seeing how things change.  And again, trying to accomplish specific goals for myself.  And again, trying to accomplish something else.
I don't agree with reviewers who say that the game is too limited and lacks replayability.  You see different stories and different options based on things you did earlier in the game.  In my most recent game, I unlocked a whole set of additional challenges that I had no idea were even possible, because I focused my attention differently in the beginning of the game.  You can play through the entire game without dying pretty easily, it's not a roguelike in that sense; but it shares with that type of game the quality of being different and challenging in a different way every time you play through it.  You need to replay it in order to see the whole game, and I think it's pretty clear that it was designed that way.
I also have to say there's something really appealing about the cartoony art juxtaposed with the silhouetted characters.  The soundtrack works perfectly.  Like Papers, Please (another favorite of mine) Beholder makes some statements about the cost of living in and cooperating with totalitarianism through gameplay, without beating you over the head with them.

Squad is a good game and a great simulator of what it would be like to work as a squad and act as a team in large scale enviroments and battles.. Some games in squad may also be some of the quietest games, only if your squad leader wants to build a super base that may never be used before the game ends or if you find yourself squadless and far away from the area of battle...This is not a run and gun type of game, you can not expect to run into places all the time or kill everyone you see before they kill you. "This game requires patience"
You may die a lot having first started the game especially if you are still learning the ropes and the mechanics of the game and how it all works.. I recommend to always stick with your squad and listen to what your squad leader tells you to do, not only to increase your survivability but for the success of your sqaud and the games outcome.
You can play with friends or you can simply join a squad, make friends and have a good time. The battles that you can encounter in the game on a 50vs50 server are truly one of a kind.
Each scenario you play will be completely different from the last time you played. No battle is the same. You will always find yourself In a different experience.
It is the squad and your whole team that defines how a battle is played and determines the outcome of how you enjoy this game. Yes there are glitches, yes there are issues and minor bugs but nothing that can't be fixed with more updates as the devs work on progressing towards a more stable and enjoyable experience, even though it's already an enjoyable experience in my opinion.
If you do not like experiencing these minor bugs and glitches i recommend for you to not by this game because you will only ruin it for youself. I'd advice to wait for a more stable experience.. As for me im happy with the performance i get and the gameplay itself. Sqaud truly makes me feel at war. 10/10 would go to war again.

Here's how to tell if you'll like this game:
If you're just looking for a sandbox to build robots with weapons and play around a bit, you'll find Robocraft incredibly frustrating. The parts are not fully balanced (and maybe never will be), there's a certain strategy to building that's the only competitive way to win in multiplayer, and the progress system is somewhat pay2win (although everything you can pay for, you can also grind for).
However, if you're competitive enough and you really enjoy winning a game with the unique bot that only you built, it's an incredibly satisfying experience to optimize and strategize your robot over and over again, and win. I usually only play it once every few months to satisfy this urge.
One day it might be a great game. It's sort of just okay right now.
EDIT: They keep making decisions that, while logical according to the competitiveness of the game, just make it unfun. As of Dec. 2017, they've gotten rid of all radar modules and the minimap, a totally unfun change. Yes, everyone just stacked the jamming modules but it was also fun to be the spotter for the team. They also changed it so only 4 of the same weapon increase your fire rate now, so no gunboats :( they ALSO have brought back tiered building blocks, which was of the worst aspects of the 2015 version that I was glad to have seen gone.
This in retrospect, is just the developers modus operandi. They've turned a fun sandbox team fight mash em up into an unfun competitive slugfest.
I don't even really mind the loot updates or the premium membership - the devs have to make money somehow. But by removing features like weapon stacking and other modules entirely, they've turned a very unbalanced, fun game into a slightly less unbalanced snorefest.

Hero Siege is kinda like those WC3 Hero Defense custom maps back in the day--it's just about running around grinding waves of enemies until you hit a boss. This game is pretty much a portmanteau of Diablo 3 and Binding of Isaac gameplay.
This game is really addicting and has the potential to be great, but there are a few glaring issues holding it back.
The first--going back to where I said it's like Diablo 3, this game has an unhealthy obsession with Blizzard crap. Expect to encounter Diablo/Warcraft references (including Acolyte quotes and a Frostmourne item) which are amusing at first but become tiresome quickly.
The second is the Diablo 3-like difficulty scaling. The game rips off their elite/boss system in which dead bosses sometimes shoot stuff at you after they're dead. One of these is a giant spinning laser which is obviously taken straight from D3. My main contention is not that the ripoffs ruin the game, but that it introduces the same problem that D3 had--you can go multiple levels without taking too much damage, and then you get a spinning laser put right on top of you in a hallway, or some super-damaging projectile hidden amongst the hundreds of other projectiles littering the screen and die immediately, sometimes without knowing what caused it (and allocating your stats defensively does not mitigate this at all). In this way the game is unbalanced because the game will be a walk in the park for 30 minutes straight and then have a massive difficulty spike for a few seconds which kills you because your reactions are only human.
The third is the stat system. Str and Dex (or was is Speed? whatever the equivalent was) are completely useless and only increase the stats by the smallest possible fraction. As a result, builds that rely on attack speed or attack damage are useless, and subsequently, so are 50% of the items in the game that increase these stats. Thus the success of a character build invariably falls on "whose flat-damage abilities scale the best?" (Hint: it's probably Pyromancer.)
So, those are the main issues. Other than that, the awful voice acting contributes a lot to the annoyance factor of the game. I'd have to guess that the devs decided to do the voices themselves--which was a bad decision considering their broken English (they're from Finland). The soliloquies are stupid too ("Are you losing it? I am not." "It's good to be on this side of the bow.").
I've sunk a decent amount of hours into this game (30+ at this time of writing), so the game was still a lot of fun despite my complaints. I think I got to Nightmare mode and then stopped because of all the random unavoidable deaths. I don't think I will be spending much more time playing this game, unless they hopefully fix some of these problems with the upcoming expansion. Overall I still definitely recommend this game for a lot of hours of fun (even more so with co-op) especially given its low price.
TL;DR: Devs are obsessed with Blizzard games. Insane difficulty spikes. Broken stat system. Still a fun co-op experience for many hours.
EDIT: They added a mana management system that sucks all the fun out of the game. I don't recommend this anymore.

I got this game wanting something along the lines of Dwarf Fortress but more approachable, and that's exactly what I got.  I just lost my first colony to a pack of beavers who wanted revenge since I killed two of their own (I was trying to kill them so they wouldn't eat every tree in the area).  It was a sad moment for me.  I've spent five hours working on this colony, planning things, trying to keep everyone alive until I finally felt like I was on top of things.  My three colonists who could shoot were badly injured and knocked out from the beaver assault, the only person left concious was my doctor and he only had a knife.  He surprisingly managed to survive and kill all but one of the remaining beavers who had retreated.  My doctor was badly wounded, carrying one of my colonists to safety as rain poured down around him until eventually he collapsed from his injuries.  My newest colonist, the doctor's brother, who had been hunting the beavers was the first to go down and despite being rescued by my doctor he bled to death in his bed.  My colonist who built everything was the next to go--his yorkie, Loyalty, had already died from the beaver attack.  Finally, my miner and my doctor followed suit and bled to death in the rain.  The good people of Priest's Borough had a rough start, they didn't always get along, but I really thought they had a chance.  I can't recommend this game enough, I plan on starting a new colony tomorrow.

Beholder is a genre-defying game in the sense that it feels like a mashup of a bunch of ideas taken from several other contexts and put together into one nice package. The game takes place in a dystopian setting, which is heavily characterized by the authoritarian regime and, for some reason, I can’t shake the feeling that this takes place in an alternate/imaginary cold war setting somewhere along Eastern Europe.
Beholder starts out with you, Carl Stein, and your family being sent by the Ministry of Allocation to a new district, where you’ll assume the role of a landlord of an apartment block. Your job is to accommodate new tenants, make sure the building is in order but, most important of all, spy and gather information about the people living there and report back to the Ministry, in the name of the Great Leader!
Before starting a new game you get to choose which mode/difficulty you want to play. There’s the Trainee mode, in which you have increased income and reduced costs, and then there’s the Government Elite mode, which is pretty much the way it’s meant to be played and that will pit you against some difficult challenges and choices.
The tutorial is pretty good at explaining how each individual mechanic works and you can take your time with it. You’ll be receiving orders from the Ministry via phone calls and completing these will grant you a reward and increase your influence. Missions can either have a certain time limit on them or be timeless, thus providing some sort of change of pace in terms of gameplay. At the same time, your tenants and your family will also ask things of you and these can be simple tasks but they can also be something that breaks the law and it’s up to you to decide what to do and accept the consequences of your actions. Even if you choose to do X instead of Y, sometimes the consequences of those actions won’t surface until very late in the game. I found this to be a really interesting sort of plot twist that has made me curious to play the game more times in order to see the different results that different actions can yield. There are also some sort of “special events” that will occur at certain parts of the game that manage to illustrate in a very good way the state of things, thus providing some sort of narrative to what’s really going on the country.
The way the game combines the atmosphere, drama and tension of games such as Papers, Please with a weird mixture of management and spying is really well done. You’ll be spying on tenants by peeking through their keyhole, breaking into their apartments when they’re not there in order to gather evidence, and placing cameras in smoke alarms in the hopes of catching them doing something illegal. The information you gather about them is then used for profiling purposes and, potentially, for reporting them to the authorities. This is where the game gets really interesting because every few days the State will issue a new directive and these can be something such as the prohibition of political propaganda or that the possession of apples or crying is prohibited, there’s all sorts of silly things used to portray such an authoritarian regime. Anything can be used to incriminate your tenants, including blackmail and planting evidence.
In terms of narrative and story, I think that the game does a wonderful job in creating a believable world, albeit silly at times. The occasional cutscenes are pretty well done but I wished there were more of them throughout the game. The line of communication between Carl and the Ministry, the newspapers you receive in the mail, the other mysterious callers and the conversations between the tenants and Carl’s family really do an excellent job in creating a living world behind all the main gameplay mechanics. I just find it a shame that the dialogue between Carl and other characters isn’t voice acted, but then again,  the voice acting isn’t really that good in my opinion, so it’s probably for the best to leave it the way it is. One thing I did notice but I didn’t thought to be that huge of a deal were some minor grammar mistakes, but that doesn’t in any way retracted me from understanding what the game was trying to transmit to me. Now, there was something about the ending I got that didn’t quite make sense, which I won’t mention for the sake of spoilers, but I can safely say that there’s some work that could be done in polishing some loose ends. In any case, this is one of those games that made me care about certain people and, at certain times, regretting treating some of them the way I did.

'Tales from the Borderlands' is a brilliant convergence of Telltale Games' unique point-and-click, episodic format and the  well established fictional world of the Borderlands universe as developed by Gearbox Software and 2K Games.
Taking a step away from Telltale Games' very successful primary genre - drama, as evidenced by the universal critical acclaim received by 'The Walking Dead' - the developers this time step into the realm of farcical comedy, befitting for the Borderlands universe; and they do it very well. With dialogue throughout consistently reflecting a Borderlandesque (sorry) flair, it is plain to see that no expense has been spared to ensure this collaboration is true to its source material.
As well as Telltale Games' normal knack for dialogue, the balance of pace and tone throughout weaves effortlessly alongside the well constructed plot.
With two playable characters whose paths cross through respective misdeeds, 'Tales from the Borderlands' pushes Telltale Games to its creative limits. The world of Pandora is explored through the eyes of criminals and Hyperion employees (although the two are not necessarily mutually exclusive *cough*), taking a fresh stance on those originally considered enemies in the Borderlands series,  adding to its thought-provoking spectrum of personalities that eliminates the false dichotomy of 'good and evil'.
I could go on.
But, in short, three episodes down and I feel Telltale Games have outdone themselves in their partnership with the Borderlands development teams. To those of you who have played the Borderlands series, it really will feel like you're coming home. If you haven't played the Borderlands series, the game stands on its own two legs to provide a thrilling, story driven comedy adventure; the exposition alone covers all the backstory you need to know.
So come on and play; show the Borderlands universe your name is 'Ten Million Dollars'.

In this interconnected world where every political, international, and minuscule thing is shared via thirty different social media accounts, it really isn't a surprise that privacy and confidentiality are a hot topic. You can't turn on the news without hearing about leaked information, deleted E-mails, and how big is somebody's butt is these days. So it's interesting when a game developer takes these issues head on and translates them into a video game. Beholder has drawn quite a bit of attention because of this and it makes one think about their own privacy; how external forces can affect that.
Beholder is a game about spying on your neighbors. Not because you're a creep, but because your government is asking you to do it for the good of the country. One can see how this already translates into reality in rather terrifying ways. Now this game comes along in the same vein as other games that have had similar political or social commentary, such as Papers, Please or This War of Mine. The trick about these games, at least for me, is that while the message comes through loud and clear that these games still retain a level of enjoyment and don't get preachy to the point where I wanna kill myself. Looking at you, This War of Mine.
Beholder, I am happy to say does accomplish this using a whimsical, if not sinister, art style and fairly easy to grasp mechanics. The story/scope of the game all takes place in an apartment building and between its tenants. Espionage is key and knowing how to use that information you've gathered effectively is the name of the game.
Tackling the story first, Beholder has MANY possible endings, multiple ways to handle a situation and it lends itself to replay and seeing what new outcomes you can get. I would love to say I got all of the endings, but that would take quite a while. You can play the game as a completely evil bastige, who cares for nothing but himself and his family. This is by far the easiest route to be honest. However, being a good person is possible. It's difficult and will have a cost of either money or possibly the life of someone you love. The chips are always stacked against you and the house usually always wins. This is a mindset that is extremely important to bear in mind as you play Beholder. You are battling your morality and the clock.
To overcome the odds, you are going to have get your hands dirty. Beholder plays with its monotone colors for a reason. Your actions are going to end being shades of grey. Blackmail your neighbor to save your daughter? Steal an illegal firearm to protect a young woman? These are questions you will have to answer quickly and that have immediate consequences. This is Beholder's greatest strength as a game. It mixes hundreds of possible narratives and decisions seamlessly with something new to discover around every corner.
From a functionality standpoint Beholder is on the simple side.(No controller required) You left click with the environment to plant cameras or evidence. Also to discover information about your tenants and make reports. There are two sources of income in the game, one is straight up cash, the main resource, and credibility which allows you purchase more cameras and get out of a jam in certain events/conversations. The game has a decent tutorial that teaches you the basics, but the rest is kind of learned as you go. The most important thing I felt the tutorial ignored was the placement of items inside of other containers. This is vitally important as framing your tenants is key way to make money or get rid of somebody.
While there are many facets that require a bit to wrap your head around, once you do figure it all out it becomes easier to rig the system in your favor. The save system also makes is rather easy to abuse as you can reload often to a previous point if you screw up. Not saying that I did, but the temptation was there on occasion. Aside from that, which is hardly a gripe, Beholder is extremely well put together. I didn't run into any bugs and all the mechanics are easy to understand.
One thing I will say is that the games difficulty can be called into question. Your main problem is never having enough money to accomplish some story related issue. Gameplay itself never really challenges you in the same way something like Papers Please did, where a keen eye was pivotal as more scrutiny was involved with passing people. Beholder is far more decision and story based. Nothing is wrong with that but felt it should be noted. The game does have two game modes, including one that reduces the amount of money/credit you get per action/blackmail etc. This just stacks the chips higher against you and makes decisions more stressful but doesn't change the overall difficulty of the game.
The art style of Beholder is an absolute treat. The game needed to capture many emotions using its black and white sprites, from terror to being adorable. I was utterly amazed by the kaleidoscope of  emotions/tone of the game could shift through. From being stabbed, to giving your wife a candy bar, and an entire range in between. The eyes of each sprite are used effectively and it just spoke to me, the way the characters were all unique in this dreadful totalitarian setting. The apartment itself is drawn well and serves as a nice back drop. It comes off very dreary so it never really caught my attention too much. There are also well illustrated cut scenes that are shown occasionally. While there are plenty of gloomy events in the game such as your daughter dying or tenants leaving penniless, the game rides a fine line but never forgets that its still a game, which to me is as important as the subject matter.
One area I wasn't a huge fan of was the music which does come off very gritty and low key. It matches the over all theme of the game but it just isn't all that pleasant on the ears. It may not be meant to in all honesty, but I found myself just turning it down and focusing on completing tasks. There are some other areas that do well though, sound effects are very well done and there is even a little bit of voice acting that is delivered quite well.
Overall game length is going to vary from game to game due to the branching narrative but the game has high replayability as I mentioned earlier. You're looking at somewhere between two to four hours for one game session. I would say and that all really depends on your familiarity with the mechanics and how you want events to play out. There is a fast forward that does make the game go a hell of lot faster that I would use on occasion. So that may drastically alter your game length as well.
Beholder is a game that makes you think about the ramifications of your decisions. It doesn't get preachy but it doesn't shy away from its subject matter. The game retains its level of fun from beginning to end and I found it to be a very satisfying experience. Games that look to deliver a message on social/political commentary can go wrong in many ways, but Beholder avoids all the pitfalls in style. I believe that the developer was very innovative in the way they tackled this subject matter and I hope to see more games like this in the future. Games are after al,87ul another form of freedom of speech, one that we must not take for granted.
At the low price of $9.99, Beholder is quite a steal if you are looking for a game that has a message but does things in its own way. With Steam cards, achievements and the developer putting out more updates and patches to tackle any issues that arise, I can easily recommend this title. So check the game out, in the meantime I am going to put on my tinfoil hat and check for bugs.

Sure, there's still skill involved and you could beat the game with none - but when your game starts with four special powers the play is so much visibly easier than otherwise that it's almost not worth continuing if your first few levels don't have anything.
All in all, I liked it. I'm working on beating it with the last few characters, and it was totally worth the price.

When I first bought this game I enjoyed it, I really did. But that quickly wore off as it was more of an excitement from trying something new than actual fun. The game is NOT a bad game, but that does not mean it is a good game. I currently feel like the game has a lot of potential, but is underdeveloped, underplanned, and at some points just completely half-a**ed.
There are a good ammount of characters to choose from, each with their own set of active and passive abilities. But besides that they can all be grouped into one of two categories: Melee and Ranged. Melee characters get close to the enemies and swing at them, Ranged characters stay farther away and shoot. The only real variation are the abilities, which most of the actually useful ones are passives that usually have a 1% chance of activating per point put into the skill, or are actives that do not scale in damage per point as well as they should and sometimes make the character a "press x to win" type of character. Besides the abilities characters get seperate attribute points that can be used to make the character have more health, do more damage, attack faster, or take less damage. Like the abilities, these scale very poorly per point spent, requiring many points to actually have a decent effect.
Besides the abilities relics are found in the game, usually by defeating the level boss, and also affect the game somehow. Some of the relics are passives that affect either the character or the enemies. Others are active abilities that are used and then are put on cooldown for a short ammount of time. Some of the relics are extremely powerful and borderline OP. Most of the relics, including the powerful ones, are really not that important and often inspire feelings of "oh, that relic." instead of "YES! I got this relic!"
Combat is pretty basic. Characters can attack either left, right, up, or down. Combat mostly consists of the character being close enough to hit the enemies, and backing up so that they are not hit themselves (also known as kiting). The only real threats are enemies with ranged attacks, or certain enemies with special abilities. From my experience the most variation in combat has been activating a relic, potion, or active ability, or a passive ability activating. The potion system is pretty standard for some rogue-likes and rogue-lites. If a potion is picked up for the first time, the effects of that potion is unknown until it has been drunk. Afterwards the effect has been learned and other potions of that color will display the effect. Note: The effects of the potions change from run to run. Once a character dies, whether hardcore or not, the effects of all potions are changed.
Multiplayer: I have not tried multiplayer, as I have felt no desire to. The game is not good enough to keep me wanting to play as it is currently, and joining a server with strangers is very unlikely to make me want to play the game more.
All in all, this game feels too simplified, like someone took a great game, and stripped away anything "complicated" only the bare bones of the game were left. This game is good for people looking for a simple casual game, but it is not for people looking for a good diablo-style game.

Run around and slay hordes of monsters in this twin-stick style top-down game. There’s a few classes to pick from, some melee, some ranged, with a basic auto attack and a small plethora of cool down abilities to use.
All those components could build up to a fun experience, but here’s the main issues with this title: Leveling up means nothing, since a 0.2% stat increase is inappreciable; fighting enemies (the meat of the game) is a visual mess of enemies, traps and projectiles; getting hit a couple of times means death, and since actually seeing threats is the difficult part, it just becomes frustrating; the basic auto attack is laughably weak, so enjoy kiting the most basic of enemies for more time than it’s worth.
In the end, it could be salvageable, but it would need serious rebalancing and reworking. To add insult to injury, please don’t remind me there’s DLC classes and stages every time I start a new run.

I played Nexus The Jupiter Incident, henceforth shortened to Nexus, long ago. I never finished it as far as I can remember. Now I have the chance to complete it and I will keep at it till I do! The graphics look great when I think back to the original, the story is OK, not the best but pretty good. The voice acting I assume is the same as the original but I can't remember how they sounded back then; it is again not the best but then I am not playing it for that reason.
It is very story led with nothing to do outside of the story to speak of but this is not a problem in my opinion. Which is surprising as I normally like much more open play games.
I did get it in the sale but I don't think this is colouring my judgement too much, full price would still be worth it especially if you are looking at Nexus for its nostalgia quality. It was released around 2004 I thnk so it is now about 12 years old. Don't let this put you off though. It has been brought up to modern standards as far as possible I think.
PROS
====
Much nicer graphics than the original.
Cinematic feel as the missions can be quite long. (Bit of a double edged sword maybe)
Decent physics.
Great models, especially Angelwing :-)
CONS
====
The missions can be a bit long. (The distances that you have to cross can be large before you are able to engage.)
Possibly a steep learning curve. (It is gradually coming back to me)
Not many CONS in my opinion, I reckon that if, like me, you were playing Nexus when it first came out, you won't regret handing over the cash for this version.
BTW, it is working fine on my Win 10 laptop with, so far, no crashes or stuttering or any of the other annoying things that seem to crop up every so often.
So, you've read my opinion, why are you not already paying for your own copy? :-)

Ashes of the Singularity is a heavily macro oriented RTS; i would argue even more so than games such as supreme commander or TA. i have not played the campaign but have played around 30 hours of the multiplayer and the community is alive and well(it takes about 8 min max to find game), the gameplay is very much about outbuilding your opponent and also maintaining a good variety of unit types, the game is full of rock paper scissor hard counters so spamming the same unit is not really an option against a good opponent, resources are distributed accross the entire map and their is a victory condition for map control so it is a game that encourages early aggression rather than turtling making for busy chaotic games right from the 3-4 min mark in smaller maps. One major criticism i have as an sc2 player is if one does need to micro some units take your orders more as suggestions than intructions moving units around is fine fine but getting them to focus down a large unit or building is much more taxing as they seem to reaggro constantly. This aside however i would reccomend for anyone who is looking for a more thoughtful but still fast paced rts experience.

In my review of Ashes of the Singularity I said, "This is not SupCom reborn, but it sure as hell evoked that feeling of managing more than just units, but whole armies."
With a bigger roster, strategic zoom, and the upcoming T4 units that were recently teased, when it comes to AotS: Escalation, the same feeling is evoked but with even more SupCom vibes than ever before. In short, I'm fully recommending this title. If you have the original, the cost to "upgrade" is more than worth the price of admission. If you are new to the series, and want something that is not all about your APM (aka Starcraft-esque), take the plunge.
The chart on the information page sums up how much is new, and there is more coming. Like I stated before, T4 units were teased, which are going to be bigger, badder, and naturally even more of a destructive force to add to your armies.
While a feature I absolutely love, the economy system will give some players a hard time. There are 2 basic mined resources, Metal and Radioactive materials. This works on a per tick basis, so infinite resources but it works on a positive/negative status. If you are mining +4 and your production is running at +4, you are all good. If you are mining +4 and your production is -5, you will lose stored materials until you run out, and production comes at a dangerously slow pace. Once you get the hang of it, you will intuitively know when you need more resource miners, or more factories.
With the variety of units, it is easy to be overwhelmed by what to build, when to build it, etc. I enjoy the variety, and many units can suit a playstyle or strategy pretty well, but no one unit is "OP Meta" or whatever that overly competitive friend of yours wants to say. Some say the variety is not enough, but I think it is at the right spot, with enough counters that a player will never feel they went down the wrong "tech tree" mid match.
Speaking of tech trees, it is pretty straight forward. The special "Orbital" abilites need special buildings, but for the most part all production is from a handful of buildings, which depending on race varies only slightly. I have not found one race to be more "OP" than the other, but playstyle does mean you will likely prefer one over the other.
Lastly, let us talk about the AI, because "The AI does not cheat, you just suck." No, that is not some elitist bull either. I have watched the insane AI play, and it does not magically have more resources. What is does do is multi-task insanely well. A really good player can keep up, but can not afford costly mistakes. Sure maybe flub a skirmish over a resource node, but fail a push and you may as well gg, because the AI will punish you. Granted, I like that. It means the lower level AI is still fun to play against, but the toughest AI will make you earn your win.
I encountered some bugs, where the game locked up (always during a cutscene in SP, no crashes in MP so far), but after some troubleshooting on the forums, they have been minimal. It was not any old drivers or anything, but I did have to ensure the game ran with a high resource priority. I may still tweak some settings, but the game runs quite well otherwise with high settings. My specs are listed below.
To bring it full circle, do I recommend this title? Absolutely.

SOME GENERAL SPOILERS:
Purchased and re-playing this on PC after originally owning it for PC.
As somebody that played the original Wolfenstein as a kid in the 90s, I originally recoiled at this re-imagining of the series considering it's past disappointments. The 2009 game had some great ideas but it was overall bland and couldn't set itself apart from every other shooter that came out that year. - Wonderful level and character design.
- Fun action balanced out by some great stealth elements that don't get too old.
- NAZI PRISON ESCAPE. SPACE NAZI BASE. ROBOT DOGS
Cons
- The controls feel loose in some ways. It takes a bit to get used to.
- The cover system [is it a cover system?] doesn't really work that well.
- With how gorgeous the game looks, I couldn't help but notice that there could have been some improvement on the graphical options front.

The Silent Age is a retro-style point-and-click retro 70's adventure. It has retro-style minimalist artwork, and... no. Stop. The Silent Age attempts to capture some of the darker corners of the '70's - the brutality that resulted from the Cold War, the greed of the men who tried to take advantage of it, and their combined consequences. The puzzles aren't especially challenging, and you can't exactly say that it's one of those adventure games that's eschews puzzles to tell a story, because the story isn't amazing, either. But it is still compelling, if point-and-clicks are your jam, and the artwork is very well-done. A lot of the elements look flat, like paper cutouts, relying on shading to give them texture and dimension, and this non-descript artwork plays into the theme of an anonymous hero ("literally, the average Joe") in a world that seems much too big and imposing for him to make a difference. The soundtrack promotes the same feeling. The game definitely isn't creepy enough to be even mild horror, but it's just enough to be imposing and intriguing.
tl;dr
The bad:
- The voiceovers. Listening to them caused me pain
- Puzzles aren't particularly challenging
- Not extremely innovative story
The good:
- It's retro
- Minimalistic artwork is simple and elegant without being dull
- Artwork fits the period and plays into the themes
- The game seems to capture the spirit of the time
- Great if you're into point-and-clicks
- Great ambience/atmosphere
Overall:
It's a classic point-and-click adventure with a flair for design.

I've always liked sweet and short indie/doujin visual novels without choices. Season of 12 Colors seemed appealing to me due to its warm rural summer setting. After finishing the game, though, I was a bit disappointed.
The story starts off light and then turns into a bittersweet tragedy with magical fantasy elements. What I didn't like about it is pretty close to what bothered me in "Ame no Marginal" and "40 Days and 40 Night of Rain": The fantasy elements primary seem to serve to purpose of creating the drama; they aren't part of the world until they are needed, and inventing whatever rules are needed to give the story some emotional twists feels artificial to me.
I also wasn't too pleased with the writing quality. The translation was okay in general, but there were quite a few typos, grammar mistakes and awkward-sounding phrases – probably lines translated too close to the original text that don't sound good in English. Example:
"She has a simple life.
She has the 'current' moment.
She has a cute child with a laughter like sunshine."
Line 2 sounds really unnatural and line 3 makes no sense at all; it should probably be "was" instead of has.
The writing style is pretty simple, and while that's not necissarily a problem, "Season of 12 Colors" has (like most visual novels) no recognizable style which makes it feel a bit generic.
The art is pretty good. Warm colors, beautiful backgrounds, nice characters designs. The music was also decent.
Overall it's not a bad story, but if feels constructed and the writing style is fairly generic. I can see why people find "Season of 12 Colors" appealing – and I genuinely like some of its ideas –, but it just doesn't work for me. I can't say I regret the purchase, though, the pricing is very fair.
Recommendations for people who liked "Season of 12 Colors":
- Ame no Marginal -Rain Marginal- (short visual novel (~2-3h) available on Steam in the same style, but with more elaborate world building)
- 40 Days and Nights of Rain (short (~1h) free visual novel in the same style)
- planetarian (short visual novel (~5h) available on Steam with very good world and character building)
- True Remembrance (free short visual novel (~6h) with excellent writing, good world building and very sweet and warm character interactions –
)

A very low price tag for a brilliant piece of work. And although not everything about it was entirely great, I stand by my statement that this is well worth the £2 and I would happily have paid more for it.
The story is short but sweet; about three children who can only meet a few times during their lifetimes and under certain conditions, bound by time. The ending leaves room for interpretation and, for what it's worth, it was a fairly touching story. The "main story" is only a part of this and it should probably have been called something else because if you only play the "main story", you're going to think this game was a pile of garbage. Because not only is it not the whole story, but it is also fairly bland and has a lot of holes. You have to read the rest in order for things to make sense. All in all, I enjoyed the story.
The art, in my opinion, was pretty damn good. The simplistic style really seems to fit, especially considering it is Chinese and not Japanese. It was not made to be like other visual novels with a Japanese art style and I am happy they didn't take that route. Because of the art, this visual novel stood out to me. Not in any words I could put together to make comprehensible sense, but it stood out to me.
The music, going from one end of the spectrum of the other, at times, was damn irritating. The music box song in particular was verging on "difficult to bear". The rest of the music was nice and when combined with the art, created an atmosphere quite different from a lot of other stories.
There isn't much to say about the characters. We don't go into much depth about them since the story is the main focus and it is about what has happened to these characters during this time. There is very little character development and personality building and I suppose, that is okay. What we do see of them though are just standard children growing up in a small village. Playful, active and in every other respect, what you expect of children, and as they age, their personalities mature.
To conclude, I think that this visual novel is very much worth the read. But it seems to suffer from the same thing that a lot of good stories suffer from: you have to look past some things that without fail, will put a great number of people off before they progress. Fault milestone one and its prologue, Steins; gate and its slow start. This has a bland start and irritating music. I'm not comparing this low price visual novel to some of these really great pieces of work that will no doubt, still be being read far into the future because this will likely, and sadly, be forgotten. But, it is still a great piece of work well worth the £2.

***EDIT***
I was having a bit of difficulty understanding the bonus points system, so I asked the Dev to explain it a little, here is his response. I'm adding this to the review, because I thought it would be very helpful for people playing the game. I also thought it would be a good way to show that the Dev is actively involved. Cheers!
DEV RESPONSE FOLLOWS:
Here's the basics...
Left Click - If you direct hit a target (over the target on fire), you get a laser blast + bonus.
If not, you'll get a pulse shot which will auto-target in a certain radius.
Right Click - If you direct hit, you get another laser blast and a larger bonus than w/ left click.
In addition, it freezes the target. You can left shoot the target to explode it
Otherwise it's an energy beam (you can hold this down).
With this beam, you can use this beam to "energize target".
Energized targets are worth more points when shot.
When energized for a second or two, will freeze like on direct hits.
After a couple of second holding, you can release for a "photon pulse".
You can shoot this pulse for a large explosion and multi-target hit.
You can use the right click beam to redirect left click shots.
A few trick shots...
- Left click shots will stick & act a proximity mines. You can place them strategically.
- Lots of special shots: bounce/ricochet, quick shots, variety bonus (many bonus types active), detonations, and others.
Other tips...
- If you feel confident, right clicking for direct hits will get you about ~2x multiplier.
- You get points and multipliers. score = multiplier * score. So, if you have a high multiplier, any points you get will mean big points.
- Keeping your streaks going is key to large scores (sounds like you figured this out already).
- Accuracy is worth a lot, so don't miss (or use the right click beam to turn a miss into a hit). "Perfect accuracy" is a streak of direct hits.
- Perfect sections have a long cool-down. And if during that section, you dont miss or even better don't miss and hit with all direct hits you get modifiers on your perfect sections & they're worth much more.
- Unlocking the secret words can help keep streaks going. Also, each level has some hidden targets often places to help you keep streaks going. It's possible to make it through every level keeping your streak going the entire time (though this is not at all easy).
That's the basics :)

In Sum:  A frustrating adventure game with a good storyline and no replay value, but is overall satisfying.  4/5.
An old classic game that has caused a lot of headaches.  Deja Vu is the story of Ace Harding, a private detective with amnesia, in a film noir setting.  It is a kind of point-and-click adventure, I believe predating games like Maniac Mansion by a few years, and it requires quite a bit of thinking to play.
Graphically, it is well-done for the time.  There are very few animations, rather the game is played with still images and a set of commands to use.  Sound is minimal.  One thing the game does to annoy even modern gamers is a primative version of QTEs.  Every now and then, a thug will come up to rob you, giving you a few seconds to react.
This game is frustrating.  There are countless ways to die, most of them are unexpected.  Unlocking the wrong thing, taking a wrong turn, or even random encounters.  You have limited resources and it is possible to block yourself from finishing the game with too many taxi rides or firing too many bullets.  Unless you are using a walkthrough, you will have to play through this game many times to learn the exact steps you need to win, and using a walkthrough ruins the game.  This also makes the game have little replay value, once you have solved the case.  The story never changes, and there's not enough depth to keep you engaged in subsequent playthroughs.  That said, it is very satisfying when you finally get to the end, and close the case.
For classic game fans, and those who want to look at the roots of adventure games, this is possibly an essential game.

Déjà Vu and all the other MacVenture series games are some of the most entertainingly written adventure games I've played. It doesn't visually depict all of the actions, but instead uses its creative writing to allow you to visualize the events yourself, creating a much more powerful image than what any animation or cutscene could accurately portray.
The porting could have done with some polishing, though, as the recreated interface looks very amateurish with its generic font, blank right click context menu and clumsily resizing windows, strongly reminiscent of a quickly made flash game UI. Fortunately, these are relatively easy to ignore as everything is still functional.
The puzzles can be quite challenging and might require use of the good ol' pen and paper to remember vital information. Overall, the game doesn't have many seemingly absurd solutions, so beating it should be doable within some hours.
The weakest part of the game is the amnesia. The game starts out only allowing you to perform a specific amount of actions before your memory deteriorates further, and keeps doing this until you lose the game, having a chance of leading to save games you can't recover from due to too many actions before finding the cure.

Quick review: If you never played the game before, keep it that way.  If you remember playing this game, and really loved it, get it for the wonderful nostalgic value.  It hasn't changed in both the best and worst ways possible.
Déjà Vu is a pioneer game in the point & click adventure genre, making a visual transition from the classic text based adventures.  At the time of it's release, it was groundbreaking in giving players a true visual sense of the items and people they are interacting with.  Vibrant and distinct colors make the world come alive from text, but text is still used to give hard definition to the characteristics of each individual object and person.  Déjà Vu, along with the other MacVenture games, also made themselves distinctively different from the other games in their genre by allowing (or requiring) players to combine inventory items within the inventory, instead of only with the environment.  Many years ago, this game was ahead of it's generation.
Now time has caught up with it, and it is more of a solid piece of nostalgia rather than a classic game.  Playing it again since the last time I played it more than a decade ago, I am getting a flashback of just how hard it is to play.  Just like the old text based adventures, it is very unforgiving, has a steep learning curve, and my require you to reset your entire game over and over again to line every event up perfectly to win the game.  Way back when these games were released, we were astounded so much by the actual colors and freedom that we wanted to suffer through hard challenge to really get the full potential out of the game.  Now that the video game market is oversaturated with more games than can need more time than a human lifetime can offer, people need to be more picky than ever for what they are going to spend their time playing.  While this game was considered a gem back in the day, it may look more like another hard rock to the newer generation of gamers.

I enjoyed the original Ashes and Escalation is an iterative improvement which makes even better grand scale macro strategy game somewhere between Supreme Commander and Sins of a Solar Empire.
PROS:
- developers seem to care about their game and fixed a bug I reported quite quickly
- your decisions are more important than your typing/clicking speed (macro > micro)
- interesting territorry/resource control not unlike Z or WH40k
- grand scale, big maps with real terrain, ridiculous amount of units
- smooth unzoom to icons only map plus nice strategic map (improved in Escalation)
- amazing take on radar as a heat map
- massive dreadnoughts of doom (kinda like capital ships in Sins)
- units are quite smart and don't need much babysitting
- each units serves its purpose and unit composition matters (new units in Escalation)
- balanced defences (upgradable turrets in Escalation for turtles)
- air is an option (tech 2 air added in Escalation)
- orbital abilities to outsmart your opponents
- most of above has fabulous animations! PEW PEW PEW
- I really love the setting and story... we are to create singularity soon in RL after all :)
- very nice and responsive AI. I bet it's neural network based which is creepily relevant to the story :D
- assymetric races (PHC and Substrate)
- half the price for original Ashes owners (66 % discount like PA:T would be more appropriate, but mkay)
- great benchmark for your shiny new PC master race graphic card
CONS
- some people expected original Ashes to look like this and now feel cheated. That is a valid point, but OTOH it's a grand game in the end, so consider forgiving Stardock it took them a little bit more time and money to finish it. Much like Uber with PA:TITANS :)
- resouce intensive, can't play with potato computer peasants
- only 2 races... better than 3 unalanced and borken, I guess
OVERALL
For me, Ashes of the Singularity: Escalation is one of the most interesting and fresh RTS games I played in a long time.
Kudos Stardock!

This is honestly one of Telltales best games yet. And i'm not just saying that because I like Borderlands.
You can clearly see a lot of thought when in to this game, and the story is amazing.
Note: this game has spoilers for Borderlands 2. As does this review.
The game takes place between two main characters: Rhys and Fiona.
Rhys works for Hyperion, and even after Handsome Jack died, the company was still hated by everyone on Pandora. One man named Rhys, with his friend Vaughn, attempt to get a promotion and move up the ranks in Hyperion, only to find their boss has been murdered by a man named Hugo Vasquez. Hugo demotes Rhys to janitor, so he decides to get revenge. After finding out Hugo is attempting to buy a vault key, he, with the help of Vaughn, steals ten million dollars to buy the vault key. Obviously, things dont go as planned. Mainly, ten million dollars explode. Now, they must survive on Pandora in an attempt to find a vault using old Atlas tech called "Gortys".
Fiona is a woman living in Hollow point with her sister Sasha and her "friend" Felix. They worked as stealers and theifs as children. Once, they tried to steal Felix's watch. Not only did he stop them, he took them in and showed them how to do it better. Fast forward a few years, they're gonna get ten million bucks off some Hyperion chumps. How? Make a fake vault key and sell it to them for money. Obviously, things dont go as planned. Such as the vault key breaking.  Now, they must survive on Pandora in an attempt to find a vault using old Atlas tech called "Gortys".
Now that you know the basic plot, the game really goes deep in to it. It goes through every detail of what happens to these "Vault Hunters" and how they recover from all the mistakes they've made. It's also nice to see that you can make choices to choose how people see you, and really affect what the characters think of you and what you think of them.
The characters dont feel bland, they feel real and lively, and its nice to see them interact with one another.
The plot also talks a lot about Atlas, the company from Borderlands 1, and what happened to Hyperion after Borderlands 2, something i'm sure were all excited to see.
The plot is great, but what about the music? The music in the game is astounding. They use a lot of songs you might have heard before, such as The Rapture - Pieces of the people we love, or Shawn Lee's Ping Pong Orchestra - Kiss the Sky. The song are amazing and fit so well in with the game you feel as if these songs were made for every awesome point they appear. As for the original music, they definetly fit in with the moment and are a nice touch to all the action scenes.
Graphics. Well, I don't really need to go over that. It's frickin' Borderlands. You already know it looks great.
Overall:
Story: 9/10
Music: 10/10
Graphics: 9/10
Choices: 8/10
Overall Gameplay: 9/10
Tales from the Borderlands is Telltales best game yet. With action, humor, fitting music and great gameplay all around, it's definetly a hit for anyone who loves Point and Click games or Borderlands. So, when you think you're man enough, click that Add to Cart button and enjoy the Telltale game of a lifetime.
