Don't be fooled by the Tron visuals, this game is as dull as it is basic.
Big areas with nothing in them. All the different environments you see in the screen shots are exactly that, environments. Empty locations with nothing going on but a few blinky lights.
Standing in for content in this game are the powers and some puzzles.
Powers are 100% contextual and are mostly used for opening doors. Blue power opens the blue doors. Green, green doors, etc... you could replace all the powers with keys or buttons and nothing would have been lost.
The puzzles are worse just because they are so lazy. A bunch of standard computer game puzzles that look like they were copied from a book. There is no real reason for them to be there and they have little context in the environments they're dropped into.
If  there is a story it's hard to get invested in. None of the areas connect to each other and there are no stakes to raise or reasons to keep moving forward.
Look, save yourself the trouble,  just tear up some Sudoku and glue the pages into a book of concept art. Then you'll have the exact experience of this game but you'll also be able to take it on the bus while you're going to do something more interesting with your life.

This part goes to those who think "this is just some angry veteran who doesn't like the change. Nobody cares!" Pretty decent game but not that great either since it has a few problems.
It's a good action/adventure game but not that great of a puzzle game, which is mainly what I was expecting from it.
+ The puzzle mechanics are pretty interesting and original
+ Really nice artstyle, the world is colorful and interesting to look at
+ Good soundtrack
+ Fairly interesting story
+ Good length. Took me about 14 hours to get through the game
+ Multiple endings don't require you to replay through the whole game or certain levels again
+ You can replay any level you want at any time using the game's hub, even after finishing the game
+ You don't have to replay through the whole levels if you just want to find the secrets, which is nice for people like me who like to find all the secrets and/or get all of the achiemevents
+ Finding secrets gives you more information about the story and characters which is a nice incentive to find them (if you're actually interested in the story)
- You can't save in the middle of a level. Which is a bit annoying sometimes considering that they pretty much all have multiple puzzles in them
- The puzzle aren't always balanced that well. Sometimes the solution will be way too easy and sometimes it will be frustrating, either because:
- Some of the environnements honestly don't make any sense, even after having finished the game and seeing all endings
- Voice acting is pretty cringy at times
- Sound design could use some work. Some sounds were either too loud, bugged or just not there
- Minor spoiler:
- Can't skip cutscenes or credits, which is fine when you're seeing them for the first time but a bit annoying when you're replaying levels or trying to get the other endings
- Even though the HUB section of the game is pretty interesting and useful, it's a bit too big in my opinion. A lot of empty space
- The jumping feels a bit clunky although you rarely need to use it so it can be overlooked
- Even though there's not a lot of them, the jumpscares are still pretty annoying and completely out of place. I have absolutely no idea what were the point of them or how they even have anything to do with the story, even after beating the game
- Game is too dark. Had the gamma all the way up the whole game otherwise I could barely see anything in some of the levels.
TLDR: As an action/adventure game, this is a pretty good game with an interesting story and nice looking world. As a puzzle game though, it has too many problems for me to recommend it.
I'd suggest waiting for it to go on sale if you intend to buy it

I cannot tell if this game was supposed to be challenging and unforgiving, or if it is simply broken. The motto for the game is "Every choice has consequences," but you'll find absolutely zero freedom in making these choices. Gameplay consists of executing tasks assigned to you by the government and by your house tenants. There is no way for you to know what the consequences will be until you are *forced* to play through the game several times. (You know how everyone just LOVES replaying the same boring dialogue over and over in games? Well, get ready to do it about a dozen times.) You'll devote hours to a playthrough, only to get caught in a loop where your character inevitably gets overcharged for a completely random fee and gets fired. When you reload, this will happen over and over again until you finally resolve to just start the entire game over. The game forces you to do this until you make the "correct" choices, at which point I assume you feel the same level of satisfaction one feels upon completing a standardized test. While the idea behind this game is brilliant, this has got to be the least fun execution one could imagine.
In short, if you want to experience what it must feel like to be a bureacrat in an Orwellian police state, this game will browbeat you into submission until you forget your own free will.

This game carefully walks the line between ARMA and Battlefield. This is not a serious military simulator or a casual arcade shoot-'em-up, if you expect either you are likely to be disappointed. This is an early access game, but the game mechanics are nearly fully flushed out and there are minimal bugs. The dev team is responsive and active in the community. The community is generally helpful and teamwork minded.
Your enjoyment will be improved if you choose servers with active admins and join a helpful Squad Lead in-game. A microphone is essentially a requirement and you shouldn't purchase this game if you are not comfortable talking with your fellow squadmates.
A few other things:
There is no leveling-up, weapon skins (aside from a few modifications for early supporters), or in-game monetization. There are vehicles in the game, but they are important team assets - so don't expect to be able to jump in one without consulting your SL.
One of my few complaints is that the Steam page does not make it crystal clear that there are currently no 50v50 servers - this is a development goal (and will certainly happen) but it is not supported at the current moment. Instead, most servers host 40v40 battles. If you are on the fence, wait for v10.

You are a beholder - a ministry-installed landlord of a war-torn totalitarian state. One that is responsible for everything that happens under your management regardless of how you may feel about those actions. As a loyal beholder, you must gather profiles on your tenants, report any wrongdoings, and strong-arm them into following the government directives (such as the ban of rubber duckies and blue ties). As the game progresses, however, you begin to develop opinions on the state of the regime and wonder whether sticking with the status-quo is absolutely necessary. To make matters more complicated, multiple dissenting groups will do their best to persuade you towards their visions for the future. Who knew spying held so much responsibility?
There are many methods available to help ensure maximum cooperation from your tenants. The first of which requires installing security cameras throughout the apartments. Alternatively, you can just as well look through an apartment door's peephole to see what may be going on within, but personally, I prefer to casually walk right in with my handy master key. Unfortunately, tenants will not allow anyone to rifle through their belongings with such wanton prejudice, so you must be sneaky about it. Honestly though, searching for evidence of criminal activity is the least of their problems. In fact, if the beholder wants someone arrested, evicted, or blackmailed, why not just plant evidence outright? After all, the beholder is an upright representative of the ministry with authority to act in the state's best interest - as long as he doesn't get caught.
Beholder paints a truly immersive world devoid of hope, happiness, or color, rife with propaganda and rebellious behavior. Daily newspapers released by the government have "Voices of Truth" attached to the back countering and revealing dark behaviors concealed by Big Brother. Assassination attempts are a plenty as you discover the alternate lives your tenants maintain. In addition, questlines clue you in on the tenants' problems just as much as your own families.  People desire entertainment to distract them from their own problems, but they also need food, bribe money, security, and favors. You are free to straddle the line between honorable ministry representative and revolutionist at will, but understand that no matter how noble your intentions may be, they may lead to unintended harm. Furthermore, Big Brother is always watching.
Regarding the actual gameplay, Beholder is a management sim with point & click controls, and it is deviously hard. For the most part, you will be provided one or two ministry/primary tasks, such as "Investigate X," "Convince X," or "Kill X," alongside 3-4 complementary side quests at any given time. Most of these tasks will have a time limit and require socializing, profiling, or blackmailing tenants to proceed. Depending on how you chose to execute these tasks, you may be fined by the ministry or police, and if you become bankrupt, the game will end prematurely. With multiple endings all wildly different from each other, additional playthoughs using differing styles of philosophy and quest progression are needed.
After achieving a somewhat "good" ending, I am left with a desire for the implementation of multiple difficulty levels. Although the story and initial playthrough was really fun and immersive, end-game became too money-oriented to care about anything else but retaining what I had and blackmailing as many tenants as I could before a deadline was up. I began choosing certain options solely on the basis of how much I might financially benefit from the situation. The moment I began to think, "I only have $X left, I need to say 'no' to everything now," is the moment Beholder becomes less impacting. Furthermore, certain endings are entirely dependent upon key choices made throughout the game, but many of these key choices all seem to be whether there was enough money to do X.

Having money be so vital to proceed is a bit of a nuisance in Beholder. It makes restarting a save from a game over very immersion-breaking because the knowledge of oncoming charges will force certain choices. This compulsion to do a particular action just for money cripples any emotional consequence in turn. Beholder should continue using the early-game style of having dire and unexpected consequences to impart the psychological agony that would persuade, not force, the player to act in a particular manner. I understand that the developers want to create a sense of harsh, soul-agonizing realism, but the story and world already did a good enough job in that aspect that I wanted to explore certain quest avenues or maintain a specific philosophy but couldn't. All because of bills and random end-game money barriers.
Even though I feel that Beholder needs to rework its money-centric nature, or add more difficulty/personalization options for it, I still found its unique spying aspect and management sim gameplay fun enough to come back for more. The thrill in having so much control over the tenants is indescribable, and catching someone in a criminal activity is empowering. The detailed world-building, strongly defined tenant characters, and surprising scripts make Beholder a worthy addition in any spy fan's library.

I love casual logic puzzles like these, non timed, non action but a lot of the time I can finish them in 1-2hrs as they are either very short or too easy - those are usually under a $1 but I found the slightly higher price here was worth it as this was the perfect level for a relaxing casual game with a cuppa.  By medium level (people and houses) most were at the level of taking anywhere from 10 -20 mins each to solve/plant fences, not hair pulling but not 'this is so boring as I don't have to work it out as its so easy'.  I did get stuck at a couple for about 45 mins each but I never felt that I was never going to get it.
Gameplay - divide the squares equally between the neighbours, by adding fences, making sure each has a person, house and eventually fruit in their area.  I really like that it has a level map so if you get stuck in a puzzle there are usually 2 other puzzles you can play.  There also is a change the view button,  you can turn and tilt it by moving it with mouse, even playing top down. You can zoom in and out using the scroll button on mouse.
It's fun, cute and there are 101 levels.  There are fun sayings on the loading scenes between the puzzles (one of them had a typo on it).  If you are looking for a hard puzzle game this isn't for you but for the rest of us who want to relax, take our time and get a few hours out of a casual game, this ticks all the boxes.
Worth every penny.

Should You Buy It; Can I Run It?
======================
I'm sure you've read plenty of reviews about what Squad is, etc.  But I'm going to take a different angle to this review.
This is because I've just upgraded my old system (well, graphics card) and will complete the upgrade of the rest of the system by June '17.
So, as the title suggests...
Do consider that I have not done any controlled testing, only using the ingame FPS/unit stat system.
When I purchased this game some time ago my specs were:
i7 930 -- HD5970 (one core disabled = 1GB vram) -- 6GB RAM -- 5400rpm HDD.
Yup, it's an old system, around seven years olds in fact!
To play Squad I had to use minimum settings and at 1080p I was getting around 35fps.  I know, right, a shocker!  The play was actually smooth enough on average but seriously let down by the 1GB vram = serious stutter/freeze loading textures.
Do realise that the freezes were for several endless seconds making it unplayable, but I'd say for the most part, I played okay.  But note, spawning in was a freeze/lag hell - urgh.
And spinning around fast stutters to f*ck.
Soooo, what happened when the aging GPU was replaced with something somewhat more modern?!  In this case I upgraded to an RX580 8GB.
Well, load in times were still long (as expected) and after bumping up the settings to max, I was getting a good steady 50fps @1080p.  Smooth as silk (for a 60hz monitor, that is) and I had no stutters.  Bliss.  I'm sure if I tweak the settings slightly, I'll get 60fps.  It can dip around heavy fighting, but not enough to effect the running of the game!
I'll return when I've upgraded my mobo, CPU, RAM and drive (will be a SSD).
CONCLUSION
=========
Aging systems can play Squad. Albeit, on lowest settings, and with suffering stutters/freezing at spawn/loading and during gameplay at certain times.  If you can deal with that sort of thing, then you may well want to try Squad at least.
And if you have an okay GPU, I'm sure it'll be a better experience on older gear.
As for Squad itself to play as a game -- joyous!  I came from Project Reality (BF2PR) and I'm glad the community spirit (in most part) made it across and I look forward to Squad getting up to par with content.

Ashes Escalation is a push of the game towards gameplay more in line with Suprème Commander.

A map editor is available and support for modding will be coming soon.
This suggests it will have all the tools to keep it a community driven game for quite a long time.

I've played RimWorld for years. It's a fascinating, and grueling simulator that inspires a true connection between the player, the colonists and their environment. It's an effective time sink and you can easily loose hours to the old "just one more thing" mentality. My initial reaction to the game was how it looked, seemingly simple, but you soon find yourself marveling at its quiet complexity.
Way back when I started playing this game (before steam), it was a fantastic and some might say seemingly complete game, but the developer has pushed on, adding more content and a better play experience. It truely is a work of genious, and I thoroughly expect great new things in RimWorld.
It is punishing though, hours into a build, you have perfectly happy colonists with epic rooms and houses, stout defences, and farms stretching for miles. Then all of a sudden a sequence of unrelenting rage quit events occur.
a) A pack of man hunting wildboars descend during a solarflare or eclipse, your turrets are out and you have to fend the beasts away yourself.
b) Shortly after the Glorious Pirate Mongoose's decide to raid bringing with them a flurry of submachine guns and molotovs.
c) Your farms are soon torched, and old Wilson is being mauled by an embittered boar near the mysterious building. The pirates have stormed the living quarters, overpowering your colonists, and stealing the women. Then the rains come dowsing the fires, the solar flare passes and power returns. Your defences kick in and Old Wilson killed the boar with his prosthetic leg Peggy. Can you reclaim your once great colony? Alex get's wilson to bed and starts treatment. The few remaining colonists quickly replant the fields and repair the damage... but whats this TOXIC FALLOUT and aliens.... fml... Wilson timet to get Peggy out again!
You've got to love RimWorld!

An under-rated gem for those who like epic space battles on a small scale. Gameplay focuses on ship level tactics rather than resource gathering and production found in other space RTS games.  You will generally control between 1 and 8 ships, ranging from fast and mobile frigates, to slow, hulking carriers, and of course support from fighters, bombers and boarding craft. Ships can be customized for specific tasks, like bringing down shields, disabling systems, and artillery etc, but is restricted by the cost of repairs and purchasing equipment between missions.
The attention to detail on the ships is still unparalleled. Weapons are mounted on specific points on a ship's hull, it must manouevre to bring them to bear on its target. When zoomed in you can even see the weapons firing indivudally. Similarly every system on a ship can be targetted for desctruction individually, with the right tools. Want to clear the way for your fighters? Take out their flak cannon, want to make them easier to target or stop a pursuit? Target their engines.
Unfortunately, some technical issues remain. Occasional scripting problems and crashing carry over from the original release, and can be quite frustrating, given the pace of the game is relatively slow. There is no option to speed up time for the sometimes slow travelling between waypoints. There is no widescreen support, and in fact, changing resolution does not seem to work at all..

Unlocking characters ingame by being better and having unlock progression and achievments is something awesome and makes me feel like a kid that just bought a game for the first time, a feeling I didn't have for many years. Warning: I uninstalled Wallpaper Engine today.
WHY: Image Stuttering even in Web Browser (fullscreen with the wallpaper stopped).
After serveral weeks of testing I found my error ... named "Wallpaper Engine"
My Setup: (old but stable)
i7 2600k
24GB RAM
GTX960 4GB
250 GB SSD
Windows 7 64bit (lastest updates)
Screens:
3* 1440p and 1* 2160p (4k)
I used Wallpaper Engine only on ONE SCREEN at 1440p with a looped Video (about 100MB -> RAM).
I noticed some stuttering images after I tested some websites and movies lately (Blu-Ray@PC).
The following seems to happen:
Wallpaper Engine is creating the Background at 25-30 FPS (see config tab - my case: 30)
If I open Firefox OR Chrome OR some desktop tools to check display stuttering on every screen I got the following results:
Test yourself at:

(they have nice tests) OR use any other tool
Left screen:  Framerate is capped at 30 FPS
Middle Screen: Framerate is stuttering between 25-60 FPS even in fullscreen.
Right screen: Framerate is nearly always at 60 FPS ~can be seen as stable
After I stopped Wallpaper Enigne the following result:
Left screen:  Framerate is capped at 30 FPS  & stable
Middle Screen: Framerate is capped at 30 FPS & stable
Right screen: Framerate is capped at 30 FPS & stable
Because the setup isnt made to run all Screens at 60 FPS I found one post which shows that 30FPS is better than unstable 30-60FPS and I can strongly confirm this. That's why Windows is forcing the IDLE setup to 30FPS which is nice and power saving.
After testing around I can confirm that even the 60FPS are stable on all screens now (not at the same time but at least one Screen at Time even high bitrate isn't a problem)
Would be nice to see this issue fixed because a laggy web experience isn't what I wanted. To fix the problem I had to close Wallpaper Engine. After I unchecked startup with Windows I uninstalled because I don't need to waste that disk space.

Borderlands is a series that puts heavy focus upon the whole "shooting and looting" thing, so some people might imagine that taking all that away would leave an uninteresting, empty husk of a game. This might be the case if the story and writing were on par with the rest of the Borderlands series, but trust me; it isn't. It's brilliant.
It plays similarly to most other Telltale games--limited time dialogue choices with a scattering of QTEs and adventure game elements, which are nothing special by themselves. So, Tales from the Borderlands relies entirely on a great story to make it work. And I can assure you, it deilvers.
Despite the fact that Gearbox have handed over the keys to Telltale on this one, it hasn't lost its soul. In my opinion, the writing is exponentially better than any Borderlands game to date! It still contains the same sort of wacky humor that BL fans know and love, but it doesn't feel like it's trying so hard to be funny and seems much more well done. Not only that, but playing as a non-vault hunter who, although capable, has reason to be afraid of all the insanity on Pandora, shows the Borderlands universe in a new light. I absolutely love it.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game. If you're a fan of the Borderlands series and have enjoyed the stories in the previous games, Tales from the Borderlands is a no-brainer. If you're not familiar with the Borderlands series, it's still a great game in its own right--however, since it contains major spoilers to the ending of Borderlands 2, I would recommend picking that up first.

Played during the free weekend to get a feel for the game, and I have to say that it was a great experience. The controls are challenging to get used to, but once you do, it becomes a real game. The learning curve is greater than CoD and Battlefield, but equally enjoyable. The community is generally willing to help out when you're new, as long as you keep in contact. The VIOP options are a little confusing at first, but you quickly get a feel for it under the pressure of the battles.
The maps are a decent size, and the heavily focused squad play is amazing. Battlefield may have introduced me, but Squad has won me.
However, I did have some slight problems while playing, such as the URE4 crashing mid game, my own hardware doing stupid things (my fault), and EAC liking to not validate and stay validated for longer periods of play.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the game, and will be keeping an eye on the development.

"Ashes of the Singularity: Escalation" plays very much like the original "Ashes", but with more content.  As a fan of "Supreme Commander", I enjoyed the addition of a strategic zoom.  There are also more units, more map types (volcanic & crystalline), and the ability to play up to 14 players on some maps.  This is a standalone, so you don't need the original "Ashes" to play this.  The only real issue I have with "Escalation" is the pricing with regards to existing "Ashes" owners.  If you don't own the original, then "Escalation" will cost $40...this is fair I think considering the amount of playtime you can get out of this.  If you do own the original however, the price is reduced to $20.  Some people may not appreciate shelling out $20 for some extra features.  While I appreciate that these kinds of things costs money to produce, I think they could have discounted the price a bit more to benefit loyal customers.  All in all though, "Escalation" is a wonderful looking RTS that I'd recommend to any RTS player, even to those folks like me who refuse to use hotkeys.  ;)

I'm a long time fan of epic RTS like Supreme Commander, Sins of a Solar Empire. So I was really excited when the developer of Sins released Ashes of Singularity in April. Unfortunately I was quite dissapointed at the time because the game was very simplified and all it comes down to is building blubs of units and pushes the blubs back and forth on the map. After playing for about two hours I requested a refund.
I decided to give it another try after the developer gathered enough feedbacks from vet RTS players and released Escalation. I'm more satisfied this time around as there are more variety of specialized units and more different tactics you can employ. The defense structures are more boosted that makes it less tedious and frustrating to hold key strategic positions. It plays a lot like Sins of a Solar Empire Rebellion now, although it is not in space the spirit of the gameplay is truly there, something I couldn't say about the original Ashes. It is not quite a Supreme Commander sequel, instead much more like Sins in terms of the feel and the flow of the game.
Graphically it is a treat as I'm a big fan of giant energy beams flashing back and forth, the scale of the battle is truely epic even in short skirmishes. The AI is very smart and competent, a rare thing in modern RTS's when most developers don't care much about single players anymore. I also like a lot the new strategic zoom which is very easy to use.
I think a few things can be improved. The audio is meh and I wish I can play custom music. and there is no random map generator, a thing I really liked in Sins, but according the the developer that is because most of the machines today don't have 64GB RAM required for a RMG. I also wish I can land the air units because they circles when idle and is quite difficult to select with mouse.
These are small complaints but the overall game is quite good and worthy to recommand now. If you are a fan of Sins of a Solar Empire then you can't go wrong buying this one.

Rimworld is a game where you can make your own stories. These stories go down branches that you and Ai Storyteller lay down for your colonists, watch and guide them into making an thriving community.
The game has a good concept of how you control the fate of individuals who have been stranded on a suppose deserted planet, you can make the experience into that of a story. It's amazing how things go, sometimes you can make flourishing trade outposts, though the story tellers won't always allow that. They will sometimes go out of their way to make your colonists' lives to be a living hell. Raiders will loot, raze and slaughter those of your colony. Packs of beast run in through your colony and maul your loved characters to bare bone. Dormant machines will wake and vaporize intruders who trespass in their ancient bases. All of this for the sake of story.
One can survive these odds at times if they prepare well, stock up on food and forge new weapons to arm your colonists. Though all doesn't need to be bloodshed, there are storytellers who provide you more times of peace and a calmer setting for stories. While others will seek to make it an living hell like dear Randy, he is such a sadist. Though you, the player have control of the outcome, based on all that you do and how you do it.
You can make tales of adventure, drama, love, and tragedy through most of your actions. The outcomes are based on your decisions and planning, building bases, managing the supplies, and maintaining relations with other factions is up to you. Tired of some elements? Download some mods and spice up the atmosphere of your story further. As it can be a story of many things, it's your story.
With the updates the game is running more and more smoothly it is definitely a game to get if you like police officers, firefighters, and EMS workers.

Got the game for €8 instead of €20 in the Steam Halloween Sales 2016. After exactly 2 hours, I asked for a refund, but the threshold timing is coincidence.
Random game-breaking bug(s?) in combination with a ridiculous savegame concept where you have to do a whole mission again if you abort it (and, only slightly annoying, you start over in the mission hub, not at the start of the mission), so e.g. you can't stop at some point in a mission, because the missions' checkpoint concept only applies in-memory. The hub world's checkpoint concept is persistent, but those checkpoints are far apart; can't say if that matters, didn't play enough to find out if this can result in annoying situations, so far it was alright.
At first, I had trouble finding emotional access to the game, because there was no context of how to interpret the literally otherworldly situations, but then eventually the world was explained and made sense. At this point, I was finally beginning to actually be interested, but before this could gain momentum, I reached the hub and chose one of the missions - the leftmost one - and, far in, encountered a game-breaking bug that, based on a video I saw where it didn't occur, seems to happen randomly.
The only thing I could do was to exit to the menu and then click "continue" - which placed me in the hub again. When I had first entered the mission and turned around to touch the exit, I had already seen the message that says the mission would completely reset if I leave it before completing it, and I assume this applies to all missions. The video showing the first mission was almost 7 minutes long, but the person playing it knew exactly what to do at all times, so expect 10-25 minutes while you still need to figure out what's what. And you can't interrupt, or you have to do it all over again, place the platforms, push the buttons, carefully navigate above the abyss.
Far in the first mission, there was a pipeline-like puzzle where I had to arrange two sets of pipes. When I was done with the left set, I fiddled with the right set, but suddenly those pipes stopped being interactive. So I had to start
over. The savegame concept is unacceptable as it is, but when game-breaking bugs like this are in the mix, the only winning move is not to play.
It would feel like walking a tightrope, constantly thinking "I hope the game doesn't break". How are you supposed to enjoy the world / story with that load on your mind, gnawing at your nerves? You're constantly threatened with extreme frustration - why should I put up with this when there are hundreds of other games I could play or spend money on?
Fixing the game-breaking bug(s?) would help, too, but that's secondary.
You see your body when looking down (at least the legs). You can walk, run (optionally as a toggle), crouch (optionally as a toggle; I found the process of crouching down a bit too slow, and it also doesn't go down far enough for my taste), jump. There's no mantling/climbing, so if you meet a wall that's a wee bit to high for your jump, you're out of luck.
The footstep sounds of normal ground (e.g. in hub) seem to be the original Dark Engine sounds (Thief, System Shock 2), which I liked a lot. I'm not sure if I find them completely apt, and I guess the reason is that as opposed to the Dark Engine games, you're just a levitating camera (With legs.) in Soul Axiom: The natural walk-sway isn't there. I know some people have problems with such things, but making such effects optional has been normal in gaming for the longest time.
You will attain powers that you can use at any time, but they are only effective on specific (clearly marked, once you know what to look for) objects. I agree with the complaint of another reviewer: The powers are delayed too much, you feel hindered. This is ok most of the time, but at other times you feel imprisoned (e.g. when turning the pipes in that game-breaking bug situation). After handling several dozens of objects with the green power, due to the delay I still don't know if the reset animation of objects always plays in full or if I can interrupt it. The delay makes use of the powers feel wooden. It would also have been a lot better if the powers' sounds would not play when you're not actually affecting an object: You can make the power gesture at any time, and if you do that while aiming at the right type of object, the effect this has on the object makes the sound fit well, and that's why it feels wrong when the sound plays even if you're just aiming at thin air. Silence or an alternative sound would be better.
You can reconfigure the input. I think I also saw options for controllers but don't remember. I moved all controls from WASD to arrow keys with no problems.
Mouse is not accelerated - just like it has to be. Mouse speed is adjustable.
Thankfully, and this is rare enough, the game has FOV controls that go far enough for my needs. I use a 49" 16:9 screen at arm's length distance, because as opposed to the vast majority, I have understood that a 3D 1st person interface is meant to
your real-world 1st person, so a bigger screen means better use of / better working interface, which e.g. expresses in the fact that I have no problems doing 1st person 3D platforming, because due to higher FOV, objects that are further away are clearly smaller, so I can estimate distances properly. I like to be immersed when I play, so I try to be
instead of just looking at it on a rectangle somewhere over there in front of me.
I had to crank up the FOV slider to max, which showed "100", and I am convinced that this is vertical FOV, because 100° horizontal (at 16:9) would be way too low for me. When standing with my back in a 90° corner in this game, I could see
walls, even when I reduced the FOV to "90", so it's definitely higher than 90° horizontal.
I tried to play at 4K with all settings maxed, but my (powerful) machine couldn't give me full 60 FPS, which is normal, so the game's rendering doesn't seem to either be slow or lightning-fast. Playing at 1920x1080 was just fine.
The graphics are very dark, but there's a gamma slider which helps a little. The darkness is in the design, not in the rendering. With your powers "out", you emit a bit of light, so you can amend this when standing close to stuff. The darkness is not really a problem, it's just a bit much overall, I find.
The graphics are simple and (mainly due to their glow and glowing lines) remind a lot of the awesome
while by far not reaching their heights (at least up to the point where I played), but they are also not bad: They have proper game studio level, not just amateur level.
Don't buy unless the savegame concept is completely overhauled, or considerable frustration from time to time is guaranteed.
If they fix those problems, and if they also reduce the powers' delay that feels so wooden, it might be a great 3D 1st person story campaign puzzler. Can't tell because I stopped at 2 hours.

VIDEO VERSION:
STORY:
According to the Steam page, “You’re a State-installed Landlord in a totalitarian State. You must spy on tenants, peep, eavesdrop and profile! You must report on anyone capable of plotting subversion against the State. You MUST! But WILL you?”. You play as Carl Stein, the new Landlord/Public servant of the Class D apartment block on Krushvitze 6 and need to spy on your tenants and report to the Ministry of Order. You and your family just moved in and were given an apartment on the building's first floor and as you are entering it, you face the predecessor being taken by the police in handcuffs. As new government directives are being released during the month of September 1984, you need to check if said tenants are following the rules and aren’t making or under possession of anything illegal, even if it takes you to eavesdrop them, get inside their homes and install surveillance hidden cameras to keep an eye on them. Even when they are not committing any crimes, the Ministry might decide to order you to evict some of them, so it is up to you to convince them to leave or frame them in order to report them to the police. But before you can say “I won’t be corrupted, I’ll play by the rules”, remember this: You have two kids and one of them might get sick and need a treatment that’s worth 20,000 bucks at the same time the other will be kicked from the university if you don’t pay 15,000 in order to get them to do research for the dean. Yep. Life’s tough.
GAMEPLAY:
In Beholder, you need to manage your building’s issues and get its residents to obey the Law. So not only you need to fill files with their activities and hobbies, you’ll also need to help them find their glasses and get them girl’s numbers. Your help increases your Reputation points, which can help you to convince tenants to do what you want (at a high cost, but will do). Also, depending on what you choose to let or prohibit them to do, will cause the Ministry to order you to evacuate them for disturbance.
You need to click on people, doors and furniture in order to interact with them. You can talk to them, repair apartments, rent them, search for clues, put items in different places, steal items, unlock doors, look through keyholes, knock on doors and, amazingly enough, you can double click to run to the hills when the apartment owner you’re sneaking in has just arrived. You should also be thoughtful on your decisions, since they can get people to threaten you or even go further.
Also, your tenants sometimes are glad to help you, so it stands up to your ethical decisions on what to do with them. No pressure.
To eavesdrop, install cameras and search rooms is pretty easy, the hard part is to notice how you can report information to your boss. At least for me.
Something that got me♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥was the characters layers, at times I couldn’t talk to a character or search a piece of furniture because there was more than one element at the same location. It is also important to point out that Beholder can easily be compared to Papers, Please style of game, especially its bureaucracy towards filling reports with correct information! No, it’s DEFINITELY FUN, OK!?
DESIGN, PRESENTATION AND MUSIC:
As a George Orwell fan, I couldn’t help but notice the references to the to-ta-litA-ri-a-nism in “1984”, same year when Carl moves to the building. One of the most relevant element on the game is the characters’ design: They all look like shadows, simply being painted black with white eyes and having different body shapes and pieces of clothing for the player to tell them apart. The color palette is pretty simple but helps you when you need to pay close attention to something.
The character’s thoughts and intentions show when they are somewhere everyone can see them or when you have cameras inside their apartments.
The soundtrack fits the game and the atmosphere and kinda helps you to get in the mood. The sound effects are a bit too simple and generic, sometimes missing when you open a door or being too exaggerated when you get mail and turn it around.
CONCLUSION:
Considering that I’ve played this game for 4 hours, have unlocked 11% of its achievements and still wanna see how far I can go for at least another 2-3 hours; the 7,99 dollars spent are worth being caught a few times, fired another couple and killed once.
As “boring” as it may sound, Beholder is super enjoyable for its many possibilities, after all, it is a game about spying your neighbors, reporting and getting them to jail, but it might also be seen as a survival game in a Totalitarian State, which is extremely hard sometimes!
Like ARMA? Want a better game than ARMA? SQUAD is here to help.

Borderlands is a series that puts heavy focus upon the whole "shooting and looting" thing, so some people might imagine that taking all that away would leave an uninteresting, empty husk of a game. This might be the case if the story and writing were on par with the rest of the Borderlands series, but trust me; it isn't. It's brilliant.
It plays similarly to most other Telltale games--limited time dialogue choices with a scattering of QTEs and adventure game elements, which are nothing special by themselves. So, Tales from the Borderlands relies entirely on a great story to make it work. And I can assure you, it deilvers.
Despite the fact that Gearbox have handed over the keys to Telltale on this one, it hasn't lost its soul. In my opinion, the writing is exponentially better than any Borderlands game to date! It still contains the same sort of wacky humor that BL fans know and love, but it doesn't feel like it's trying so hard to be funny and seems much more well done. Not only that, but playing as a non-vault hunter who, although capable, has reason to be afraid of all the insanity on Pandora, shows the Borderlands universe in a new light. I absolutely love it.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game. If you're a fan of the Borderlands series and have enjoyed the stories in the previous games, Tales from the Borderlands is a no-brainer. If you're not familiar with the Borderlands series, it's still a great game in its own right--however, since it contains major spoilers to the ending of Borderlands 2, I would recommend picking that up first.
If you want a game where teamwork is essential and a fantastic community that follows through with the games values, but is more relaxed than Arma, this is the game for you.

A great game with limits, and if those limits were bypassed then this game would go from great to amazing.
Anyone who has played this game several times after the likely unavoidable deaths knows what I'm talking about.  This game desperately needs a sandbox/endless mode where events and outcomes are randomized, as well as tenants and their traits, etc.  If this were in the game it would seriously push this game to greater heights.
As it stands however the game itself is still quite good.  The characters are very basic looking, very LIMBO'esque, but they serve their purpose and I think given the atmosphere in general it's very suiting.
The premise of the game is as follows : you get greeted with quests gradually that are typically the same with each playthrough, the order which can be jumbled slightly depending who you choose to rent apartments to.  These quests usually have a timer, in which if you do not meet the requirements it's typically game over.   You'll learn from your mistakes in the game from your first couple play-throughs and adapt accordingly to keep getting further.
If this game ever adds an endless/sandbox mode where you just constantly spy on new tenants that are always different, that'd add so much replayability to this game, and I really hope it's a feature added later in the game and if so I think everyone who has purchased this game or anyone on the fence with this game will greatly appreciate it.
If such a feature were added, a larger house to look after would be great, as well as possibly Steam Workshop support for users to create/modify tenants and/or scenarios to constantly add new fresh content to this game would be outstanding.  Here's to hoping anyways.  *crosses fingers*

This game is neither Mario Kart nor CTR; it is not an attempt at a clone thereof. This is an entirely different game. More accurately, this game runs along the vein of Crash Tag Team racing, but this game is not about racing: it is a battle game. Remember the Battle Mode of Mario Kart and CTR/Crash Nitro Kart and how it always seemed so slow-paced, with everyone running around in circles trying to hit everyone? This game takes the battle mode to a higher pace, forcing everyone to be close together going around in a circuit. There are no laps, just points accumulated with respect to survival. This game is extremely fun, but like I said, set aside all preconceived notions that this might be a Mario Kart/CTR clone and accept that this is a battle game within the setting of moving vehicles.
Furthermore, the vehicle dynamics seem different than other racing games I've played: I feel like I'm racing in a zero-turn vehicle rather than a front-wheel drive vehicle, but that just might be the character I've been playing with. The weapons are suitable, unique, and fun. Though the game revolves around "survival", any race does not end with the victor, but goes through a series of rounds so that the first to meet the highest score is the winner.
The graphics are unfortunately more demanding than I would have hoped, but I seem to notice little difference between low, medium, and high quality settings to have a significant impact on the enjoyability of the game. The artistic style is self-identifying, set apart from others within its genre. I would recommend this game to anybody who appreciates these games within the genre and is willing to leave the confines of nostalgia to play another fun game within Steam.

I finished the entire campaign and played several multiplayer matches with friends.  The campaign is pretty much garbage.  The sole redeeming factor of the campaign is that it introduces you to the modifiers that you can enable in custom races with friends, but you're far better off just playing the game with friends and experimenting for yourself.  Finishing the campaign does not unlock any content or race modifiers.
This game gets pretty chaotic when you have the maximum player count racing (16 players!)  You can sync tablets and phones to be used as controllers, so you could conceivably have a 16-player local competition if you wanted, or just play online.
Knockout is by far my favorite game mode.  I found the game most enjoyable with about 8-10 racers, high speed, and some form of elimination.  I didn't really like Endurance because it's too easy to lose track of where you are, but I like the elimination modes because they are short and make your focus on surviving a bit more important.  Plus, it's fun to shoot the map's cannon at your friends after your'e dead!
The different game modes are:
Survival - be the last man alive
Knockout - earn points for eliminating other racers
Leader - earn points by being in the front of the pack
Endurance - endless race, race, earn points for eliminating other racers

This game runs very well with extreme amounts of units on the battlefield at once.  I've played 14 player FFA games vs computer opponents with well over ten thousand units active on the map at once with no perceptible slowdown.  The nitrous engine which was developed for this game by oxide studios is amazing- the AI gets it's own CPU core instead of being forced to calculate everything between frames (the typical method used for AI to keep system requirements down).  This leads to an astonishingly capable AI opponent on normal difficulty.  It will flank, it will change builds and tactics if it sees weakness, it, it will attack from several directions at once.  I can obliterate the most powerful AI in Starcraft 2 with ease and I find this AI challenging on normal difficulty.  You can of course turn the AI down until you're ready for more challenge, but the point is that it's extremely entertaining for a solo player and a good option for leveling up your skills for multiplayer.
The game is beautiful in scope as well as vision, you can have five mega battles involving hundreds of units in each battle happening simultaneously.  The strategic zoom makes this easy to manage and easy to que up and move even larger armies into position.  This game is similar to supreme commander in that respect, although supreme commander still has them beat on variety of units and structures.
A few disclaimers:
I haven't played the campaign for this expansion, but the campaign for the first ashes was lackluster in some respects.  I enjoyed it, but it could have been improved.  I've heard that the campaign for this sequel is better, but still a bit underwhelming in general.
Be aware what kind of game this is.  It is strategic rather than tactical.  You manage many large armies of units rather than the clickfest of microing each individual unit.  You COULD micro each individual unit and this is somewhat helpful in the very early game, but it will quickly become pointless due to the sheer numbers you would have to manage.  Macro is the skill you need for this game.  You outproduce and counter builds to win.  Flanking an enemy force is also desirable as they will naturally put meat shield type units to the front and higher dps units behind them (you can select a group of units and click a button to get them to self organise into an army group).  Massive sneak attacks and breakthroughs along a large front are things you need to worry about.  Losing units means little; losing resource nodes can be devastating.
Finally, there are still some bugs with the game.  I have never experienced anything remotely game breaking, but occasionally unit pathing will screw up and cause individuals to get caught up on terrain.  It ends up meaning nothing in the general scheme of things unless it's something massive like a dreadnought, but it's still annoying.

I enjoyed Master Reboot so I decided to pick this game up and I'm glad I did. Soul Axiom is a first-person puzzle game wheere you solve puzzles by interacting with them with different special powers, represented by changing the color of your hands. I found the puzzles to be mostly enjoyable, some were really obvious and some were sort of non-intuitive, but most found a happy medium and I loved the "duh" moment you get when you solve a challenging one. The visuals and soundtrack really add to the game, my only complaint is some levels were a bit too dark, although you can use your hands as "flashlights." The atmostphere was great to, and there are some jump scares but I think they were well done. The game is made up of a diverse group of enviroments, all with neat little details and the design overall is very abstract. Playing the first game isn't required to get into the story although it will help, and there's lots of little references which were fun to discover. The story is very nonlinear, don't expect to understand everything at once. Although like MR, once you piece everything together it really shines. Performance was mostly good except I noticed the engine struggled a bit when you shatter something, like wood or ice, but the game was never unplayable. My biggest complaint is probably the lack of save files, if you exit the level you have to start over which is kind of annoying. Overall a very fun puzzle game with an great story and aesthetic.

First things first, this game will play on Windows 10 even though it was orginally released in 2008.
This is a classic time management game that has the player completing various tasks before the timer runs out for the level.  It has a bit of sim city vibe in the sense that the player has to make sure that each house is supported with water and power, but the levels seem fairly rigid in structure; you won't be building wondeours cities of your own design.
No, at it's heart Jane's Reality is a time management, and one that demands a frenzy of clicking at that.  There is no relaxed mode or carrying on with a level if the time runs out.  The player has to complete various goals while keeping track of tenet happiness and random events that necessitate a clean up or repair order.  It starts out slowly enough that learning the gameplay is easy enough, but I soon found out that this is a game that doesn't really like the concept of downtime or taking a moment to breath.  Think and work fast!
I didn't play more than an hour when I wrote this review, so I don't know about all the  issues that might crop up.  I did encounter a situation where I one of my goals was to upgrade a house, and getting the ability to do so was difficult.  I finally figured out that you have to give enough presents to your tenents to get them to send the request, but it seemed kinds of overly random to me to get the option to full the requirement of the level.
The graphics are pretty much what one would expect from a 2008 game.  Servicable and not ugly, but hardly cutting edge either.  The sound effects are fine, and the music is easily mutable, which is how I play all my games.  It seems there are only 24 levels, but since the game only costs $2.99 that doesn't seem unreasonable.
In short, if the idea of a fairly difficult, very fast paced time management game appeals to you, then for the price this one is a solid, if not perfect, investment.

Definitely worth the price, no contest--can easily sink forty hours into trying all the different choices. The time spent trying all the different combinations won't feel like a chore either.
Within solid storylines and gameplay on a macro level (overall decision making), you always feel as though you could have moved more efficiently than last time, been a bit sharper from second to second in order to scrape together every advantage you can to protect your family (or screw everyone, thoroughly). Although the individual events may be the same, different combinations can result in many different "endings," which creates a satisfying sense of freedom. Although the ending does come down to a summarizing set of cutscenes, differences in who you save or betray and how you do so are what make each result feel different.
There is just enough RNG so that each playthrough is different, but not to the extent that previous experience could not be applied to future playthroughs.
The
is that the save system is automatic so the timings may not always be in your favor, forcing you to be careful with when to time event triggers (you trigger to save).
- The fast forward feature is excellent but if you fast forward while searching, when the inventory pops up, you cannot click the fast forward button (to turn it off). This can result in frustrating moments where the resident returns suddenly while you're fumbling to close the inventory screen to return time to normal.
- The cutscene narrator sounds sort of silly on some occasions; I don't know if I've been playing this for too many consecutive hours but it sounded like he said 'boiling' instead of 'bodies'. It seems as though he tries to sound smooth and dramatic, but on occasion loses control of his mouth and slurs.

[Currently reviewed up to Episode 3]
I'm going to be honest: this is probably my favorite Telltale  game.  Yeah, I said it.   It's not because I'm a fan of the Borderlands series, which admitedly hasn't had the best of story telling, but rather because this game has managed to make me want to learn more about Pandora and all of it's stories.
It has everything you'd expect from a quality Telltale game series, with a lot of the weird/funny bits that come from the Borderlands series.  It's a very unlikely match but I think that's one of the many reasons it succeeds.
Episode 1 was a fantastic introduction that made me realize that this was going to be a keeper of a series, and it had everything I could ask for.   Episode 2 was a little slower, but it introduces more character development and begins to tie the story into the greater Borderlands mythos.   Episode 3 went back to being more action packed, while also giving us a lot of fan favorite appearances from previous characters, and tying the story more into the Borderlands mythos while also introducing new characters that, dare I say are even more compelling than the older and more established ones.
As a Telltale game, this is more or less what you might expect.  Perhaps even more, if you came into this game with mixed or skeptical feelings on the IP.  I have to say, as a fan of Telltale I think one of the reasons I love this probably the most out of anything they've put is that it puts a refreshing shift of mood from their normal style.  The Walking Dead, Wolf Among us and Game of Thrones are all great and quality stuff, but they always had that somber, depressing or even painful atmosphere.  Dark and gritty is great, realistic is good, and tension is nice.   Tales from the Borderland is almost on the entirely different end of the spectrum.  Wacky (but not in a lol so randumb way), funny, charming with it's own sense of dark humor that you'd expect from Borderlands, it's very refreshing to see this in a sea of debbie downer moods.  Variety is the spice of life, after all.
The only negatives I have to say so far are the usual stuff you might see in Telltale games; an aging engine that is showing it's age more and more with every game, with so-so animations at times and weird little bugs that can annoy you if you've been a veteran of Telltale and have seen them in multiple games.   It's more of a nitpick, but I do hope that they can pump out a new, or at least vastly improved engine soon.   Tales is a little better about it, but when the stuff starts to show, boy does it show.   Oh, and the wait times for new episodes.   If you're one of the types that like to wait until all of the episodes are out, you're going to probably be waiting for a while; this entry is one of the worst offenders of making you wait so far.   However, that can't ultimately pull away from how highly I recommend this game.
As a bonus, don't be afraid to play if you've never played Borderlands or even remember the story from the Borderlands games; this game does a fairly good job of keeping you up to speed, and while some background knowledge is appreciated and rewarded (especially for long-time fans of the series), it isn't essential in the slightest.
Oh, and I should have 6 more hours played but Steam bugged out for whatever reason with my Episode 1 playthroughs.
Pros:
+ Well written characters and story
+ Exciting
+ Genuinely funny at times
+ Great voice acting

While Hero Siege can provide fun for a few hours, it is not a game with much replay value and I only found myself sick of it after a few hours.  While I didn't max out any characters or make it to the later acts, I was able to complete act 1 without much difficulty and played a good deal of act 2.  The game itself is a hack 'n' slash (which I respect), but it has so many balance issues there is only one way to approach gameplay.  You can't create a brash tank, a wily theif, a sinister necromancer, or a restoring cleric.  All you can create are glass cannons.
Gameplay involves circlestrafing enemies in an arena for hours on end and hoping not to get 1shot by something you literally cannot see.  Projectiles are 1000x more lethal than melee attacks, and the amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥on screen after act 1 means that in order to survive you are relying more on luck than any actual skill.  Unfortunately, the pacing for act 1 is so slow that you spend more time hunting down stray enemies than you do anything else.  Do not make the mistake of trying to conquor a random dungeon, as they are usually a suicide mission.  Enemies will randomly spawn on you, or you will get stuck fighting off a horde of enemies in a diagional hallway when you can only attack NSEW.  Most bosses in the game are laughably easy, being much slower than you and often having no projectile attacks.  Other bosses will spawn and start casting a spell.  The boss will just say ♥♥♥♥ the channel time and instantly 1shot you with a cross-screen NSEW laser attack that pierces all terrain.  I'm pretty sure he just waits for you to get NSEW of him then he lets loose with an instagib.
I created several characters, and even when putting EVERY stat point into HP and defense you will still get 1shot or 2shot by any enemy in the game.  It makes stat points feel irrelevent when the stat distribution does nothing to affect gameplay.  Your skill build is pretty relevant, but some skills and passives are totally useless or bonkers overpowered.  Some low cooldown aoe skills have +500 damage per skillpoint, while some single target abilities have +40 damge per skillpoint.  At least a respec is cheap.  Trying to grind for a level advantage is pretty impossible.  Luckily for me, a type of elete enemy spawns waves of weak flies, and killing a small swarm of these will net you 1-3 levels in experience.  Fly swarms have probably given me 60-75% of my total character xp.
Items are pretty underwhelming in most cases, and give you a paltry amount of +stats.  Picking up charms and potions is a deathwish in many situations.  Trying to pickup a charm pops up an equipment comparison window, but while you compare stats, you find yourself getting brutalized by terrain hazards.  Potions on the other hand cause you to pause in place and hold them over your head (item get!), while enemies swoop in for free killing blows on your character.  When you are actively running away from enemies, it's really obnoxious to have a minefield of potions littering the battlefield, and many of them are totally obscured behind houses, trees, and particle effects.
This isn't the worst game I've ever played, and I may try playing again sometime, but it has serious issues that make it hard to enjoy.  I feel like I've given it a decent chance, and while the game has its merits, I will make a point of doing more research on games I buy in the future becuase I don't like my steam library cluttered up with games I don't enjoy.

The game was good in its original state but it felt shallow, overly simplified and not too long. Escalation simply remedies all that and truly feels like a viable replacement for Supreme Commander 2. Whilst it does not have the depth of SupCom FA it is an absolutly beautiful game and the seemless transition from game map to tactical overview is wonderful.
You can feel the extra depth the game has been given and for a strategy game in 2016 to cater so much to single player is phenomenal. We can't all spend hours of our lives practicing specific build orders or mouse clicks in order to become passable online. Sometimes you just want to kick back and take on a challenging AI or even an easy AI; and you want to have plenty of different opportunities in which to do that and AotSE provides a wonderful platform for this.
Whilst this game is not a spiritual successor to SupCom it heavily takes away from it:
- Units are wildly indespensible save for you 'Titan Class'
- There are resource nodes doted around the map and control of them is critical
- The tactical overlay builds on SupCom's as if it used it as a base and just beautified it
- Defenses are good to hold off raids but terrible if anything with some oomph comes at you
All very SupCom-ey to me. :)
The only downside I can think of is that this game takes a lot of computing power to even run. Casual gaming devices won't stand a chance of running this.
Otherwise, very recommended.

I've played RimWorld for years. It's a fascinating, and grueling simulator that inspires a true connection between the player, the colonists and their environment. It's an effective time sink and you can easily loose hours to the old "just one more thing" mentality. My initial reaction to the game was how it looked, seemingly simple, but you soon find yourself marveling at its quiet complexity.
Way back when I started playing this game (before steam), it was a fantastic and some might say seemingly complete game, but the developer has pushed on, adding more content and a better play experience. It truely is a work of genious, and I thoroughly expect great new things in RimWorld.
It is punishing though, hours into a build, you have perfectly happy colonists with epic rooms and houses, stout defences, and farms stretching for miles. Then all of a sudden a sequence of unrelenting rage quit events occur.
a) A pack of man hunting wildboars descend during a solarflare or eclipse, your turrets are out and you have to fend the beasts away yourself.
b) Shortly after the Glorious Pirate Mongoose's decide to raid bringing with them a flurry of submachine guns and molotovs.
c) Your farms are soon torched, and old Wilson is being mauled by an embittered boar near the mysterious building. The pirates have stormed the living quarters, overpowering your colonists, and stealing the women. Then the rains come dowsing the fires, the solar flare passes and power returns. Your defences kick in and Old Wilson killed the boar with his prosthetic leg Peggy. Can you reclaim your once great colony? Alex get's wilson to bed and starts treatment. The few remaining colonists quickly replant the fields and repair the damage... but whats this TOXIC FALLOUT and aliens.... fml... Wilson timet to get Peggy out again!
You've got to love RimWorld!

Rimworld is a game where you can make your own stories. These stories go down branches that you and Ai Storyteller lay down for your colonists, watch and guide them into making an thriving community.
The game has a good concept of how you control the fate of individuals who have been stranded on a suppose deserted planet, you can make the experience into that of a story. It's amazing how things go, sometimes you can make flourishing trade outposts, though the story tellers won't always allow that. They will sometimes go out of their way to make your colonists' lives to be a living hell. Raiders will loot, raze and slaughter those of your colony. Packs of beast run in through your colony and maul your loved characters to bare bone. Dormant machines will wake and vaporize intruders who trespass in their ancient bases. All of this for the sake of story.
One can survive these odds at times if they prepare well, stock up on food and forge new weapons to arm your colonists. Though all doesn't need to be bloodshed, there are storytellers who provide you more times of peace and a calmer setting for stories. While others will seek to make it an living hell like dear Randy, he is such a sadist. Though you, the player have control of the outcome, based on all that you do and how you do it.
You can make tales of adventure, drama, love, and tragedy through most of your actions. The outcomes are based on your decisions and planning, building bases, managing the supplies, and maintaining relations with other factions is up to you. Tired of some elements? Download some mods and spice up the atmosphere of your story further. As it can be a story of many things, it's your story.

This game is weird, and can be really hard to follow sometimes, but it does a lot of really cool things and has an interesting story to tell if you take the time to unravel it.
PROS:
-Interesting mechanics (phasing objects in and out of existance, "playing" and "pausing" objects to move them along a pathway to solve a puzzle, etc.)
-Challenging puzzles
-Nice visual style in gameplay
-Layered story (meaning you complete a level and get a cutscene, but only later is that cutscene made relevant in the story)
-Good music
-Mysterious atmosphere
CONS:
-Controls are a bit clunky and take some getting used to
-Sound design is wonky (audio cues play over other sound effects, or sometimes don't play at all, volume mixing can be off sometimes)
-Backtracking (there are 12 "normal" levels in the hub, and after completing them, you're required to go back inside each one of them in order to find 12 more "corrupt" variations on the level. Now the corrupt levels are very different than the normal ones, but you still have to dig around in an already explored environment just to get to something new)
-Framerate drops (maybe this is just my rig, but I was having some issues where the game would lose 15-20 frames whenever I would sprint around or turn quickly. I have a pretty hefty setup capable of running pretty much anything pretty well at the moment, so I'm not too keen to blame it on my setup, but I haven't seen anyone else mention this so maybe it is on my end)
CONNCLUSION:
Despite its few flaws Soul Axiom is a pretty great little game that I've hade a lot of fun with. Its atmospheric, challenging, and interesting, and yeah, I'd say its worth your time if you like games like The Talos Principle and are willing to look past a few minor production problems.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game after finding it by chance. It's a lot of fun spying on the tenants and trying to collect the required information about them, while also completing the side missions that the game presents.
The surveillance camera mechanic is very interesting: the other apartments are usually obscured when you're not inside them, but when a camera is installed, you can still watch a small part of the house after you've left. You can also peek through the keyhole, or use a master key to investigate personally when the apartment is empty.
The game has quite a few small English mistakes like odd word choices or using "he" or "she" to refer to inanimate objects. This is justified since the developers are based in Russia, but they should fix it for the full release.

Played for free during the free weekend. I am very impressed with what Squad wants to accomplish, but at this time it is VERY rough around the edges. The weapon animations and the mechanics of the game are sound and conducive to the overal realistic style the developers want to achieve, but there are so many issues regarding player model actions that it detracts from the experience, namely entering water (I haven't noticed any swimming or wading mechanics), moving past obstacles and corners, vaulting, etc. These things are a given on modern shooters and it is incredible that they haven't implemented these things satisfactorily as of yet.
Vehicles are interesting and varied but in order to prevent vehicle stealing the devs decided to make a squad "own" a vehicle, making it unnecessarily cumbersome to find available transport even if the squad has been wiped out or just abandoned it somewhere in the map.
I am willing to revisit this review as the game evolves as I think it has tremendous potential,  but as it is right now, I just can't recommend it.

Pros:

+Generally good level design, with some really fun areas. You'll be reminded of HL2 in many ways.
+It's pretty fun...mostly.
+Immersive world, it really fleshes out a lot of backstory and really brings the 1960s Nazi-dominated world to life. Even finding things like
. The game is full of little bits and pieces of backstory, most of which are quite entertaining, and some are even hilarious.
+Great writing, dialogue and voice acting, although Blazcowicz whispers like a depressed Batman constantly for some reason. The supporting cast are much more fun to listen to.
+The campaign is fairly long, but I don't much feel like replaying.
+Gunplay is mostly fun and satisfying, but the heavier enemies are generally NOT fun.
+A lot of areas allow you to approach them stealthily at the start. The game thent takes on a somewhat Dishonored vibe.
+The only game where I've seen the word 'radgie' used.
Cons
-That HEAD-BOB! You cannot switch it off, and it is really awful! It hurts my eyes just thinking about it.
-Not much variation in enemies. Heavy soldiers are not much fun to fight.
-Too easy to exploit enemies, especially bosses.
-Having to scroll the mouse wheel to equip some weapons/tools.
-Too many areas where you must fight wave-after-wave of enemies. That is not fun and slows the pace of the game in a bad way.
-Some of the enemies and encounters are just cheap enemy spam-fests with bullet sponges walking slowly toward you.
-The energy charging points for laser weapons felt really lame. They become a life-line and you will find yourself using them constantly, especially on the higher difficulties. The energy weapons are just not fun.
-Sometimes it can be irritating to find your objective. If not for the map, this would be regularly frustrating.

-You're basically a terrorist and your actions get tons of innocent people killed. I mean, the Nazis have earned their victory at this point, and Blazcowicz is just causing hell for a bit of revenge. Since Ashes of the Singularity: Escalation is a bigger, better version of the original Ashes of the Singularity, I am reposting this review as it is entirely applicable to this new version.
Ashes of the Singularity is a real-time strategy (RTS) game at an epic scale based in the far future.
What is Great about this game:
- Very strong RTS game mechanics with solid tactical and strategic elements
- An elegant combination of various other great RTS games (Supreme Commander, Company of Heroes, etc) but still with an authentic flavor of its own
- Incredible replayability and playstyle variety - particularly in skirmish mode
- The unit management for such a large-scale game is second to none. Put units into an army, and they simply work smartly together. No micromanagement!
- Micromanagement is at a minimal level for a game of this scale. Armies are generally smart enough (assuming decent unit composition) to actually follow orders and execute on them relatively well
- The games visuals and tech are amazing. The Nitous engine (which is what this game runs on) is a beauty and looks so lovely that I switched graphics cards to run it better
What is Good about this game:
- Good unit variety with excellent hard counters (e.g. Apollo > Bomber > Zeus > Apollo across several different combinations of units etc)
- Dreadnoughts look and play amazingly - good depth and satisfaction to their upgrade tree, just fun to watch blow stuff up
- There is almost unlimited skill-ceiling even against the AI as the skirmish AI is quite excellent
- A good game of skirmish can feel epic and still be done in 30-60 minutes
What could be improved in this game:
- Some of the controls can be a little fiddly:
- The dreadnaught upgrades can be a little tedious on very large maps. Would be nice if there was an icon in the GUI similar to the idle engineer icon to simply auto-find them and select them to upgrade faster with less hunting, even if you find them, can sometimes be hard to select the exact ship among a large group
- The AI can be tough even at lower difficulties until you learn the game pretty well
- Would love more large skirmish maps
Conclusion:
This is simply the best skirmish RTS game to come out probably since Supreme Commander. And even so, the devs are working on it constantly to improve on the game, and the progress continues to show. If you like RTS games, and particularly RTS games that focus on the skirmish mode or large-to-epic scale RTS games, this game is really second to none right now.

Note: I have a free copy of the game to giveaway to
lucky subscriber (see video for details).  Full written review below.
Ashes of Singularity was released in March of this year - a real time strategy game where you could play as one of two warring factions and set off on futuristic space battles of massive scale.  And when I mean massive, I mean it.  Hundreds, hell even thousands of individual units swirling and dancing around in all out war was a sight to behold.  It was well received for the most part, but the general consensus was that the game was a little too simple.  The community called out for some major improvements and additions to be developed into the game to grant it more depth, and thus we have Escalation.
First, we’ve got the long awaited Strategic Zoom a’la Supreme Commander and Sins of a Solar Empire.  This is so helpful to compensate for the newly expanded player map size, now allowing for now a ridiculous 14 players.  It’s so clean looking, so futuristic, and aptly mutes the background music as if you’re viewing the battle in orbit on a satellite.  And the bonus, it never hitches the frame rate or takes any loading time to transition to and from.
Secondly, the developers have added new specialized units for each race such as advanced aircraft with bombing or support functions, lots of new upgrade-able defensive structures that allow players to participate in area denial and siege strategies, two new world environments - volcanic and crystalline, new start up configurations, and a slew of new global abilities to use from your HUD.
Movement speed is deliberately paced to make you feel not in control of an army, but a commander of the battlefield.  Most units move slow enough for you to make your orders and have enough time to see to your base construction, manage your upgrades and make sure that you’re constantly pumping out that train of units.
It’s important that the game begs you to be strategic.  Lopsided battles can be won with proper positioning and patience, as all units have varying movement speeds and smart players will use multiple unit groups to make sure spongy units stay up front and soak damage, airships with air-to-air missiles only engage while enemy aircraft are present, and your dreadnoughts stay well protected.
As such, it’s less about your micromanagement of units and more about your macro control over the entirity of the map that insures your success.
Game modes include 3 story mode options with scripted missions, a skirmish mode with tons of personal modifiers for you to shape the worlds and battles of your choosing, and a competitive multiplayer.
Wow, the graphics.  It’s no denying that this one is a looker on the surface, moreso by the rich color depth and variation moreso than by flexing its tecnical muscles.  The units and environments are plain, for the most part, but its because of their association to such huge amounts of enemies that they seem more interesting and vibrant.  The throngs of armies raining down onto each other create just a wonder of eyecandy - the colors, the animations, the sound design.  It’s a treat for the eyes.
But it’s going to cost you.  The game requires a rig to run it well.  On the screen are the specs of my machine.  I’m able to run the game at 60 fps on High settings with some stressing effects such as shading and post processing turned down to medium.  Thankfully, a very detailed benchmark tool is available to guide you to selecting the appropriate graphical settings to make sure you maintain a consistant framerate because you’re not going to want it dipping when the big fights break out.
Some units look pretty similiar and some of the detail is hard to see because you're mostly zoomed out so high (not really a bad thing, but notable).
Lastly, I think the voice acting is a little second-rate.  Although more was added to the campaign it often feels a bit oddly paced.  But, because Skirmish is the best way to play the game outside of multiplayer anyway, It wasn’t a deal breaker for me.
With the additions of the tactical zoom new units and structures, alongside fleshing out the campaign,  I think it’s safe to say Escalation has really made some huge improvements on Ashes.  I loved it and I’m excited to continue my time with Ashes of Singularity: Escalation. This one gets the thumbs up from me.
