INGREDIENTS
1.5kg (3lb) loin pork, with fat attached and rind removed, tied with string
2tbsp olive oil
1.5l (48fl oz) milk
50g (1¾oz) butter
6 cloves garlic, peeled and split in half
2 unwaxed lemons, peel removed
METHOD
Heat the oven to 160°C (gas mark 2-3). Season the pork well with salt and freshly ground black pepper. Heat the oil in the bottom of a large casserole or frying pan over a medium heat. Add the pork and slowly cook until golden. Remove it from the pan and wipe out the excess fat with kitchen paper.
Bring the milk to just under the boil in a large saucepan. Heat the butter in the casserole. Add the garlic and cook for 1-2 minutes, then add the pork.
Add enough of the milk to come about a third of the way up the side of the pork. Drop the strips of lemon peel (minus any white pith) into the milk and bring to the boil.
Cover with foil or a lid, and transfer to the oven. Cook for 1 hour then remove the cover and continue to cook for a further 30 minutes. Spoon off and discard any fat. Serve the pork in slices, accompanied with the reduced milk.
top tips
The milk will reduce to a lovely, soft, golden, lemony curd. Spoon this around the meat when you serve it.

If you want to step up your casual gaming from The Sims series to something more extreme, RimWorld is it. Its difficulty rivals Dwarf Fortress, but there are easier difficulties (and three different 'storytellers' that control what happens) that you could pretend like you're playing The Sims. Plus, there's no household cap of 8! Anyone that survives, crashing into your colony - or enemies you capture from a raid - you can *convince* them to join your colony and become a part of the family. :)
Once you're comfortable with observing your Sims, I mean, colonists get cozy - bump up the difficulty for hordes of your neighbors, space pirates, and even space alien robots. No one could make fun of you for that.
This game is really addictive and there are so many ways you can play it. You can treat it like a Sims game with minimal horrifying events, or a challenge to keep the longest standing colony despite waves and waves of things-trying-to-kill-you, or.. you can just see if you can make it past one colony, over and over again.
The community is very active! Reddit, Discord, and other forums. The dev(s) communicate with the community and they love the game as much as we do. There are so, so, so many mods - and some that are practically expansion packs to the game!
With randomization (seeds & events), high quality mods, and the ongoing major update - the game has so much replayability. It's really, really fun - I really can't recommend it enough. This is the most amount of hours I've put into a Steam game. I really recommend it.

For a small studio, this game has excellent graphic and sound design, and a decent, if somewhat stale, sci-fi plot.
However, the game falls completely flat in the realm of puzzle design.  All of the puzzles fall somewhere on a spectrum between trivial and simple.  Some puzzles require a bit of thought only because it's often not clear what you're supposed to do.  In many cases, the puzzles are arbitrary non-sequitors having nothing to do with the narrative.  The game contains the worst kind of timing puzzles -- frustrating and lots of waiting for things to reset, coupled with clunky controls.  This game wants to be challenging and fun in the same way as Portal or Talos but misses the mark widely.
Also, you cannot save in the middle of levels, which just seems barbaric in the year 2016.
I'm so bored with the puzzles that I'm quitting at around the halfway point and won't finish.  In spite of the excellent production effort, I can't recommend this game.

Dark Train is a beautifully mysterious point-and-click adventure game. Its world never really becomes familiar: of course you know what a squid is, or what a train is, also the basic physics seems to work and there are familiar icons near train controls, like thunderbolts and water droplets... but why is this squid chained to the train, where does this train go, and why is there a little city inside of an ordinary cargo container?
Given time, you'll get the answers to these questions, only to find out that the game has the new ones prepared. And the thing is, it is not frustrating, it's more wonderous, really. The exchange is done with a good pace, and the things you discover are always interesting and sometimes pleasantly unexpected. Dark Train shows definite and solid understanding of exploration-based gameplay.
And there are lots and lots of things to explore. First and foremost, the train is a big world-in-itself. Apart from obvious functional parts, it has four cargo containers, each with a little world inside. At first, this seems pretty limited: there's a town, a garden, a church and, errrrrm... a freezer, which is frozen shut and will take some dedication to break into. Once you unlock a special interlocking device on your train, you'll discover that worlds in adjacent containers actually influence each other! For example, your garden, when influenced by the town, becomes an iron plant, and you can use it to forge some tools that will help you in other worlds. Other worlds are affected in a similar manner.
Each new device unlocks new world possibilities -- next you find a magnet which allows you to move the containers, creating new combinations. Sometimes, differences  are subtle, sometimes very drastic, but there are always some new discoveries. It's very useful to write down the combinations -- some world variations will need several visits over the course of the game.
Because train constantly moves towards some unknown destination, everything above may sound like you have a lot to do. However, there's no need to rush and frantically try everything as soon as you unlock new devices. The game has a good and easy to follow system to track the train's progress in a natural way, so you always know how much time do you have to do stuff. And while you can sometimes get confused in a particular room, for the most part you know what to do next: compartments where you can do something inside are highlighted, and when you've done everything you need to do inside, the game will visibly open the hatch leading outside. Consequently, when you clear all rooms, something will happen in the outside world that will give you new ways to progress.
What I must mention is that there's no in-game guide or hint system. And, as the game's community is pretty small, there're no comprehensive player guides to each and every room, which means that if you're stuck, you're on your own. Still, the game is definitely clearable without external help, sometimes you just need to be more rigorous in searching for interactive objects. And so, I completed the main storyline in about 5 hours...
...and missed a lot of content on my first walkthrough, actually. Did I mention that the train has
? It definitely does have two sets of them: one on the front and one on the back cart respectively. It sounds trivival, yes. However, you get introduced to them in a pretty weird way: when it happens, you are not required to slow down or stop -- you need to use the heat and sparkles produced by friction to recharge your heat accumulator. Which makes it easy to dismiss the main obvious function, especially with the game world being so bizarre -- maybe that's just how people and robots produce heat there, after all, they also seem to collect electricity from lightning bolts. Heat collection requires one set of brakes. But if you engage both sets -- the train will actually stop.

Now, why stop? For more exploration, of course! Don't forget to look out for the things in the outside world and sometimes make a stop to examine some of them closer
. It's also useful to spend some time moving at half-speed, with one of the brake sets engaged, so you can momentary stop at any point of interest by activating the second set. While all of this is optional, it provides a whole lot more of substance to the game world.
Dark Train is the game with a lot of heart and a lot of imagination. Knowing this, it's a bit sad that the game hasn't sold well. According to Steamspy its sales are somewhere around 10-11k at the moment of this review. It would be more interesting to solve the mysteries and build up theories on the game's world in a bigger community. On the other hand, you can save all the mysteries for yourself and play it spoiler-free. Whatever fits you best, I definitely recommend Dark Train if you like exploration-based games.

Beautiful, absolutely beautiful, an amazing successor to SAIS. So much has been improved and it feels like the first game, but better. For starters you have the game start up, there are 3 ships to choose from, Science Vessel, Corvette, and Frigatte, and each changes the game fundamentally (more on that ahead), you still have the nebulae density and combat difficulty scales, but they've also added a map size adjustment as well, which increases your mission years and makes the map scale exponentially larger (each also has a separate score board). There aren't really any downsides to the start up, in my opinion. As for core game concepts, the combat remains the same at a core level, but they've added many more options and combat functions, the've also upped the difficulty (i.e., much smarter AI) and added more ships, more creatures, more scenarios, more systems, more tech, just more everything, except bugs. The UI is the worst part, tiny♥♥♥♥♥buttons ♥♥♥♥ my combat up and get me killed all the time, try to pause with space and recloak, fail to cloak and get killed in seconds. As for the ships changing the game. The science vessel gives you much more points for collecting creatures and exploring, it also only gets 1 gun and has the least expansion slots and most inventory space. The Corvette remains the same, 2 guns and just enough slots, with 3 rows for cargo with exploration and combat rewarded and more value placed on tech and artifacts than anything else. Finally the Frigatte, this one has the most expansion slots, 3 weapons, 2 cargo rows, places most value from points and barter on guns and implements of war and rewards mostly combat. Saying it doesn't do nearly as much justice to how much these simple things change the game, the only way to understand truly is to go pick up the download of SAIS and play that then to try this (which after playing SAIS you'll know will take less than 2 hours) and judging the game accordingly.
Honestly a clear improvement on the first game and deserves your $5.

I've had many expirences with this game that I cannot get from any other. From the roaring machine gun fire, to people yelling out contacts, to the stealth push through the forest, this game portrays very well what it wants. Chaos of battle. You may argue battlefield or arma does that too, but not in the heart pounding way this game does. It has an intensity that is more so than those games. Every firefight is memorable because of the sometimes long periods in between them. With a good squad lead and communication, it boosts that even higher. Its like a big game of chess, with big boy toys at your disposal.
Overall, this game provides an excellent expirence. A lot of the cons that are listed are probably being worked on as we speak, and I can't complain too much about it. Compared to project reality, this game is a beautiful upgrade. Worth the investement. WARNING: Dont expect this game to be of AAA quality, which it almost is, this is a smaller team that is doing an amazing job. A lot of reviews I see are from the wave of free weekenders that didnt understand the game completley, or doesnt realize its a work in progress. Over half probably didnt even read or watch the guides that were provided to them once they launch the game. With that said, its good to have feedback to work from.

Overall I like this game. It offers pretty unique ideas and the artstyle is fitting. (reminded me of the bleaker parts of Little Inferno)
You get a "Papers, Please" vibe with the story, athmosphere, filling out reports and needing to get the smaller details right and decisions you have to make.
You can definitely play this through more than once, but that also brings me to one of the more negative parts:
Each tenant is tied to certain story pieces and the first 3 are always the same, with the ones you let move in following a similar part (with that I mean you CAN decide who to move in after the initial ones, but you choose between 2 or 3 that will stay the same til everyone was there at least once), so every replay has big chunks of repetition.
If you compare that to "papers, please" where you had randomized NPCs, but also a few storydriven ones that show up every playthrough, only in this game they all are story NPCs.
That brings me to something where I'm not sure if its good or bad and probably depends on opinion:
Since they all have a story purpose, they also often tie together and the game is more a puzzle of which NPCs work together instead of a management game that leaves you a little more freedom to breathe.
I would have loved the game to be more leniant with the time you get and also add some random non-story NPCs that are just there to get money for. (Just put in tenants with few text lines that randomly have illegal goods you can spot and report to get money)
The game mostly teaches you the stuff you need to know, but for example I had a NPC that needed a gun and I knew another one had one. I could even ask him about it and marked it in his report earlier, but I could not figure out how to get it (asking him about, trying to tell the other about it, searched the room) and then the timer of the quest ran out and i lost both tenants (the one with the gun got removed by the police, guess cause there was no more story to him?)
Also some things simply didn't work as I thought they would, which I blame on the game NOT telling me how to do it.
Example: I put illegal goods into the room of someone, but never figured out how to snitch him to the police about it.
It would also be nice if already sent files stayed archived so you can just add new info to them instead of rewriting them completly.
So in summary: Unique game with nice style and good story.
Good for several playthroughs, but repetetive parts and not much freedom in the progression, since you have timers on the quests and with some things you need to figure out how the game wants you to handle it, instead of being intuitive.

Played for free during the free weekend. I am very impressed with what Squad wants to accomplish, but at this time it is VERY rough around the edges. The weapon animations and the mechanics of the game are sound and conducive to the overal realistic style the developers want to achieve, but there are so many issues regarding player model actions that it detracts from the experience, namely entering water (I haven't noticed any swimming or wading mechanics), moving past obstacles and corners, vaulting, etc. These things are a given on modern shooters and it is incredible that they haven't implemented these things satisfactorily as of yet.
Vehicles are interesting and varied but in order to prevent vehicle stealing the devs decided to make a squad "own" a vehicle, making it unnecessarily cumbersome to find available transport even if the squad has been wiped out or just abandoned it somewhere in the map.
I am willing to revisit this review as the game evolves as I think it has tremendous potential,  but as it is right now, I just can't recommend it.

Binding of Isaac-like random powerups, level progression and hack'n'slash, sounds great!
Too bad the basic gameplay is crazy repetitive and the feeling of progression is not there with the current skill/attribute system. Example: The Viking has a skill Stoneskin unlocked somewhere around level 18, which gives you 1% chance to "gain a massive boost" to armor. This massive boost is 5 points of armor, which translates into 1% damage reduction. The skill doesn't mention when does this happen, nor how long does the effect last. Most of the skills and attributes are equally underwhelming and most of the information is either hidden or wrong (Pirate lvl1 skill at rank 1 claims to do 25000 damage, lvl28 skill at rank 1 claims to do around 40, neither is even near correct).
The main thing you're collecting is money, but the only place to spend it appears randomly (high chance that you'll get too much money to spend). Most of the items sold are just minor stat gains for this particular run. When your Pirate has a good chance to shoot a cannonball for 1000 damage, you really don't care about that +5 strength which would give you about 2 damage per attack.
Chances are, that the game is balanced for "end game", but I can't seem to find the fun in trying to reach there. Was fun for a few hours, could've been way better (and apparently has been, if other reviews can be believed).
TL;DR: Your generic minion available to all classes hits harder than you. If you don't care about any details how the game progression works and like hacking away, this game might still suit your needs.

Well, this is the first game I have ever really felt compelled to write a review for, so I guess that says something about the quality of it compared to the roughly 200 other games in my inventory.
First up, since I place empasis on story over gameplay or graphics at any time, this game shouldn't surprise anyone as being to my liking. (The clue is kinda in the name of the company: Telltale)
The game plays so well into the Borderlands universe, which happens to be well coordinated with the people at Gearbox, which in itself is pretty darn awesome. It serves to sort of fill in a few blanks between the established canon of the three Borderlands games, particularly (SPOILERS!) in the third episode where we get to know how Athena winds up a prisoner of the BL2 Vault Hunters and thus sets the story for the beginning of the Pre-Sequel. It does so all the while telling a fantastic new story fully in line with the original Borderlands humour, which (personal opinion, feel free to disagree) makes it feel more like Borderlands than the Pre-Sequel did to me.
So, yeah, in short, if you like story driven games and you have bothered to read through all this, chances are you have probably already either bought the game or you will be doing it shortly. It is definitely worth the money.

TL;DR - Like FPS's with good stories? Pick this baby up.
====
Don't let that 81/100 scare you on the metacritic score. If you want a solid FPS that is highly polished with a great story, buy this.
Graphics: 9/10 - They didn't blow me away but they look fantastic. Nothing more to be said here.
Sound/Music: 7.5/10 - A bunch of the sounds in the game felt weird to me, mostly ambient ones. Some sounds didn't really match the environment piece they were attached to (like a bridge wire ejecting from it's latch). Music is overall solid but nothing hugely memorable. There were a couple scenes where they played an interesting song that you expected something big to happen because of the song. This is not the case.
Voice acting is top notch.
Story: 9/10 - The Nazis have found technology 100s of years ahead of the current time period (WW2 era). This enables them to win the war and take over the world. You play as an American who took Shrapnel to the brain and suffered 14 years of kinda-comatose only to finally come back to reality to the world the nazis have created. Resistance time. I won't say anymore beyond that. Time for you to start playing and take it back.
Characters are solid, but could use a bit more development in my opinion.
Gameplay: 7.5/10 - Gameplay is fairly standard FPS with some heavy polish on everything the Main Character does with his hands (like stabbing people or pulling levers). For the most part, it looks great and feels great. Nothing that blows me away and nothing that makes me utterly hate it (except the shotgun badguys. ♥♥♥♥ those guys).
Gripes: This game takes some questionable approaches when it comes to reality. Putting aside the fact that it's a fiction based on future technology and that the nazis won the war, there are a few things that could've been handled better. I won't go into detail of the number of things they did, but as an example...you can't jump out of a plane going 100+ mph into another plane (very beginning of the game) and not have wind friction totally latch onto you and basically blowing you away so to speak. You'll see what I mean when you play it.
Overall: 8.5/10 - Regardless of whether you let things like that slide (my gripes above), this game is still fantastic. Like FPS's with good stories? Pick This baby up.

I've played this game since it was in Closed Beta in 2015. To start you to know that this game was made as a response to WoT and WT, both of them by russian developers. This is important due to the mindset that these 2 russian devs have towards their playerbase. Basically it amounts to "Don't like what we're doing? Don't play." AW was marketed from the beginning as a modern arcade tank game by a western developer. What we didn't realise was that
, the publisher, is run by a russian company. So much for that. The other thing is that it was designed to directly address the criticisms both playerbases had for their games. You'd expect that this setup meant AW was destined to fail.
You'd be partly right but not in the way you might think. The game mechanics were designed to be more fair overall with a lower RNG swing (10% compared to WoT's 25%) and an emphasis on gun accuracy and speed of play. These major changes along with several other minor ones created a game that was tons of fun for all skill levels. What was even better was that Obsidian Entertainment actually wanted to create an overarching story to the game and to bring some RPG elements as well. They really wanted to take the good from WoT and WT while eliminating the bad and drive this kind of game well beyond the original scope. I personally have spoken to developers from obsidian all the way up to the project director for AW about this and heard nothing but amazing things from them about their goals for AW.
Then
started to push back. All they ever wanted was a WoT clone and they started to make that abundantly clear right after the game launched in late 2015. From launch the game went steadily downhill as massive tank and tier imbalances were ignored, map issues were ignored, and game mode imbalances were ignored. They tried to cover up the problems with new tanks, new maps and new game modes but the core issues remained.
Finally the other shoe dropped. OE got cut by
. Despite what it says here on steam this is NOT a game currently developed by Obsidian Entertainment. It is now an in house development team at
. And as far as I can currently tell, they are stumbling their way around trying to make this game even more like WoT than it already was. AW coming to steam is nothing more than an attempt to drum up support for a game that has already lost its playerbase. Cannot recommend AGAINST this game enough.

Beholder is a surprising little gem. It's a mash up between Papers Please, the old Thief Series and a Detective thriller.
You're a bureaucrat, stuck spying on people in secret for a totalitarian regime in the role of landlord, sneaking into people's miserable personal lives, to put together the clues you find to manipulate events on both individual and national scale for morally good or bad. You need to support your own family by ratting people out, taking bribes, blackmail, planting evidence or building a case. Sometimes that means putting murderers and drugdealers behind bars, sometimes that means stabbing nice old folk in the back.
Meanwhile, all your tenants have their own interesting personal lives that you can bud into. Most of these stories really are quite good, with fleshed out characters and lots of intrigue, up to the point where they are not so much gameplay goals to me, as just story-arcs I want to see resolved. I arranged a wedding in my apartment, followed shortly by several funerals as characters in my antfarm had their own motivations that I didn't see coming. And when the day is done, it is incredibly satisfying that unbeknown to these fleshed out characters with a believable lives, you're secretly in control over them, with the ability to invade their privacy to see how something turned out, to have them either dragged off by the regime at a moment's notice, or help them into a brighter future.
There are a few cons to this product. Across the board, this is not a native English game and the dialogue and translations are a bit wonky, while the spoken dialogue in cut scenes awkwardly hilarious with thick accents and blatant mispronunciation. It also takes a fair bit to get used to as the game refuses to hold your hand and throws you into the deep end with a surprising amount to do, usually backed by several timers that not always match up with each other. At first, I just went in doing the main mission and I quickly lost all my money, several family members and my chance at following up on good endings. It's only slowly that I understood that there are a lot of spinning plates to keep up simultaneously.
Gathering info on your tenants - their hobbies, interests, vices and activities - to leak back to the regime for pocket change, through cameras, looking through keyholes or rummaging through their belongings when they're not home, is already a full-time job. Add to that getting specific missions done for the regime or resistance, keeping track of events, interceding at the right time and scheming to get some quick extra cash for your family and it can get a little overwhelming quickly and hard to enjoy the personal drama.
There are missions where you can just freeze the progression of the game to get some breathing space, but then it starts to feel like the game's own systems can be chanced or exploited. Certain quests peter out without an end, or quests that depend on each other for a good outcome don't match together, when stumbling upon the wrong set of circumstances and the timers of your chosen progression allign poorly or not at all, which deprive the game of some of its weight and feeling of solid design. Some options rather harshly roadblock you with an instant character death, facilitating a reload in a checkpoint system you have no manual control over.
It all comes together in this feeling that the game REALLY has the heart in the right place, but the mechanics and systems are a little too loose to get a good grip on them. It's too easy for everything to spin out of control for lack of player oversight or the game's own organization.
Despite this, the game simply is too novel and the core of it too charming in a creepy, dystopian way, for me to not wholeheartedly recommend it. If you liked Papers Please, detective puzzles or the Thief thrill of sneaking around people's personal space, you need to buy this one.

Weird Worlds is a remake of an older 2002 indie game called Strange Adventures in Infinite Space. SAIS was fairly popular back in the day of Palms, Pocket PCs, and PDAs. It's meant to be a fun little distraction in sizable chucks perfect for a lunch break. To give you an idea, SAIS's tagline literally was "Explore the galaxy in 20 minutes or less!" Weird Worlds is basically SAIS plus more content.
With the above in mind, a lot of reviewers are somewhat unfairly comparing Weird Worlds to FTL. If you're looking at it as a FTL clone, or an immersive game you can play for hours, or a game that requires great strategy, you're completely missing the point.
On the other hand, if you're feeling nostalgic and want a faithful sequel to SAIS, or a quick game you can pickup and put down, or a distraction to escape the drudgery of boring work, Weird Worlds is perfect for you. If you're still unsure, go download SAIS; it's been open sourced since 2005.

TL;DR: The much advertised visuals are nice, but there's little logic to the game and the controls are actively fighting against you. I strongly advise to not buy.
Movement feels more like controlling one of Octodad's tentacles or the hand in Surgeon Simulator rather than making deliberate movements; You don't really move the droid, but rather you guide it and hope that it'll hit your target. For a puzzle game designed around interacting with the world, this is a huge problem.
The droid picks up things and interacts with objects, but the mechanics are inconsistent. The droid will easily miss targets and drop objects for no apparent reason. Sometimes moving near a target will automatically do something, sometimes you have to press A/click, sometimes nothing happens unless you hover over for a while. Foreground and background also often obscure the important things.
But worst of all, the game does not explain itself in any way, nor will it guide you in a helpful manner. There's a difference between "no hints, no help - solve it" and having a game go beyond old-school Sierra moon logic. The game requires you to constantly stumble into one-shot mechanics by mere chance.

Soul Axiom is a first-person sci-fi puzzle game set inside a cyber-world. The gameplay in Soul Axiom revolves VERY heavily around solving puzzles. As you progress through the game, you will discover new powers that you need to use to manipulate, and destroy parts of the environment.
Once you reach the HUB in Elysia, there are 12 memories for you to learn about and experience. Each memory is set in a unique world to explore, with it’s own set of puzzles to figure out. If you are paying attention to your surroundings, there are plenty of clues that will help you greatly in finding the solutions.
The story starts as a mystery, and you have no idea who you are or how you wound up in the digital afterlife of Elysia. The story was interesting once I figured it all out, but it takes quite a while to put some of the mysteries of the game to rest.
I spent over 15 hours playing the game to complete everything, and then about another half an hour to experience each of the endings that the game has to offer. The game has a TON of unique puzzles. However, due to the nature of a puzzle game, I cannot see replaying the game once you fully complete it.
Soul Axiom is a game that is meant for people who love puzzles, and if you do, you will probably enjoy it. I got a lot of enjoyment out of the gameplay, and I feel that I got my money’s worth in content. If you are not a big fan of puzzles, and problem solving, then you will probably not enjoy this game.

Paperash Studio is an indie Chzec team formed in 2013, whose goal is to develop video games that offer different experience and gameplay. To achieve this, they combine various types of art and technology such as hand-made illustrations, paper creations, writings and also high-quality audiovisual digital post-production.  Dark Train is the first and only developed game for now; it was released in 2016 for Windows and you can buy it on Steam.
Developers gently gave me a Steam key, so before playing it, I had no idea of what to expect.
Well, I was immediately impressed by game aesthetics. It's all made of paper and illustrations, and obviuosly they used digital effects for lights and colors. They privileged dark scenarios, sometimes with cyberpunk elements, but there are also a few bright and colored environments. It has the really special flavor of a handmade product. You can admire for yourself Paperash handmade development work here, it's really worth of watching:
.
The first detail that impressed me when i started to play was the animation of my strange avatar, a female squid robot, obviously made of paper! Animation was really fluid and perfectly responsive to player's inputs. I have immediately connected such handmade animation to the great Czech tradition in animated films; it reminded me of Švankmajer and Trnka artworks. Not by chance, Dark Train won the prize for Czech Art Game Of The Year in 2016; in the same year Samorost 3 won the prize for Best Czech Game Of The Year. I mentioned Samorost because Dark Train is also a puzzle game, but it's not a point&click adventure, it has something more of a platform and a bit of a hidden objects game. Developers stated it is a railroad tamagotchi!
Well, here begins the difficult part of the review!
After my eyes have become accustomed to aesthetics beauty, i started wondering what to do: what's this game about? I was abruptly projected in the oppressive world of DT controlling this strange robotic squid avatar and driving the weird cyberpunk train without any sort of instruction, tutorial or explanation; i was even ignoring it was a female squid! There are no texts or documents to be read, no dialogues, no voice over; narration is intended to be only carried out through situations and scenarios, but it is too criptic. Well, i started to explore the imaginative scenarios and went crazy for understanding what to do and mostly why! Yes, after a while i was missing the urge to continue playing. Too difficult, not for casual players for sure, and i'm not a casual player! You have to search for objects to interact with and puzzles to be solved, but in the end you are not able to understand what you are doing, what you have just done and why; you are simply solving incomprehensible puzzles by chance, through a trial and error process. You are not even able to understand if you correctly completed the puzzles and the exploration of the scenarios or you need to come back later for further actions.
Who or what is the squid  supposed to be and to do? Why and where am I driving this weird train? Why, when i go through the holes on the train, do i find myself in new suggestive scenarios, what kind of magic is that? Is there some metaphor, symbolism or message i cannot understand?
After more than one hour i stopped and went looking for a walkthrough! But first of all i needed to understand what i was playing! I found all the explanations on the developers web site
, but i could  relate in no way such explanations to my game experience!
Here we have four problems: 1) Players are not supposed to search for external resources in order to understand and get involved with the game experience; 2) It's better avoiding frustrating, not so clear and annoying gameplay; 3) If a game artist has something to express, he must be able to express it trough the artwork itself, no need to explain gameplay, story or contents outside the artwork; 4) Form and content, gameplay and story, they have to be coherent and well integrated.
Probably DT is plenty of metaphors, messages and symbolism, but i was not able to understand any of them.
This is a case of an artwork with superlative aesthetics and oustanding art technique, but with bad gameplay and  not well expressed story and contents. So after the first enjoyment of the eyes, the experience results frustrating.
On the developers web site i found the following link to a previous project, an interesting animated film:
I think the guys at Paperash come from cinema school or academy or at least from expierences in animated films. They probably made the mistake to develop the game as it was an animated film.
Making art through a film is not the same of making art through a game. In a game you have to engage players in virtual immersive interactive experiences; players are supposed to partially shape the artwork itself. So a game artist is a creator of virtual interactive experiences, he has to grant the best experience to the player and be able to express aesthetics, story, emotions, thoughts and contents through such experience.
I think that video games market absolutely need the outstanding artistic skills of the guys at Paperash, it would be a pity to leave them to cinema! So i hope they are going to “adjust the shot” and develop more and better games.
I can suggest DT only for its marvellous aesthetics and its astonishing handmade scenarios and animations. I think the actual price of  15 euro is too much, i would suggest developers to lower the price.
Rating: 70/100

Soul Axiom (you heard that in math class, right?) is, as it's officially stated, the spiritual successor of Master Reboot, like the connection between Bioshock Infinite and the ones before the masterpiece. Master Reboot became one of my favorite games mainly because it was a good example of a successfull execution of a creative idea presented as a video
game with artistic value. Soul Axiom borrows everything that is worthy in Master Reboot and makes them better.
The story is loosely tied to Master Reboot and any issue of interest required from that plot is integrated into Soul Axiom's storyline. While the main story is told piece by piece in cutscenes at the end of every memory (memory=level), the theme and the plot is largely explained through collectibles, in the form of toy monkeys called PEMOs, like ducks in
Master Reboot. Pretty much like every other video game which contains collectible items, you sometimes forget about whatever it is you're doing and start to look for them so that you don't miss any critical part of the story. Unfortunately that has become an unwritten rule nobody seems to guestion (an axiom?) in modern video game design and since I can't
really think of a better alternative, I'm not complaining, and to be honest the "hunting" process in Soul Axiom is a lot less tiresome than it is in similar games.
New with Soul Axiom, now the protagonist has several powers which increases the amount of interaction and variety of puzzles. Together with the length (more than twice Master Reboot) and diversity of the story and the abandoned horror elements, this new feature makes Soul Axiom an all-around adventure experience.
Beacuse the game takes place in some kind of virtual reality, the emphasis on graphical design is artistic rather than realistic. Soul Axiom has overall nice graphics, but from a subjective point of view, the game looks great. Especially the DoF effect really enhances the unreal and abstract atmosphere. The cutscene videos are a new addition to the series
and although, being an older adventure gamer, I enjoyed watching them, I must say the level of quality was lower than the rest of the game. There are also a few non-game-breaking technical issues (like dysfunctioning AA options) right now which will probably be resolved in the near future.
There are many other games promising to provide unique psychological/philosophical experiences and almost all of them fall short. Soul Axiom is a great game that does everything it's supposed to do without going too deep (something I wouldn't mind if it did) and manages to keep you interested throughout the 20 hours you spend on this work of art. If you like adventure games in general you absolutely have to play this game. Starting with Master Reboot is recommended.

This game, I cannot tell you how much I've played this game when I was a child. I saw this on the Steam Winter sale with the price tag of $10 for a 4 pack. I knew what I was getting, so, why not share the joy and give to my other friends? Well, a few of us tried to set up a game, but we got an error message that was not allowing us to start games up. It was a bit saddening to say the least, but hey, I got a game I played for hours when I was in secondary school. So I picked up my chinese knock off X360 controller, plugged it in the PC, started playing an old classic.
I guess the past never changes, I used a combo when I first started playing and I have never staved away from it, X+Y repeat X in the air until the EXP bar increases no more. This is how I usually beat the game casually within 2-3 hours (probably should video myself). I just, repeat the same actions as any other character; no magic, mid-low attack, no agility, high defense, I usually beat the game when I get to level 25-27.
The gameplay is pretty dang good for a flash game. It's a medieval themed Double Dragon type of fighting game that opens up more options the more you progress. The more you put attributes into your stats, the more your character improves. With the stats capping off at level 78, you still learn new combos even after the stats being maxed out, with the level cap being 99.
The difficulty is at this point for me, pretty easy, but when I first played when I was 3rd grader, it was still pretty easy. This game isn't really that hard, unless your massochist like me who plays insane mode after the normal adventure. I remember little me playing it on the Xbox with the Snakem Knight, reaching level 80 and getting stuck in the Swamp level for weeks on end. I remember never stopping, I remember saying to myself "I got this far so why stop now?". Well, I'm still stuck on the Swamp level, mostly because it got overshadowed by Terraria in middle school.
The story is nothing special, get the girl from the Barbs, get the black one from the Cyc (that's the wrong number!), save Elsa from the Joker in blue attire, and then save the clown from chest Cthulu and then look at the clown. Simple as showing a 1700s man how to cook a microwave burrito. They won't understand what the heck you are talking about until you show them.
Time for the negatives, this game has some copy and paste character styles, not every character is unique. Grey Knight is just Cone Knight, Demon is the same as Fire Knight, there's a few others to point out, but I can't think of them on the top of my head. Not only that, the animal orbs are relatively broken early game, I feel like the animal orbs should be locked off like the weapons until you reach a certain level or location.
This game isn't perfect, but I do hold this game dear to myself as it one of the first games I've ever truly gotten large addiction to. I'd give this game a 7.9/10, it's really good.

The whole game seems very well done at the first glance. The plot is engaging but easy enough to follow, gameplay is solid and the soundtrack is absolutely amazing.
But there's a lot of stuff that makes no sense if you thing about it and it kinda kills it in the end. Protagonist routinely survives events that definitely surely with 100% certainty should have left him dead or at least unable to function normally. If it happened once it could be attributed to luck or strength or some other quality of the character, but as it happens in every other chapter you soon run out of excuses and have to assume it's just plot armor and devs haven't figured a better way to up the stakes without having the main character being stabbed or thrown out of the 10th story window without suffering any lasting damage. Also, for a game that treats itself that seriously, it's hard to believe there's not a single redeemable person on the other side of the barricades. But nah, everyone is evil and deserve to die, no exceptions, no morally grey areas, no ambivalency.
Gameplay is still fun though. Well, except the final boss fight, which is atrocious. There are other ways to make a fight challenging than just making the enemy a bullet sponge. Heck, even all the other boss fights in this very game got it right. But here, there's no different approach, no alternative strategy, no weak point to exploit. You just stand there and shoot at him and pray all the extra health you picked up will be enough for you to survive when the enemy lights the room on fire.
At least they got Polish right, both in speech and in writing, nothing kills immersion like hearing your native language butchered by characters that were supposed to speak it fluently (I'm looking at you, X-Men: Apocalypse). Can't say about other languages/ethnicities but I assume they tried to do it properly all across the board.
All in all, it's decent as far as action games go. But nothing to write home about.

A pretty unique game (a first for concepts that I never seen before) that does deliver some mildly interesting content for a free game. But while the aesthetics are quite colourful, it gets pretty bland fast as you'll realise it's pretty minimalistic, content-wise. But that shouldn't be surprising considering the game is barely above 100MB in size.
Project Rhombus pits you in the middle of a diamond / rhombus as you try to block arrows from reaching the middle and making you fail. The arrows have variable approach rates and some can jump to the side opposite it originally came from, to add to difficulty. As a rhythm game, such concept is unique (at least for me) as I never seen it executed before. But that is just about it for the variability of gameplay as you seemingly block arrows to no end. The lack of progress / stat-tracking bar the timer gives little incentive to keep retrying.
As mentioned before, Project Rhombus is very minimalistic in its current state when it comes to content as there are only 3 available levels with 1 harder one locked behind some time dedication. Since there is a lack of progress-stat related features except the timer, there is little incentive to get to it. (I did it anyway, but I personally believe this would ward away casual players)
- Minimalistic design that's pretty aesthetic; pleasing on the eye except for the epileptic ones
- (A bit of a con) incredibly simple gameplay means no need for a tutorial
- (A bit of a con) highly variable arrows allows gameplay to be based on skills. Their random appearances throughtout the song COMPLETELY demolishes the thought of memorising the song to beat it, which is sort of nice.
- Music sounds pretty nice, needs more variety though.
- Since there was no tutorial, gameplay was initially confusing. Despite the incredibly simple gaming, a well-highlighted tutorial with maybe slow-motion and / or a simple page describing the game with gameplay gifs would have new players, since all games ought to have some sort of a tutorial
-The variability of the arrows means that not only you can't memorise the level, but you also can't play-match the arrows to the beat in your head when it does appear. Some sections are loaded with arrows while others are also bare, sometimes in the part of song when you expect it to be "heavy". That can sometimes throw you off.
- Except for yesterday (11/12/17) update, the game has literally no configuration ability which can block enjoyment of users who likes to customise their game experience. The option should be revised in the future again in accordance with new changes.
-Lack of progress tracking: Project Rhombus has only one way to track highscore and that's via a timer; how long you have survived into the song. The lack of scoring - points, checkpoints, leaderboards gives little incentive to retry, except for the expert level. Even then it's almost not enough.
Project Rhombus is a neat, indie rhythmic game that is worth a try as there is literally no "risk" even among F2P games, as it is only ~110 MB as of now. However when compared to other popular mainstream entries like Cytus, Osu, or even Geometry Dash, it is pretty "stale". I suggest trying it and adopt a "wait-n-see approach", hence why I am recommending this game for everybody.
P.S: The developer(s) should have a Trello page to detail the game development plans and / or discuss future features with other players. Steam discussion can be a start as a forum.

I was hesistant to buy this game as I do not enjoy singleplayer games as much as multiplayer games, but I am thankful for making this purchase.  The gunplay and gun progression in this game flows very well.  The side peak mechanics are very unique and interesting and also work very well.  Last but not least, the melee in this game is absolutely brutal and morbidly fun to do.  The setting of an alternate history where the Germans won the war is, admittedly, a little overused but this game is able to make it interesting by adding steam punk elements and the amazing graphics really push that narrative.
However, the downfall of this game. in my opinion, is the story is a little weak.  Don't get me wrong though, the story is one of the best stories I have seen for an FPS shoot'em ups, but as a story that competes with gaming in general you will see it lacks a few things.  Things like strong character building, and the biggest offense of making me suspend my belief and on multiple ocassions made me say, "How the hell did he survive that."  SPOILER ALERT!!! In many cutscenes the protagonist is stabbed in the chest or has an explosion go off right next to him and just keeps going like nothing ever happened.  However, if you can get past these two things the game is worth the buy and I hope you can enjoy as much I have.
***Note**** As full disclosure I did buy this game on sale and that may have influenced my opinion slightly

Originally I wasn't going to recommend this game since in the very beginning it wasn't all that fun. This would mainly be because I came to this game looking for a PvP experience. If your looking for a PvP experience I will happily tell you to go to World of Tanks instead. The PvP aspect of this game is quite dead, with que times reaching past 2 minutes and most games just being 3v3's. And if your not playing a Main Battle Tank, you won't be able to do a thing.
The heart of this game is in it's PvE. The mass player base is located there. While I cannot say the PvE is the most challenging, it can still be a lot of fun and would be a blast if you were to get a couple of friends with you to play with.
My computer doesn't have the best graphics card so I can't judge the graphics but I hear they're great. The majority of the sounds ingame can be pretty repetitive which makes them sometimes annoying to listen to but the roaring "BOOM" of your cannon is nice.
Overall the game has variety both in maps, play styles, tanks, and ammo types which means that there is a good amount to learn. Not every ammo type will work in every situation meaning you can't just spam the same type of ammo and expect to get something out of it each time; and to add, unlike World of Tanks there is no gold ammunition. So your forced to use all the ammo types and not just one.
In the end its a fun game and if your into a modern day World of Tanks then this may be the game for you.

If you want to step up your casual gaming from The Sims series to something more extreme, RimWorld is it. Its difficulty rivals Dwarf Fortress, but there are easier difficulties (and three different 'storytellers' that control what happens) that you could pretend like you're playing The Sims. Plus, there's no household cap of 8! Anyone that survives, crashing into your colony - or enemies you capture from a raid - you can *convince* them to join your colony and become a part of the family. :)
Once you're comfortable with observing your Sims, I mean, colonists get cozy - bump up the difficulty for hordes of your neighbors, space pirates, and even space alien robots. No one could make fun of you for that.
This game is really addictive and there are so many ways you can play it. You can treat it like a Sims game with minimal horrifying events, or a challenge to keep the longest standing colony despite waves and waves of things-trying-to-kill-you, or.. you can just see if you can make it past one colony, over and over again.
The community is very active! Reddit, Discord, and other forums. The dev(s) communicate with the community and they love the game as much as we do. There are so, so, so many mods - and some that are practically expansion packs to the game!
With randomization (seeds & events), high quality mods, and the ongoing major update - the game has so much replayability. It's really, really fun - I really can't recommend it enough. This is the most amount of hours I've put into a Steam game. I really recommend it.
Of course, sure, you can make people into hats.

The way to achieve these goals require trial and error, 2hrs in the game, you're given a choice, you select the wrong choice and your daughter dies, so you restart. You reach that point again and take the 'correct' choice, then another choice comes up and you mess that one up, your daughter dies, restart. This is how the game progresses, it's pure frustration.
This isn't a puzzle game or strategy, it's trial and error, and without a save feature, you'll be restarting the game over and over until you get sick of it. The devs should've taken a closer look at TWOM, that game has choice.

I really wanted to like this game, but after 2 hours it became obvious that the game mechanics only work in theory.
Other reviewers already mentioned the frustrating pacing and the ridiculous tasks which hit you right in the beginning. After 3 restarts I still haven't find a way to
and at first I didn't want to continue playing, but at some point I just wanted the story to continue and didn't care anymore. That's a really bad thing for this kind of game.
Dying and failing is incredibly easy. But you can instantly reload and replay it anyway, so there's no point. Everything is scripted, so playing the same events over and over again is boring and frustrating. Considering that alternative choices often are deadly, there is hardly any replayability. That's the biggest problem: The excellent atmosphere created by music and graphic style is completely ruined by repetition and frustration.
What I also didn't like is the fact they could not decide between a serious tone or a comedic one. Some aspects of the game are so ridiculous and over the top that I really can't take the opressive atmosphere seriously.
Installing cameras is hardly ever necessary. Most of your time is spent by clicking exclamation marks and bringing stuff from A to B. There's always a ridiculous rush. It's just tedious, not fun.
The profiling mechanic is another missed opportunity. Putting in the basic details over and over again is neither challenging nor fun. I see what they were trying to do here with the directives, comparing evidence with regulations like in Papers, Please. I feel like they stopped developing that area, as it's completely underdeveloped, not challenging and - again - just tedious.
Speaking of which, it's really obvious that Beholder is influenced by Papers, Please and This War of Mine. But while it has some interesting ideas, execution simply falls short.

Robocraft is a game about designing your own robot and battling other robots in a variety of different game modes. It has (or had) opportunity, but has gradually become a terribly designed pay-to-win.
Early game progression has become a frustrating endeavor that leads nowhere. If you are a free to play player, then you will be delighted to know that the devs have once again taken away the free, limited-time premium previously handed to new players. The reason this existed in the first place was to enable new players to progress to a state where they were able to compete with other players who have had the game and already have decent equipment. Now that the free premium is gone, new players are left with this:
you get three medium cpu robots with common weapons and no shields. You also get an absurdly large amount of building blocks to create your own bots if you so wish (although you should just sell these blocks to buy a few decent weapons to start you off). other than that, all you are left with is a free protonium crate from the tutorial, and your daily crate.
Crates are a curse that should never have even been discussed by the developers. The crates are rigged to give players a better chance of winning the powerball than getting a legendary from a protonium crate. The drops are random to an extent, but they are heavily HEAVILY weighted toward common and uncommon items. This weighted drop system is to be expected, and is used effectively in many games, but robocraft is not one of them. Robocraft's loot system has a huge problem. New players often do the worst on their team, which gives them the worst crate, which gives them the worst items. The worse the item, the less money you get for selling it, and since the only way you can get robits anymore is by selling items, this leaves new players begging for change. This will then snowball out of proportion, as those who were given the better items now have vastly more money than those given crappy items, and will now continue to gain higher amounts of money, while players with little money to begin with will have to continue getting crappy items until they save up enough robits for a good setup and are able to pull themselves away from the f2p poverty line.
Luckily there is a way to make all of your dreams come true! All you have to do is throw your hard earned cash into the hands of the sleazy devs, and then BAM, you have premium! Premium gives you many advantages over free to play players: one example is the full access to colors, allowing you to paint your robots black, which means nobody can tell how hurt your robot is. You also get twice as many items from crates, which means double the profits right? WRONG! it actually means you get 6x the profit of normal players, as you are now able to sell items for 3x more than f2p players. You know that legendary item that you were saving for for weeks as a f2p player? well now that you have a decent way to make robits thanks to premium, you are able to buy that legendary item in a matter of hours! That is assuming you havent already been handed a legendary in the totally-not-rigged-for-premium loot system.
When you get premium, you finally have a game that is fun and playable. However, if you do not buy premium, you do not exist to the developers. You will constantly be left struggling to find that you are taking 2 steps and getting half-no no, 1/3 of the distance as anyone who funds this terrible game.
In the end, I recommend the game to anyone who is willing to spend more money on this game than it will ever be worth, but for anyone who is not planning on emptying their wallet on a free game in early access, turn around and find a different MOBA because this one will never treat you with any kindness no matter how long you play.
Also, the whole early access thing is a load of bull, this game used to be a finished, playable game that you would very rarely get tired of. The developers then changed everything about that game and will now forever be stuck in a state of fixing one thing only to break another, and then another, and another.... This game will never again be finished, and will forever remain in "early access" limbo,  allowing the devs to continue fixing their mistakes.

Dark Train is a beautiful, wonderful game.  While the developers have termed it "tamagotchi"-style, this description woefully underdescribes the gameplay, which is very much puzzle-oriented.  Nominally, one must keep the train supplied with electricity, fire, and water, but there are no dire consequences to allowing any of these to run out: One must simply wait for the required resources to come along, and then once any puzzle at hand has been solved, one is gothily chugging away down the tracks once again.  There are a few "secret" areas that can be missed if you aren't actively trying to find them, but bypassing them won't impede gameplay.
The puzzles aren't incredibly hard or anything, but they're all enjoyable and certainly nontrivial, and the art and sound are an absolute feast.  It's worth playing Dark Train simply to absorb the delicious atmosphere; Dark Train is replayable simply for that experience.  My only real complaint is that the game ends abruptly -- one may be expecting two more equally-sized parts to the game based on visual clues in the control box, but those are apparently planned for future updates, which I will hungrily devour when released.

Weird Worlds is a fun little rogue-like set in space. On your quest to explore unknown frontiers, you will fly from star to star, finding ramdomized loot, trading with friendly species, battling not-so-friendly alien armadas, hiring mercenaries who are not very helpful and die like flies in a flamethrower spray, and getting your loot stolen repeatedly by a mysterious Esmeralda. Most likely, many of your quests will end in failure and untimely death, but with a little bit of luck and persistence, you could become a legendary hero known throughout the galaxy. With just over a dozen stars, even the longest quest would last only about 30 minutes, and in about 5-6 hours even the most unlucky captain should see every piece of randomized loot, experience every randomized event, and thoroughly master Weird Worlds. The galaxy is a small place with little going on, but for a measly 5 bucks, exploring it is very addictive and a great way to kill a few hours.

TLDR (you should read); I was pleasantly surprised by this title and that doesn't happen often.  It's definitely worth it at a sale price and probably just the same at full price.  This moved the Wolfenstein franchise forward in a lot of ways and set the bar higher than it’s ever been for Wolfenstein games.  Now they have more to live up to.
I pretty much never post reviews but this game was worth a bit of time.  I've been rather disappointed for quite a while with the quality of games; almost everything is just some cliche or imitation of something else.  The New Order was refreshing in this regard.

At its core, it's a Wolfenstein game.  The default mode of operation is light everybody up and leave nothing standing.  I did like in this game, however, that you are able to decide how you want to crack that egg.  You can sneak without the game fully investing in tired stealth mechanics (I like stealth but no game has advanced that genre in years), you can search for flanking opportunities, or you can dual wield and just be carnage incarnate.
This game has a well put together narrative.  It's not overbearing and it doesn't feel like the focal point but it's well developed and one appreciates it. I usually find romantic elements for FPS stories obnoxious by The New Order does it perfectly.  You fully grasp the authenticity and realness of their affection but it's not over done; it's exactly how you imagine a couple would be in a time like this.  They are super focused on the mission/task at hand, but take time to indulge.

I hate collectibles in FPS or third person games, it always feel like artificial content extension that is mostly just making you do chores or run errands.  I collected most of them in the first run through without really trying, most are in rather expected places and that's good.  Still don't think they should be in every game, but The New Order didn't go overboard, thankfully.

The villains are sufficiently creepy and have personality, even if that personality makes you dislike them more.

The soundtrack is phenomenal and the audio effects are spot on.  Most of the guns sound just as they should and the directional/distortion effects throughout the game were anywhere between very good and outright impressive.

But what made this game really good is the variety of situations.  Each idea for a different setting, mechanic, mission the designers had, were fully fleshed out and not just a re-skin of existing code.  They spent the extra time to do it right.  So whether it's driving a car, piloting an underwater submarine, or jumping around off world, you can tell explicit care was placed on each area and we all should appreciate that.  It's super rare anymore.
Just when I thought the game was going to end or the level was about to finish up, a curveball was thrown to introduce something new, and that's how a game like this should be. You should be frequently surprised.  Then when it ended, I wanted more.

Only a few of my deaths were annoying, mostly having to do with poor clipping/modeling on surfaces that forced me to fall off a cliff.  Most of my deaths made me laugh given the shock of it or how preposterous it was.
Late in the game a large number of heavy enemies caused multiple deaths and reloads which was frustrating but in the end, the proper strategy was to play it as if it were real; careful, methodical, and actually respecting the adversaries.

Yes, like all FPS games there's difficulty created simply by having enemies that take a lot of hits and the boss fights smell of Metal Gear Solid due to the "do this to weaken, do this to harm, do this to remove protection shield, run from cover to cover" instead of a raw bullet filled finish.  They're not great in all forms but The New Order didn't break any rules, didn't make them worse, but did not devise any new experience here.

I experienced no bugs during the game despite having an older rig with a new video card, the previously mentioned clipping/modeling issues are about the only technical grievance.
And in the end, one never grows tired of throwing knives into Nazi groins over and over.

-----

What is Armored Wafare?:
To put it up simply, AW is a tank vs tank arcade game. It is closer to WoT than WT. AW has a thing for everyone. Do you like to fight verse players in a TDM? Then you want to do pvp. Do you like to capture and hold? Then you want to do Glops( Global Operations). Are you more of a pve player? Then you want to PVE. Pve puts you up against bots as you do a mix of objectives.
Pros:
No pay to win.
No gold ammo.
Premium tanks are = progession tanks.
Premiums tanks do not cost an absurd amount.
No Garage slots.
Commanders can be assigned to many tanks at once without having to relevel them up or convert them over.
Generous events.
Lootboxes - The better you do, the higher chance to earn the better ones. Each box has a 10% chance to uptiered. Loot boxes can you you premium too.
A playstyle for everyone.
Low RNG
Optimization
You can actually farm at tier 10.
Cons:
A couple nasty bugs from EA still exist
No endgame focus yet. - I see this coming soon.

I didn't want to put these under pros or cons.

It's not that I didn't like the game. I thought it was good in places, the introduction was fantastic and made you really hate the main villains behind it all. The combat, at the start, was fairly exciting. Except it's overdone. My main issue with The New Order is just how bland the shooting is after a while. It feels like you're being forced to deal with every single encounter in such a similar way: be the Nazis' b*tch and slowly chip away from behind a convenient wall.
If you try going in guns blazing, you will be killed. You absolutely must fight every encounter of more than a couple of Nazis in his way. Stealth is an alternative, but a lot of the time the game is designed for you to have to fight swathes of enemies, and (lo and behold!) you'll have to crouch behind a waist high wall and pick off each goon individually. And don't even get me started on when they call for back up and you have to do it all over again! It really seems like they have tried to inflate the difficulty by merely piling on more enemies. Individual bossfights are incredibly easy since you can just go into cover and chip away at them until they die (the Heavy Robot being a huge offender!) , but a few goons becomes an impossible chore as they reinforce their ranks over and over again.
I really wanted to like this game, but IMHO MachineGames managed, somehow, to make KILLING NAZIS seem bland and boring. The story was good, and if you're prepared to deal with monotonous gameplay, I'd say you should go for it while it's on sale. Otherwise I'd wait and see if the new game brings anything interesting to the FPS genre and pass on this carbon copy shooter with a Nazi facelift.
TLDR:
Pros:
+Decent story
+Strong start (See spoilers section below)
+Hateable villains
Cons:
-It's just too damn slow
-Forces every fight to be the same
-There are so many enemies that you are likely to get bored of fighting

Borderlands 2 and The Wolf Among Us are two of my all time favorite games so Tales from the Borderlands was obviously a must-buy title.
TftB remains overwhelmingly loyal to the general feel of the Borderlands franchise, but with TellTale's tried and true choose-your-own adventure narrative story telling.
You play as two characters this time around in a twist on the standard formula:
Rhys - a Hyperion "code monkey" who dreams of becoming the next Handsome Jack and may end up getting exactly what he wished for (in a sense).
Fiona - a professional con artist with aspirations of getting off of Pandora, or at least becoming stupidly rich.
These two characters are drawn together by these aspirations of theirs and inadvertently become wannabe vault hunters in the process - alongside Rhys's best friend, Fiona's sister, and a jail broken Loader Bot that is becoming increasingly self-aware and has a habit of referencing pop culture as it kills your enemies for you. Oh. And Handsome Jack, your new best frenemy.
Tales from the Borderlands is looking to be an absolute rush from start to finish complete with Borderlands' typical over-the-top, insane, Mad Max on mushrooms, satirical toilet humor and violence.
You should pick this up if you're a fan of Borderlands, TellTale, narrative driven games, or simply always wanted an increasingly intelligent robot buddy that murders things while pondering war's purpose.

Yes, the game has its flaws and the devs make some bad decisions, nevertheless, its quite fun to play :D
A big problem is that even though you dont mind the "design" problems, there is a problematic lack of players and bad advertising :(
PS: The actual fun only starts in T5, with Global Operations, which includes respawn and dynamic missions (+"killstreaks")
Imagine like Battlefield (in other words: You can respawn endlessly, but it costs your team tickets and you have to capture "flags") but with a dynamic world, so about every ~5 minutes the flags switch (some flags "disappear" and others show up).
As you can imagine, that game mode is also the most profitable, as you can also kill endlessly (on PvP a dead enemy cannot be killed again. But on GLOPS, he respawns, so you can kill him over and over again :P ).
Some matches feature a small number of bots on strategic objectives (they spawn, for example, on bases/"flags" or killstreaks you can capture and defend it from both teams. They are easily killed, so they are a great way to farm money and XP).
If you win, you get a lot more XP and Credits (in fact, the last player on the winning team often gets MORE rewards than the best on the losing team).
And TEAMWORK is the key to success.
You work as a team = you win = you get more money and XP = it's better for YOU and for the team :D
+ if you work as a team, that also means that you are very likely to perform a lot better, so even if you end up losing (if the other team "worked better" together), you  will get more rewards than if you played like lonewolves.
A tank that deals 600HP per shot will do 600 DMG per shot as long as he is alive. The same tank with 1HP or with 2000HP is the same threat.
BUUUT: A dead tank cannot kill, or even damage, you.
Do not go for damage, but for kills, so you save your teammates and yourself ;)
+ on GLOPS, "injured" tanks dont cost tickets. Dead tanks do.

Notice: While Steam may say I have little to no hours on Armored Warfare, this is due to the fact I play off the standalone launcher for the game. I've been around for well over two years and I am also one of the administrators for the Armored Warfare Wiki (link at the bottom of the review if you'd like to learn more about AW).
Also if you're an NA player, the
launcher has a habit of defaulting you to EU, so check that before you launch the game if you want to play on the NA server.

Armored Warfare is a arena style MMO in the same vein of concept as World of Tanks and War Thunder, but with marked improvements to gameplay and mechanics. While there are similarities to the other two major vehicle based combat games, the areas where AW shines in my opinion is in the much more (free to play) player friendly experience offered compared to its competition.

Armored Warfare has three main modes available; PvE, PvP, and Global Operations, or GLOPS.
is a cooperative mode based around completing missions in exchange for credits and reputation. It consists of a five person team which work together to achieve the goals set out by over thirty unique scenarios across three difficulties.
is a team deathmatch battle to the death where two teams of up to fifteen players each do battle across over a dozen sprawling maps, from the deserts of the Middle East to the frozen oil fields of the Caucuses.
is another PvP based mode, but takes place on one of a five huge maps. These maps are filled with strategic points, each needing to be captured and defended from enemy attack. Fight on the flight deck of a Nimitz Class aircraft carrier or in the ruined remains of a long abandoned Russian village.

As one of those games that is easy to learn, hard to master, Armored Warfare's intuitive controls, and unique classes, weaponry, and abilities offer tons of fun. From lightning fast scouts to seventy ton main battle tanks, the variety is very clear. Unlike its competition, Armored Warfare does not come with premium ammunition or pay to win vehicles, with most in game purchases only going towards either cosmetic changes or progression acceleration in one form or another. Premium vehicles, which are available in game, are for the most part either
, instead of being a clear pay to win mechanic. One important point is that you will
No game is perfect though, and the development cycle of AW has been anything but smooth. Around a year ago, Obsidian Entertainment, the former developer studio for the game, did not have their contract renewed due to conceptual differences between themselves and
, the publisher. Since the split (and Obsidian's turbulent exit that involved certain childish acts by them which cannot be shared without breaking an NDA),
has rebuilt a lot of the game from the ground up, and is currently in the ending stages of completely rebalancing the game.
With these things in mind though, I'd implore potential players to not judge AW off other
offerings, and to judge it off of what it offers. In the end it is a free to play game, so other than the time it would take to play the game you're out nothing for giving it a try.
If you wish to know more about AW before diving into the download, here are some links to the Armored Warfare Wiki, Offical AW Discord, and the main Armored Warfare website to give you more information.

If you have played World of Tanks before, then you'd feel right at home with this tank shooter. Health bars, weak spots on tanks and disabling components by shooting them? All here. The game mixes it up a bit by introducing more ammo types and making them useful against certain armor types. The game isn't aiming realism as much as, say, War Thunder tries. At its core, its an arcade-y tank game; you get a tank, you drive around and you shoot things. And try not to get shoot. Too much.
Graphics wise..game looks decent. Nothing too fancy. Runs ok too. Don't expect cutting edge graphics.
A few issues though. Playerbase is a bit lacking, like at max i see 30 players queued up. To be honest I expected the population to be worse, but I guess the game moving to Steam helps it out a bit. Other than that, I did encounter one bug that's annoying during the tutorial phase. All the tanks are 'reserved' as default, save for the Type 59 that came along free. This is very annoying especially when one of the tutorial stages asks you to take your new tank that you just bought out for a spin. You'd have to filter the settings out a bit to find it. Or not do the tut. But there goes your rewards. Nothing too major, actually, just gotta dig around a bit.
Oh and the game comes with a PvE mode which, honestly, is pretty fun although it might get old after a bit. Shoot X enemies, destroy X objectives, capture X points...all the usual stuff. If you're just here to blow stuff up and collect all the cool tanks then this is the mode for you.
P.S. A merging option for those coming from the standalone version would be pretty dope, since both playerbases are already playing together. Prolly in the works.
Worth a try. It's free anyways.

A unique little game made by Paradox, doomed by not being supported anymore.
Now, don't get me wrong. The only reason why you would want to buy and subsequently play this game is if you had a bunch of friends who also want to do so. As it is, the game is dead. There's very few people who still play and since this game is absolutely horrible with AI (and even if it had decent AI, it wouldn't be fun for long) you'll have a bad time.
The gameplay involves you either dungeoncrawling through a fun, cartoony dungeon filled with monsters and traps while playing one of three classes (who also split up into 3 specializations). All of those have a very different role: The warrior is clearly the tank, the rogue is perfect for annihilating big foes and the mage is support and AoE damage.
The group dynamic between the 3 players is great and lots of fun, but it's way more fun to be the 4th one: The Dungeon Maestro. In this gamemode you get to direct the dungeon! You can use spells to actively harm the players, you can place monsters and even minibosses to create obstacles or make already premade monsterpacks even scarier and at the end you even get to control a huge Boss yourself!
You can take different kinds of "cards" (which are either monsterpacks or spells) with you, and the variety and combo-potential is pretty cool. Almost all of the 22 hours I have put into this game are from this mode, aside from farming for some hero items via an exploit (which has been fixed though). I'd still be playing it, if other people were to, too.
As it stands, the game isn't really playable anymore. If you do have 3 friends and a bunch of free time, get a 4 pack. Now. The game's tons of fun and very unique, and you'll laugh your asses off (while cursing the wretched Dungeon master, of course)!
If you do not though...Don't bother. Paradox, if you ever revive a game, do a Dungeonland 2 and support it like crazy!

Played Runaway 1 and 2 waaaay back in the days, so bought the trilogy to complete the experience.

Cons:
1. Seriously? they change the voice actors again?
2. The confusing beginning made me search the web couple of times, thinking that I might have missed some DLC or something. I get it that the game is trying to tell the story in a non linear way, but the way they unfold the plot is really bad.
3. Everything that I have done and achieved in Runaway 2, POOF! gone. The developer axed most of the story in Runaway 2 due to an outcry of fans, which i totally understand. but the explanation that they gave in Runaway 3 is just... lazy. And bad. God It leaves a bad taste in my mouth.

In conclusion, you should still buy this if you want to complete your experience. but this game, on its own, is bad.
