So some background first, I was a part of the closed alpha, the closed beta, and the open beta over the past almost three years now. I've obtained almost every vehicle in the game and am currently working on obtaining the rest, as new vehicles seem to get added every few patches. This is not my first tank game, I've also played World of Tanks, World of Tanks Blitz (Both phone and PC), and War Thunder to some extent. Yet, I keep coming back to Armored Warfare to play, here's why.
Vehicles:
Let's start with the vehicles. This game's vehicles are modern. (Oh really? Stay with me here) The earliest existing vehicles are from the late 1940's onwards, which means that the "One tank for all roles" idea is ingrained in tank development, so all vehicles in the game feel mobile and the majority of the guns are very accurate. This creates a much more fast-paced combat experience, where speed is available to all players in a game, encouraging movement, and if you hold still; all of the other tanks are accurate enough to root you out of your comfy camping spot the instant you make a mistake. Add on top of this the inclusion of wheeled vehicles, and now you have a battle experience that moves quickly and has both vehicles for all play styles and skill levels. Each tank I've played has had its strengths and weaknesses some tanks are great at close range and brawling tactics, some are better snipers and flankers, others are good at finding targets and providing support fire, even others are very good at finishing off targets that get themselves caught away from the rest of the team. I can honestly say that I have never played a tank that was ever really bad at it's tier, there's ones that are easier to do well in, but there'sno tank I can think of that cannot hold its own in a fight. That alone is worth a significant amount of respect from me. If you like to play a certain way, there's a vehicle perfect for you.
Now for the gamemodes:
PvP - It's your standard 15 vs. 15 player vs. player gamemode, can be played alone or in a platoon of up to 3 players. The
maps for this mode are larger than I expected, and that is very welcome. I never feel as though i'm limited in my
options for where to go, and most vehicles are fast enough to be able to reposition on a whim. This prevents me
from ever feeling like i'm stuck having to defend a flank.
TL:DR: Nothing special, but nothing bad either
PvE - This is the mode I spend the most of my time playing. This is a 5 players vs. a single mission. This also can be played either alone or in a platoon, but the platoons can be up to 5 players. So you can pick your team as you go out and take on AI opponents doing their best to prevent you from completing your objective. The game is still in open beta, so the AI can sometimes be the dumbest sack of rocks on the planet, or they can snap off a shot at you and send you to an early grave in an unforgiving amount of time. Their biggest flaw, in my opinion, currently is their over effectiveness when using missiles. They can still be beaten, but they manage to hold their own a lot better than they should when using these weapons.
TL:DR: Very good for when playing in larger groups, or when you just want to relax while
mowing down targets. It still has some bugs with the AI, though nothing
gamebreaking.
GLOPS - (Global Operations) This mode is BY FAR, the crowning achievement of this game. You play just as you would a PvP mode, but everything else changes. The maps are larger, and there are multiple capture points around the map, each point is guarded by a small garrison of AI-Controlled vehicles, which will attack both teams, either damaging enemies for you or preventing you from capturing a point. Every few minutes the locations of the capture points change, forcing the teams to move into attempting to capture and hold different portions of the map than what they have managed to hold so far. To further add some madness to the conflict, special abilites may spawn around the map, capturing these activates and advantage for whichever player captured the ability. The abilites range from building ATGM bunkers in certain areas, providing a scout drone to spot enemies in a certain area, and calling in a bomber to carpet bomb a small area of the map. To top it all off, if you make a mistake you can respawn and get back into the fight within a few seconds, don't die too much though as the timer gets longer the more you die This mode is absolute chaos and is the most fun I have had in any tank game in a while. The only catch is that it is only available to vehicles tier 5+, which I think takes almost no time at all, and basically acts as training players a bit before throwing them into the madness.
TL:DR: The best mode in the game, this gameplay is what you see in the trailers, though
you do need to get tier 5+ to play it, which should not be an issue at all.
Technical Aspects:
This is still a beta and it can show. Tank stats and balancing changes consistently, so if you like a tank, it may be nerfed in the future. The good news is, whenever this is done, players are allowed a "Progress Reset" This refunds you EVERYTHING you spent on every tank, research, purchase, and equipment at once. (You keep your premium vehicles, and insignias, and boosts)
Allowing you to speed up another line if the line you were currently on gets turned into a different playstyle that you do not enjoy. Framerates can occationally take a dive on certain maps and some visual bugs occur from time to time. As for audio, occationally some in-game voices will clip into a loop at the end of a game, but overall every gun and engine sounds different. There will also be the occational game crash, but if you relaunch the game fast enough, you will be reconnected to the match you left. The rate of crashing improves over time, but takes a little spike right after each patch is launched.
Other: A few Things that don't fit a category, but should be mentioned
-World of Tanks players rejoice! Artillery cannot be played in PvP or GLOPS, it is restricted to
being played in PvE only, acting as a purely support class
-Pay to win? Nope. several premium vehicles have had thier tiers changed, been nerfed, and
some outright never sold again because they were too good. Half the time premium vehicles are
just reskins of vehicles that can be researched for free.
-Are loot crates as bad here?  No, the crates CANNOT be bought directly, they are sometimes
added as a bonus with buying premium vehicles, but besides that, all crates are earned from
finishing daily missions or for your performance in a match. The crates themselves only contain
boosts to your rewards after battle, speeding progression. Nothing they give effects gameplay.
(Maybe the consumables, which acts as a usable item, but those are a dime a dozen, anyone
can buy them with standard currency for a resonable amount)
Current State: A Section for any notes exclusive to a recent patch or decision in the game's development
As of the most recent patch 0.22, There are a lot of bugs. Most of which never this common before the patch. A Micro Patch is getting published on November 23rd, i'll update with what is fixed or still broken.
Conclusion:
This is the tank game I have been looking for as long as tank games were a thing. I have tanks to match all of my playstyle whims, gamemodes for when I'm feeling competative or just want to reap havoc amongst AI. It's not perfect, as it's still in Beta with bugs still being found and fixed. Plus the small player base it has garners it with what I believe is undeserved hate. But it's a great time to have I recommend any action game player to hop into a tank and engage in Armored Warfare themselves.

Note: I am speaking as a veteran player from the non-Steam version of the game.
Armored Warfare is a tank-based arena shooter that offers you the chance to drive Cold War and modern day tanks in a simple to pick up but well-realized arcade model. It's a game that I highly reccomend.
Basic user experience:
On the user experience side, you will find the game has bright, pleasing graphics, effective sound design, and controls quite nicely. The tanks (even the sluggish early Cold War era Main Battle Tanks) are swift and respond well to your inputs, leading to a quick pace and rapidly decided battles, although nowhere near to the extent of requiring the twitch reflexes of traditional shooters. Advanced systems like guided missiles, explosive reactive armour, and autoloaders and ready racks promote varied, unpredictable gameplay. There is also a decent variety of vehicles on offer, with more to be added as the game continues development. RNG associated with hitting, penetrating, and damaging the enemy is kept to a minimum, and the amount of advantage players can add to any given tank from grinding for experienced crew members or adding special equipment pieces that provide buffs (known as retrofits) is kept limited, ensuring that player skill is always of paramount importance. The garrage user interface that allows you to manage and upgrade your tanks in preparation for battle can be a bit clunky, but is functional and does what it ought to.
On the downside, the game CAN be very buggy. Most patches have significant issues that are repaired in subsequent hotfixes. This is certainly a game you have to be somewhat paitent with in order to get the best possible user experience. The general trend, however, is virtually always towards improvement. If you bare with AW, it will do right by you. But if you have no paitence for games that lack a certain level of polish, you would be best off staying away, as AW is the very definition of a diamond in the rough.
Update: A couple of hotfixes have ocurred since I posted this review that fixed some nagging stability issues.
Gameplay and game modes:
The three main game modes are PvP (which is a traditional 15 v 15 1 life deathmatch battle, with an option for 3 v 3 - 5v 5 "skimish" gameplay when there are fewer players in the queue), PvE (essentially a hoarde mode pitting 5 players against waves of AI enemies), and Global Operations (15 v 15, but players can respawn and win by capturing objectives and holding them long enough to make the enemy team's point tracker tick down). I wasn't a fan of Armored Warfare's PvP for a long time, but I've been more impressed with it in recent patches. The vehicles are fairly well-balanced and the fast-paced gameplay allows you to play more battles in a session, reducing the frustation of losses. Beyond this PvP is what you would expect from an arena shooter, so if these make you salty I would hesitate to reccomend PvP. If you like that sort of thing, however, then go for your life. PvE, meanwhile, offers a satisfying co-op experience. Easy and Medium difficulties are relaxing and allow you to just have fun driving a tank (which can be quite the breath of fresh air considering that many of AW's contemporaries are quite unrelenting games all told), while Hard difficulty offers a satisfactory challenge even for experienced players and has been plenty engaging enough to remain fun and keep me coming back to the game. To me, PvE is AW's finest USP, though there is nothing inherently wrong with any of the three modes.
The only drawback is that AW has had issues with player retention, so until more new blood enters the game in light of the Steam release, you may find it difficult to find a PvP game if you play at odd hours, which has held the game back quite a lot over the last couple of years. PvE, however, is always active owing to the fact that it requires only 5 players per match.
Progression and economy:
Armored Warfare is an extremely generous game. It utilises a free to play model under the "pay 2 skip" concept, wherein everything you can purchase for premium currency exists only to ensure that you can access new tanks and upgrades for existing ones faster than you otherwise would be able to (most prominently, premium account time merely boosts the amount of in-game resources you earn from battles). There are no pay 2 win elements (there ARE special tanks you can purchase that cannot be accessed for free, but their main purpose is that they recieve more in-game resources from battles than the free tanks do, and most are only comparable to or even inferior to the free tanks in terms of gameplay performance), and even within this pay 2 skip model the game offers a significant quantity of free premium account time, free premium tanks, discounts, and packages of boosters that provide additional bonuses to your resource income outside of what you can purchase. You will rarely find yourself starved of resources, or feel like you are being pressed to pay up or have your progress stymied. Rather, making a purchase fits into the game smoothly, and works to enhance an already good experience rather than make an otherwise intolerable grind just barely manageable as is the case with many freemium games.
There is virtually no downside to the economy and monetisation system of Armored Warfare. It genuinely is extremely well-handled and makes spending money to support the developer solely a question of how much you like the game, as opposed to a battle of impaitence vs conscience. Bundles CAN sometimes be poorly put together, but this rarely remains a problem for long as virtually every tank that was initially packaged poorly was later re-offered for a better price and with less trimmings.
Overall:
Armored Warfare is a beautiful, flawed gem that deeply deserves to have more people playing it. If it had a larger playerbase, it would truly be something special. As it is, it's merely a good game as opposed to a great one, with a great deal of untapped potential. If the concept behind the game interests you enough that you'd like to see that potential realized, I highly encourage you to give Armored Warfare a try. Worst case scenario, play in PvE mode as a stress reliever game to cool off after you're done playing more stressful games. AW, with its welcoming nature that quite openly WANTS you to have fun (as opposed to many other arena shooters that often feel more like they MIGHT let you squeeze out a few drops of fun if you can impress them enough), is great at being that.

I've been playing this game since the early betas and I have mixed feelings about the finished product.  Though simple, the beta interface seemed easier to both see and use and the graphics, in my opinion were better back then.  I'm glad I kept one of the beta builds from when the game was being developed so that I can play that version over this one.  Notably, this is not to say that this game is bad, but it is very short and I'm not sure I like how it ended up.
So, the things I like about the game are the exploration elements...and that's just about it.  It's not a particularly good strategy game and unless you get really good luck with the randomizer, the enemy will almost always have the advantage in battle, meaning you avoid or retreat from fights a lot.  While there aren't a huge amount of things to indicate what is better than other things equipment-wise, you can rest assured that if an equipment or item says it does something, it most likely does it some way or another.
Things I don't particularly care for are many.  They are all minor things that altogether don't make the game not worth owning or playing, but they are annoyances I can't say I like.  As mentioned above, you are largely at the mercy of the randomizer.  If you get mediocre or bad item drops, you can expect to blow up at some random time or your first attempt at battle.  The variety of equipment and weapons seems significantly smaller than in the betas.  I don't know if that's true or I simply haven't encountered many of them since I started playing again.  The graphics seemed to get a downgrade for the most part, even the pictures of cats that were used as stand-in images for things that hadn't been completed yet were better than some of the final art we got.  In the beta, items had some stats you could compare to see what was better than what and gave a lot of insight on how you might want to equip your ship.  That information is now gone, making outfitting your ship rather tedious when you realize that, though something had a better rating in coins, it ended up hurting your strategy pretty significantly when you tried it in battle.
It seems like they realized they wouldn't be finished with the game anytime soon and gutted out the parts that they hadn't finished yet and then simplified a lot of graphics to finish it up.  The three ships you get to choose from at the start are all there are and they don't really affect gameplay much.  Overall, while not a bad game, it's very lackluster, nonetheless.  I had high hopes for this title, but I would have to say that I was disappointed with the end result of all that time spent in beta.

Yes buy it.
It still has very minor issues in the day to day gameplay.  It has a good balance between planning and execution, with random events taking place provided by which storyteller you choose.  I.e. the storyteller (apparently) provides the non-deterministic events in the world, which can range from pirate raids or lunar eclipses to the wildlife going crazy.
It seems to play like a D20 game.
The Good:
- Characters have to sleep each day - which usually means hitting fast forward.  This provides a casual feeling to the game - the game is not rushed.
- It might even be the most casual "chill" game I can remember.  You can pause the clock at any moment or revert to an old save.  So even when things are getting heavy you can think through what needs to happen.
- The game setting is living in the wild and pulling together a survival plan in the midst of the storyteller generating random events.  It's very easy-going this way -- not like Prison Architect which was too heavy and dark for me.
- Grizzly bears seem to just eat berries.  Now you know storyteller will make them go crazy at any moment - so try to figure out a way to deal with them.
The Bad:
- The price feels high before you buy it.  So it might take longer before many people try this game.
- The game could provide more pointers.  "Just look it up on the Wiki."  I suppose if you're hardcore you will want to figure everything out - but this is the blurry line between gameplay-based enjoyment and arbitrary recipe search-space Easter Egg hunting.
- There's no demo.  You can watch youtube videos all day - you'll think this is a Dwarf fortress thing like I did, but it's not, and all the videos don't do the game justice.  A demo would have helped me get over the price hump.
As it is this game is easily worth the asking price.  Listen - you have 2 hours to figure it out - if you still want a refund, you'll know after first hour.

Firstly, this is a kart racer through and through. If that's not something you are looking for then you might want to avoid it.
However, if you like kart games (mario kart etc) then this is a fantastic game.
There are quite a few characters to choose from which, through unlocked "mods", can have their stats changed slightly. One thing I would say is that there are deffinatly better and worse characters. Any with high boost are usually the best, and as such the ones with low boost often are not as competitive.
The tracks are mostly fun and often have multiple paths to use with some being faster and others slower. They aren't hard to remember though and can be picked up quickly. Most are rather easy to drive, with some exceptions like chilly castle and race of ages, though even these aren't too hard to learn. The number of tracks is okay, although it is bulked up with mirror tracks. Also some tracks lack the diverse transormation types of the rest (possibly due to being ported from Sonic & Sega ASR?) and as such seem much less fun, being mostly just kart mode tracks (sun shine tour, egg carrier etc).
The pick ups are well balanced and actually require some skill to use. They can be avoided with a bit of skill too, meaning you aren't at the mercy of overpowered cheap weapons like mario karts blue/spikey shell or lightning.
Controls are okay (only used a 360 pad so haven't tried KB) but collisions with other drivers can be buggy sometimes, bouncing you around like a ping pong ball. Also the boat controls sometimes seem to be a bit funky and will steer the wrong way on occasion. The stunts sometimes fail for no obvious reason as well which can be a pain.
All in all though SASRT is a good fun game, especialy if played with friends, so if you are looking for some fun and frantic arcade racing I'd deffinatly recommend it.

The twist is that they somehow fixed the series, but was it just in time?
Firstly, Runaway: A Twist of Fate is the third and latest entry in the Runaway series, the point-and-click adventure series by Pendulo Studios where you follow Brian Basco - a shy physics nerd turned into a confident adult capable to stand up for himself - and his attractive girlfriend, Gina Timmins, in their Hollywood-like adventures which take some evident inspirations from a couple of known classics, like Broken Sword in particular.
Split into a couple of acts, this time around the story starts off from nowhere with absolutely no connections to Runaway 2’s ending: Brian is dead and he left a cryptic message to Gina who was supposedly still trapped in some sort of water tank in the previous game. For the first time in this series you take control of Gina, which oddly enough feels like breath of fresh air for this series despite this mechanic being nothing new to the genre. Not only that, but the biggest complain I personally had with this series was how useless Gina was as a character in the past by bringing nothing to the story other than an incentive for Brian to save her -- damsel in distress at her finest. It also did not help her being off-screen for at least three quarters of a game each. But the developers have finally listened and addressed this issue with a newly rewritten Gina who can be clever, reliable, and funny whilst still retaining her woman qualities.
So as Gina, it is your job to find out what actually happened to Brian as you deduce that he is not actually dead. From there on, the story starts building up piece by piece into a satisfying adventure worthy of its title with enough thrills and detective work to suck you in; you really want to know what happens next. I do not know what kind of sorcery the folks at Pendulo Studios dealt with, but whatever it was, the narrative in particular is a massive improvement over the previous games. It has a certain cinematic vibe to it which works surprisingly well with what Runaway: A Twist of Fate is going for, but perhaps the best part is how you are given a certain degree of perspective from different characters on how the plot develops (or developed in the past events) over the course of the game. Without any major spoilers though, the ending does feel somewhat unsatisfying considering the events that occur in the game, even despite being a throwback to Runaway 1’s ending. At the end of the day, considering how Runaway 1’s plot took a while to hook you and how Runaway 2’s was a trainwreck after the first two or so acts, Runaway: A Twist of Fate shows that this series is capable of consistently adequate writing. In actual fact, this is perhaps the most serious Runaway game from a plot standpoint due to its evident shift in tone, but at the price of also being the most mundane from the series as it cut down on the supernatural nonsense and the number of cheesy scenarios. Therefore, fans of the original might miss some of that wacky trademark whilst those who despised Runaway 2’s “Indigo Prophecy”-like approach in storytelling might go through sensations of revelations. Cutting it to the chase, the plot is simply a retcon of the entire story of the series.
Where Runaway: A Twist of Fate truly shines is perhaps when it mocks itself. There are plenty of hilarious, tongue-in-cheek, moments and references where it acknowledges how cheesy the previous Runaway games were and even questions the clichés of the point ‘n’ click genre. Realistically, becoming self-aware of itself should have ruined any of the immersion that the game has to offer, but it actually works in its favour to drive some of the humour from this comedy-oriented flick. Still, when it works, it can generate a chunck of laughter.
Visually, the cartoonish hand drawn backgrounds in here still maintain the unique aesthetics of the series, although they do feel subjectively less memorable (than in Runaway 1) and not as vibrant (as in Runaway 2) this time around. Locations and scenes, which in fact are far less than in the previous two games, are more constrained and definitely a lot smaller in size than before. Furthermore, they are also not as exotic as before since most of setting is mainly based in urban locations. One major criticism in regards to the drawings is that some of the rooms or objects were drawn at really odd angles in respect to the camera, so to speak, making them feel out of place sometimes. The character animations are also much better now.
The puzzles follow the tradition in the Runway series of doing plenty of pixel-hunting and every so often nodding at their illogicality when characters have to “improvise” their way. For our sanity, the developers finally listened to the criticisms received from the previous games and implemented a clever hint system which gives clues (not full solutions) to the player at any given time, along with the  ability to highlight all the hotspots in the scene. This allows for a smoother experience than the previous entries without hindering much of the story’s pace. As result, this becomes the easiest and shortest Runaway to complete, clocking around 6-8 hours at most. The only noticeable annoyance with some of the puzzles is when acquiring items before any real motive, thus making certain actions not sequentially logical. This, sadly, ruins a bit of the immersion that is being built. Other than that, Runaway: A Twist of Fate has probably the best puzzles compared to the other two with less temptations of looking up a walkthrough.
As with the shift in tone, the soundtrack returns to the vibes accustomed from the original game which is a satisfying feeling for anyone who unashamedly enjoyed it, especially for its cheesily sang theme tune with synth-guitars. Talking about the audio, gone are the days when you were hearing someone talk as if they were doing so through a tin can, so it is, again, relatively better in most parts than in the previous games. But the most notable observation is the change in voice actors. For instance, Brian does sound different this time around. So you may like this change or not, but I did not find any problems with the new voice actors as far as I am concerned.
In conclusion, Runaway: A Twist of Fate is easily the best and most polished entry in this series, but sadly not the ultimate Runaway experience in my eyes. The way I personally see it is that it spends too much time doing a retcon of the entire series rather than bringing something new to the table. Many of the new features and improvements implemented in here were already present in other similar games of its genre many years prior this. It might as well have been called Runaway 3: The Apology Letter To Fans instead. The only thing that Runaway: A Twist of Fate did was to catch up with modern standards. By fixing many of the series glaring issues (which is commendable), it lost a bit of its charm that made it stand out to other adventure games from its genre, whether you liked it or not. Just when it finished cutting all its badly grown weeds, it ended. Still, I am recommending this game to anyone who fancies a point ‘n’ click adventure game with a good narrative and doable puzzles as it is easily the most accessible of the three games. Luckily, it does not require to have played the previous two to understand the story and recurring characters as everything is explained in it, but in lesser detail. For a better understanding, do play the previous two even if you have to endure their respective flaws.
I believe Pendulo Studios learnt a lot from this experience and I strongly believe, based on how this game played out, that Runaway 4 would have been that ultimate Runaway experience I am craving for. Retain the design polish of this game, but bring back some of those wacky charms of the original.
